# About the Authors

 

**Dr. Manel Martínez‐Ramón** received his Telecommunication Engineering degree from Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Spain, in 1994 and his PhD in Telecommunication Engineering from Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, Spain, in 1999. He is currently a professor of Artificial Intelligence with the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering of the University of New Mexico, NM, USA, where he holds the King Felipe VI Endowed Chair. His research interests are in the area of machine learning, where he has produced numerous contributions to kernel learning methods, Gaussian processes, and deep learning, with applications to electromagnetics and antenna array processing, smart grid, scientific particle accelerators, and others. As an instructor, he teaches graduate courses in statistical learning theory, Gaussian process learning, probabilistic machine learning, and deep learning both face‐to‐face and online.

**Dr. Meenu Ajith** earned her PhD in Electrical Engineering from the University of New Mexico, USA, in 2022. Presently, she serves as a postdoctoral research associate at the Tri‐Institutional Center for Translational Research in Neuroimaging and Data Science (TReNDS), a collaborative research institute supported by Georgia State, the Georgia Institute of Technology, and Emory University in Atlanta, GA, USA. Her research focuses on deep learning, image processing, time‐series analysis, and neuroimaging. She obtained her MS in Electrical Engineering from the University of New Mexico in 2017 and her bachelor's degree in Electronics and Communication Engineering from Amrita School of Engineering in 2015. In her current role as a postdoctoral researcher, Dr. Ajith concentrates on implementing and applying various deep‐learning models and neuroinformatic tools that leverage advanced brain imaging data. Her objective is to translate these approaches into biomarkers, addressing pertinent aspects of brain health and diseases.

**Dr. Aswathy Rajendra Kurup** earned her PhD in Electrical Engineering from the University of New Mexico USA in the year 2022, where her research focused on designing CNN‐based deep‐learning models for applications such as smart grids, medical diagnosis, and computer vision. She completed her MS in Electrical Engineering from the University of New Mexico, USA, in 2017. Currently, she serves as a Machine Learning Engineer at Intel Corporation, a leading force in the semiconductor chip manufacturing landscape. In her current role, she applies her extensive knowledge to address real‐world challenges, utilizing her expertise in handling diverse data types, including images, videos, and time‐series data. As a part of the role, she applies data mining and statistical modeling techniques along with developing Machine learning/Deep learning solutions for enabling factory decision‐making, improved equipment performance, and higher product yields.

# Foreword

 

*Deep Learning: A Practical Introduction*, authored by Manel Martínez‐Ramón, Meenu Ajith, and Aswathy Rajendra Kurup, stands as a pragmatic guide, which prepares the engaged student to digest and understand advanced deep learning concepts. Designed primarily as an educational resource for graduate‐level courses in deep learning, this book is enriched with a valuable collection of exercises and practical Python tutorials, making it an ideal educational tool.

Deep learning, a cornerstone of modern artificial intelligence, has seen a meteoric rise in usage, powering the creation of text, images, and videos, from simple prompts, and enhancing our predictive capabilities in a diverse array of applications. This book offers a thorough exploration of deep learning fundamentals, an essential component for students in engineering or computer science.

The authors begin by tracing the intriguing history of deep learning, setting the stage for a deeper dive into the subject. They skillfully introduce various methods for training and optimizing algorithms, alongside an overview of essential programming tools and libraries which are prevalent today, including Python, NumPy, TensorFlow, and Pytorch.

The book then covers a broad range of fundamental models including recurrent neural networks, transformers, unsupervised learning, and deep Bayesian networks. Within each of these chapters, there is an accessible introduction and detailed explanation of each modeling framework, which allows the reader who is new to deep learning to gain a foothold in this extraordinarily important space, while also providing practical examples including code and data as well as references for further learning. Additionally, it offers references for extended learning, bridging the gap between fundamental concepts and recent advancements in the field.

The author's provides a clear and comprehensive introduction to deep learning, making it an essential addition to the field's literature. Whether you are an instructor designing a course or a student embarking on self‐directed learning, this book is an invaluable resource for navigating the complexities and applications of deep learning.

In essence, *Deep Learning: A Practical Introduction* is not just a textbook; it is a gateway to understanding and applying one of the most influential technologies in the field of artificial intelligence today. It is a useful tool for (i) instructors who want to teach core deep learning topics to their students, (ii) researchers in a variety of fields, including my own field of neuroimaging, who want to develop domain‐specific methods, and (iii) students who are interested in self‐learning on this important topic.

Overall, I strongly endorse *Deep Learning: A Practical Introduction* as a valuable resource for both educators aiming to impart core deep learning concepts to their students and for learners pursuing self‐study in this vital area. The book's blend of theoretical insights and practical applications, including code and data examples, makes it a standout choice for anyone looking to delve into the world of deep learning.

*Vince Calhoun*

# Preface

 

The present book is intended to be a comprehensive introduction to deep learning that covers all major areas in this discipline. This document is designed to cover a full semester graduate class in deep learning, and it contains all the materials necessary to build the class. We structured our work in a classical way, starting from the fundamentals of neural networks, which are then used to describe the different elements of deep learning used in artificial intelligence, from the classic convolutional neural network and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to the transformers, plus unsupervised learning structures and algorithms. In every chapter, we follow a schema where first the structures are described, and then the criteria and algorithms to optimize them are developed. In most cases, full mathematical developments are included in the description of the structure optimization.

[Chapter 1](#c01.xhtml) is a first contact with deep learning, where we introduce the most basic type of feedforward neural network (FFNN), which is called the multilayer perception (MLP). Here, we first introduce the low‐level basic elements of most neural networks and then the structure and learning criteria.

[Chapter 2](#c02.xhtml) is complementary to [Chapter 1](#c01.xhtml), but its contents are valid for the rest of the book since it provides details about the practical training of deep learning structures, which we have omitted from the first chapter in order to make it more concise and compact.

These readers who do not have a knowledge of basic Python will benefit from using [Chapter 3](#c03.xhtml) in order to start experimenting with learning machines in this programming language. In this chapter, authors assume that the reader has reviewed [Chapter 1](#c01.xhtml), which implies that they have been introduced to the concepts of structure, criteria, and algorithms. If so, readers already had the opportunity to see some basic Python codes containing at least a class with methods and an instantiation of it to be used in the examples and exercises, without needing to understand their Python structure. In this chapter, we introduce the basic elements of Python to be used throughout the book, and we will revisit the code previously introduced in [Chapter 3](#c03.xhtml), among other examples.

The concepts and structure of convolutional neural structures are described in [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml). It starts with the concept of convolution in two dimensions and its justification for its use in deep learning, after which the structure of a convolutional neural network is described. The training of such a structure is not commonly found in the literature, assuming that the students and practitioners understand and can apply the backpropagation to them. We offer in this chapter a full development of the backpropagation for convolutional neural networks and we summarize the algorithms, so the practitioner can program it. Still, most importantly, they will understand exactly how it works.

[Chapter 5](#c05.xhtml) covers the basics of the RNN. The chapter starts off with the architecture of the RNN and then explains how these networks are used for modeling sequential information. Further into the chapter, the training criterion is introduced, which describes the feed‐forward training, loss functions, and backpropagation through time. Next, the different types of RNN and their application are discussed. The following section explains the shortcomings of RNNs and highlights the details on different types of gradient problems and the solutions to these problems. Then, the shortcomings of RNNs and highlights the details on different types of gradient problems and the solutions to these problems are explained. After that, the details on other RNN‐derived structures which were introduced to mitigate the short‐term memory problem associated with the traditional RNNs are discussed.

[Chapter 6](#c06.xhtml) provides a structured and comprehensive overview of the developments in attention‐based networks. The first section summarizes the different types of attention mechanisms based on sequence, levels, positions, and representations. Finally, we review the network architectures that widely use attention and also discuss a few applications in which attention‐based networks have shown a significant impact.

[Chapter 7](#c07.xhtml) gives a comprehensive outline of deep unsupervised learning. The overview gives an introduction to the two main categories of deep unsupervised learning such as probabilistic and nonprobabilistic models. The chapter is mainly devoted to the autoencoder, which is one of the widely used nonprobabilistic deep unsupervised learning methods. First, the basic elements, training criteria, and the extensions of autoencoders are explained. Following this, an overview of the deep belief networks (DBNs) is given and it constitutes the basic blocks (restricted Boltzmann machines), training using contrastive divergence, and the variations of DBN. Finally, we also provide different applications of unsupervised deep learning.

[Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml) briefly covers the generative adversarial networks (GANs). Primarily, it introduces the two elements of GANs namely discriminator and generator. After this, the complete architecture of the GAN is illustrated to have a higher level of understanding of the network. Next, the training criteria are outlined which describes the alternate training process between the discriminator and the generator. The loss functions that model the probability distribution of the data is also added in this section. Finally, popular models derived from GAN are presented, and the chapter is concluded by summarizing the advantages and trade‐offs of GAN.

[Chapter 9](#c09.xhtml) covers the main topics of deep Bayesian networks. Here, the authors do not intend to be exhaustive by covering the state of the art of deep Bayesian networks, Instead, we propose a chapter that gives the reader a general view of the characteristics and different philosophies of Bayesian networks with respect to previously introduced structures and algorithms. After introducing the general concepts of deep Bayesian networks, including structures and criteria (thus following the same format used in the rest of the book) we explain the main optimization algorithms used in the current literature, with several examples.

# 1  
The Multilayer Perceptron

 

## 1.1 Introduction

The concept of artificial intelligence (AI) is relatively simple to explain, and it can be enunciated as a possible answer to the question of how to make a machine that is able to perform a given task without being explicitly programmed for it, but instead, extracting the necessary information from a set of data. Let us say, for example, that a machine is needed to classify green and red apples. The machine is provided with a camera, and all the mechanisms necessary to place one apple at a time in front of it and then throw it in one of two buckets. A machine wired to do this will relay in binary operators as “IF,” “THEN.” If the color is red, throw it in bucket A, otherwise, in bucket “B.”

The limitations of this method are obvious. If a pear is mistakenly introduced in the process, it will be classified as a green apple. Also, how can we use the same or similar structure for a different or more complex task? As in the previous machine, an AI approach uses features found in the data in order to take the decision, but the algorithm is not explicitly programmed. Instead, the machine has a specific parametric structure capable of learning from data. The learning process involves the optimization of a certain measurable criterion with respect to the parameters. The deep learning (DL) structures for artificial intelligence are able to learn complex tasks from the available data, but they also have capabilities such as learning how to extract the useful features for the task at hand, provide probabilistic outputs (i.e. “the probability of apple is 97%”), and many others. The basic element of such a structure in DL is the so‐called artificial neuron, a simple concept that provides the power and nonlinear properties.

This chapter is intended to be a first contact with DL, where we introduce the most basic type of feedforward neural network (FFNN), which is called the multilayer perceptron (MLP). Here, we first introduce the low‐level basic elements of most neural network (NN)s, then the structure and learning criteria.

The elements introduced in this chapter will be used throughout the book. We start from the single perceptron, we construct a basic MLP, where the different activations are developed, and then the notation based on tensors is also justified as a generalized tool to be used throughout the book. After this, we present the maximum likelihood (ML) criterion as a general criterion, which is then particularized to the classic cases corresponding to the different output activations. Finally, the backpropagation (BP) is detailed and then summarized so that can be translated into a computer program.

In this chapter, examples and exercises are presented in a way that assumes that the student does not necessarily know about programming in Python. Examples will be focused on the behavior of the MLP, without focusing on the programming, and the exercises intended to modify, at a high‐level data, parameters, and structures in order to answer questions to different practical cases. [Chapter 3](#c03.xhtml) explains, in particular, how the different examples have been coded, thus they will be reviewed in that chapter from the point of view of practical programming.

 

## 1.2 The Concept of Neuron

The idea of the artificial neural network (ANN) is obviously inspired by the structure of the nervous system. The first attempt to understand how neural tissue works from a logical perspective was published in 1943 by Warren S. McCulloch and Walter Pitts ([1943](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0223)) ([Fig. 1.1](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0001)). They proposed the first mathematical model for a biological neuron in his paper. In this model, the neuron has two possible states, defined as 0 or 1 depending on whether the neuron is resting or it has been activated or *fired*. This represents the *axon* of the neuron. The input of this neuron model consists of a number of *dendrites* whose excitation is also binary. This elemental structure is completed with an inhibitory input. If this input is activated, the neuron cannot fire. If the inhibitory input is deactivated, the neuron can be activated if the combination of inputs is larger than a given threshold. This model is fully binary and, since it includes mathematical functions that cannot be differentiated, it cannot be treated mathematically in an easy way. Certain modifications that will be seen further give rise to what is known as the artificial neuron in use today.

![Figure 1.1 Warren S. McCulloch (left) and Walter Pitts in 1949. ¶ Source: R. Moreno‐Díaz and A. Moreno‐Díaz (2007)/with permission from Elsevier.](images/c01f001.png)

[**Figure 1.1**](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-fig-0001) Warren S. McCulloch (left) and Walter Pitts in 1949. ¶ Source: R. Moreno‐Díaz and A. Moreno‐Díaz ([2007](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0234))/with permission from Elsevier.

[Section 1.2.1](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0003) contains an introduction to the concept of artificial perceptron from an algebraic point of view. A possible way to train a single perceptron is introduced in [Sections 1.2.2](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0004) and [1.2.3](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0007), as well as the limitations of this structure as a linear classifier.

The concept of artificial NN was introduced by the psychologist Frank Rosenblatt ([Fig. 1.2](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0002)) in 1958 Rosenblatt ([1957](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0292), [1958](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0293)). In this paper, he proposed a structure of the visual cortex *perceptron* ([Fig. 1.3](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0003)). The structure presented in Rosenblatt ([1958](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0293)) contained the fundamental idea that is used in any artificial learning structure. In the first stage (Retina), the device collects the available observation or input pattern intended to be processed in order to extract knowledge of it. The second stage (Projection area) is in charge of processing this observation to extract the information needed for the task at hand. This information is commonly called the set of features of the input pattern. The third stage (Association area) is intended to process these features to map them into a given response. For example, the response may be to recognize some given object classes present in the scene. Rosenblatt is the father of the artificial perceptron. He proved that by modifying the McCulloch–Pitts neuron model, the neuron could actually learn tasks from the data. In particular, his model had weights that multiplied each of the inputs to the neuron as well as the input bias or threshold that could be adjusted for the neuron to perform a given task. He developed the Mark 1 perceptron machine, which was the first implementation of his perceptron algorithm. This device was not a computer but an electromechanical *learning machine*. The machine consisted of a camera constructed with an array of 400 photocells, the output of each one connected randomly to the dendrites of a set of neurons. The weights, or attenuations applied to these inputs, were controlled with potentiometers whose axes were connected to electric motors. During the learning procedure, the motors adjusted the input weights. This machine was able to distinguish *linearly separable* patterns, or patterns that were at one or another side of a hyperplane in the space of 400 dimensions spanned by the camera inputs depending on its binary class. The invention was then limited in its capabilities until it was proven that a perceptron constructed with more than one layer of neurons MLP had nonlinear capabilities, that is, the ability to separate patterns that could not be separated by a hyperplane. Nevertheless, the MLP could not be trained using the techniques introduced by Rosenblatt for his perceptron. It was in 1971 that Paul Werbos, in his PhD thesis (P. J. Werbos [1974](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0369)) introduced the BP algorithm, which made it possible to adjust the weights of a multilayer perceptron.

![Figure 1.2 Frank Rosenblatt. ¶ Source: https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2019/09/professors-perceptron-paved-way-ai-60-years-too-soon/ last accessed November 30, 2023.](images/c01f002.png)

[**Figure 1.2**](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-fig-0002) Frank Rosenblatt. ¶ Source: [https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2019/09/professors-perceptron-paved-way-ai-60-years-too-soon/](https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2019/09/professors-perceptron-paved-way-ai-60-years-too-soon/) last accessed November 30, 2023.

![Figure 1.3 The perceptron as described in Rosenblatt (1958)/American Psychological Association.](images/c01f003.png)

[**Figure 1.3**](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-fig-0003) The perceptron as described in Rosenblatt ([1958](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0293))/American Psychological Association.

 

### 1.2.1 The Perceptron

From a conceptual point of view, a perceptron is a function made to perform a binary classification. In order to describe this function, let us first introduce the necessary notation and concepts associated with it. Assume a given observation that consists of a collection of ![upper D](images/c01-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> magnitudes observed from a physical phenomenon. These magnitudes are stored in a column vector, which will be called ![bold x element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper D](images/c01-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>D</mi></msup></math>, which lies in a space of ![upper D](images/c01-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> dimensions. For illustrative purposes, let us construct a set of artificial data in a space of ![upper D equals 2](images/c01-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> dimensions as in [Fig. 1.4](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0004).

The figure shows a set of points with coordinates ![bold x equals left-parenthesis x 1 comma x 2 right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c01-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup></math>, where operator ![down-tack](images/c01-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></math> denotes the transpose operation, meaning that the vector is a column one even if it is written as a row vector. In this toy example, the data belongs to one of two classes (black or white) that we will label arbitrarily with the labels ![1 comma negative 1](images/c01-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, though in some cases, labels ![1 comma 0](images/c01-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></math> are more convenient. It can be seen that the data is linearly separable, that is, both classes can be separated by placing a line between the black and white clusters of data. That is, roughly speaking, the idea of the perceptron. It must be trained to place a *separating hyperplane* between both classes. We define the hyperplane (particularized to a line in the two‐dimensional example) as

[(1.1)](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-disp-0001)![bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x plus b equals 0](images/c01-math-0001.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> ![Figure 1.4 A set of observations in a space of two dimensions.](images/c01f004.png)

![Figure 1.5 A point bold x 1 lying in the semi‐space opposite to the one pointed by vector bold w.](images/c01f005.png)

[**Figure 1.5**](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-fig-0005) A point ![bold x 1](images/c01-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> lying in the semi‐space opposite to the one pointed by vector ![bold w](images/c01-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math>.

where ![bold w element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper D](images/c01-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>D</mi></msup></math> is a set of parameters, and thus operation ![bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x](images/c01-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></math> defines an inner product or dot product between two vectors. Strictly speaking, [Eq. (1.1)](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0001) defines a space affine to hyperplane ![bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x equals 0](images/c01-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, which contains the origin.

The important point here is that all vectors ![bold x](images/c01-i0014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> that belong to the hyperplane satisfy the above definition. Therefore, for all points outside the hyperplane, the result of operation ([1.1](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0001)) is different from zero. Moreover, all the points at one side of the plane have a positive response, and all the points at the opposite side have a negative response. In order to prove this, we have to notice that ![bold w](images/c01-i0015.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math> is a vector normal to the hyperplane defined by [Eq. (1.1)](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0001). Indeed, that hyperplane is trivially parallel to the hyperplane defined by ![bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x equals 0](images/c01-i0016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. Since the plane is defined as all vectors whose dot product with ![bold w](images/c01-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math> is zero, all vectors in the plane are normal to ![bold w](images/c01-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math> and, therefore, all vectors in the plane defined by [Eq. (1.1)](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0001) must be normal to ![bold w](images/c01-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math>. Now, let us assume arbitrarily that vector ![bold w](images/c01-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math> has the direction depicted in [Fig. 1.5](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0005). Assume a vector ![bold x 0](images/c01-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math> that belongs to the plane, and another vector ![bold x 1](images/c01-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> that is placed in the semi‐space opposite to the one pointed by the vector. For this vector, the response of the operation ([1.1](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0001)) is ![bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x plus b less-than 0](images/c01-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. Indeed, point ![bold x 1 equals bold x Subscript o Baseline plus bold z](images/c01-i0024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>o</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></math> where ![bold z](images/c01-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow></math> is the segment going from ![bold x 0](images/c01-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math> to ![bold x 1](images/c01-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math>. Then,

(1.2)![StartLayout 1st Row bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x 1 plus b equals bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline left-parenthesis bold x 0 plus bold z right-parenthesis plus b equals bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x 0 plus b plus bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold z equals bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold z EndLayout](images/c01-math-0002.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable class="lmatrix"><mtr><mtd class="array"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> ![Figure 1.6 A separating hyperplane that classifies among the two classes of a set of data.](images/c01f006.png)

[**Figure 1.6**](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-fig-0006) A separating hyperplane that classifies among the two classes of a set of data.

since by definition ![bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x 0 plus b equals 0](images/c01-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> because ![bold x 0](images/c01-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math> belongs to the plane. Then, notice that since ![bold x 1](images/c01-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> is opposite to ![bold w](images/c01-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math>, this vector forms an angle with ![bold z](images/c01-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow></math> higher than ![9 0 Superscript ring](images/c01-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>9</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8728;</mo></mrow></msup></math>, and thus this dot product must be negative. If point ![bold x 1](images/c01-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> was in the semi‐space pointed by ![bold w](images/c01-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math>, then the angle with ![bold z](images/c01-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow></math> would be less than ![9 0 Superscript ring](images/c01-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>9</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8728;</mo></mrow></msup></math> and the dot product would be positive. This is the principle used in binary linear classification. In conclusion, to classify the points in [Fig. 1.4](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0004), it is only necessary to place a hyperplane defined by parameters ![bold w comma b](images/c01-i0038.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></math> between the two classes as seen in [Fig. 1.6](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0006). The classification operation is then

(1.3)![f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis equals sign left-parenthesis bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x plus b right-parenthesis](images/c01-math-0003.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mtext>sign</mtext><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where ![sign left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>sign</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is an activation function whose response is 1 if ![z greater-than 0](images/c01-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>z</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and ![negative 1](images/c01-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> otherwise. The dot product of this equation can be expanded as

[(1.4)](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-disp-0004)![f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis equals sign left-parenthesis sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper D Endscripts w Subscript i Baseline x Subscript i Baseline plus b right-parenthesis](images/c01-math-0004.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mtext>sign</mtext><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>D</mi></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

and the operation can be expressed in a graphic form as the perceptron, depicted in [Fig. 1.7](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0007). In this structure, an observation consisting of a vector ![bold x](images/c01-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> with components ![normal x Subscript i](images/c01-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, ![1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to 3](images/c01-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> is element‐wise multiplied by the elements ![w Subscript i](images/c01-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> of parameter vector ![bold w](images/c01-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math>, and then a bias ![b](images/c01-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is added. The corresponding operations are represented by the arrows incoming to the first node (an addition operator) that emulate the behavior of the dendrites in a neuron. All the products are added together and then passed to a sign detector. This is equivalent to applying a threshold to dot product ![bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x](images/c01-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></math> to obtain an output equal to 1 if the dot product is higher than ![negative b](images/c01-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>b</mi></math> and ![negative 1](images/c01-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> otherwise. The sum and comparison operations emulate the behavior of the *soma* of a neuron. The output arrow represents the axon.

 

### 1.2.2 The Perceptron (Training) Rule

The training of the perceptron described by Rosenblatt, usually called the Perceptron Rule, is very easy to implement. The training procedure needs to use a *training dataset* composed by a set of samples ![bold x Subscript i](images/c01-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, ![1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper N](images/c01-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>N</mi></math> for which the corresponding labels ![y Subscript i Baseline element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet](images/c01-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> are known. Usually, we will define the labeled datasets as ![script í’Ÿ equals StartSet bold x Subscript i Baseline comma y Subscript i Baseline EndSet](images/c01-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#54431;</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, ![1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper N](images/c01-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>N</mi></math>.

![Figure 1.7 Structure of a perceptron where the input bold x has three dimensions.](images/c01f007.png)

[**Figure 1.7**](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-fig-0007) Structure of a perceptron where the input ![bold x](images/c01-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> has three dimensions.

The goal of the perceptron rule is to reduce the classification error over the training dataset. We define the error of the response to input sample ![bold x Subscript i](images/c01-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> as

(1.5)![e Subscript i Baseline equals one half left-parenthesis y Subscript i Baseline minus sign left-parenthesis bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x Subscript i Baseline plus b right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c01-math-0005.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>sign</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></math> 

This error is zero if the sample has been classified correctly. If the sample is labeled with ![y equals negative 1](images/c01-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and the classification is 1, the error is ![e Subscript i Baseline equals negative 1](images/c01-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, and if the sample is labeled with 1 and the classification is 0, then the error is ![e Subscript i Baseline equals 1](images/c01-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. That is, when a misclassification is observed, the error is equal to the true label.

The algorithm has to be initialized with some arbitrary values for ![bold w comma b](images/c01-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></math>, for example, all coefficients can be initialized at zero. Then, all samples are classified using the perceptron until an error, say for sample ![bold x Subscript k](images/c01-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub></math>, is reported. At this moment, the algorithm updates the weights using the following rule:

[(1.6)](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-disp-0006)![StartLayout 1st Row bold w left-parenthesis k plus 1 right-parenthesis equals bold w left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis plus y Subscript k Baseline bold x Subscript k Baseline 2nd Row b left-parenthesis k plus 1 right-parenthesis equals b left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis plus y Subscript i EndLayout](images/c01-math-0006.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable class="lmatrix"><mtr><mtd class="array"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="array"><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

where ![bold w left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis comma b left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> denote the values of the parameters at iteration ![k](images/c01-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>. It is relatively easy to prove that this algorithm converges to a solution if the data set is linearly separable, but convergence is not guaranteed when the data is not linearly separable. We must assume that the norm of the data vectors is bounded by some value, i.e. ![for-all i comma 1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper N](images/c01-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>N</mi></math>, ![parallel-to bold x Subscript i Baseline parallel-to less-than upper R](images/c01-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8741;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>R</mi></math>. Assume further that, since the data is linearly separable, some optimal parameters ![bold w Superscript asterisk Baseline comma b Superscript asterisk](images/c01-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></math> must exist that define a separating hyperplane able to classify the data with no errors. These parameters are thus normalized such that ![parallel-to bold w Superscript asterisk Baseline parallel-to Superscript 2 Baseline plus StartAbsoluteValue b Superscript asterisk Baseline EndAbsoluteValue squared equals 1](images/c01-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8741;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mo>&#8741;</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. For this classification hyperplane, and for some ![eta greater-than 0](images/c01-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#951;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, it must be the case that

[(1.7)](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-disp-0007)![y Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold w Superscript asterisk down-tack Baseline bold x Subscript i Baseline plus b Superscript asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis greater-than eta comma for-all i element-of left-bracket 1 comma upper N right-bracket](images/c01-math-0007.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>&#951;</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math> 

This is true for an optimal classifier since the sign of ![bold w Superscript asterisk down-tack Baseline bold x Subscript i plus b Superscript asterisk](images/c01-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></math> will be the same as the one of the labels for all samples.

 

### 1.2.3 The Minimum Mean Square Error Training Criterion

The limitations of the above‐presented perceptron are two, the first one being that it can only synthesize linear functions. The second one is that it will not converge if the data is not linearly separable.

![Figure 1.8 Example of the application of the perceptron rule in a set of separable data in dimension 2. Before the first iteration (upper left pane), the classifier is set with random parameters. The first sample in the dataset gives a misclassification, so the classifier parameters are updated in iteration 1, after which sample number nine is found to be misclassified. The algorithm goes through six iterations until it classifies all samples with no errors. In this particular example, the bound on the number of iterations is StartFraction upper R squared plus 1 Over eta EndFraction equals 228.](images/c01f008.png)

[**Figure 1.8**](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-fig-0008) Example of the application of the perceptron rule in a set of separable data in dimension 2. Before the first iteration (upper left pane), the classifier is set with random parameters. The first sample in the dataset gives a misclassification, so the classifier parameters are updated in iteration 1, after which sample number nine is found to be misclassified. The algorithm goes through six iterations until it classifies all samples with no errors. In this particular example, the bound on the number of iterations is ![StartFraction upper R squared plus 1 Over eta EndFraction equals 228](images/c01-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>228</mn></math>.

The first limitation is to be corrected by the introduction of the MLP, which will provide nonlinear properties to the classifier, but then the perceptron rule cannot be applied as it has been presented. The second limitation comes from the fact that the error measure applied to the perceptron is binary rather than continuous. The first modification applied to the structure in order to obtain a continuous measure of the error is to change the sign operator by a continuous *activation* function that tends to 1 when the machine classifies the sample as ![plus 1](images/c01-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and to 0 or ![negative 1](images/c01-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> when the sample is classified as ![negative 1](images/c01-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. Such activations are often called sigmoids because they have a shape that reminds of a stylized ![s](images/c01-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>. For this example, we use the hyperbolic tangent function, and the classification function will have the following form:

[(1.14)](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-disp-0014)![f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis equals hyperbolic tangent left-parenthesis bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x plus b right-parenthesis](images/c01-math-0014.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>tanh</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where the expression of the hyperbolic tangent is

[(1.15)](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-disp-0015)![hyperbolic tangent left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals StartFraction e Superscript z Baseline minus e Superscript negative z Baseline Over e Superscript z Baseline plus e Superscript negative z Baseline EndFraction](images/c01-math-0015.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>tanh</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>z</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>z</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></math> 

where ![z equals bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x plus b](images/c01-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></math>. It is straightforward to see that when argument ![z](images/c01-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> tends to ![infinity](images/c01-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></math>, the function approaches 1, and if ![z](images/c01-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> tends to ![negative infinity](images/c01-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>, then the function tends to ![negative 1](images/c01-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. The function is represented in [Fig 1.9](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0009)a.

![Figure 1.9 Hyperbolic tangent function (a) and logistic function (b).](images/c01f009.png)

[**Figure 1.9**](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-fig-0009) Hyperbolic tangent function (a) and logistic function (b).

Its derivative will be needed in the construction of the algorithm, and it has the expression

[(1.16)](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-disp-0016)![StartFraction d hyperbolic tangent left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis Over d z EndFraction equals 1 minus hyperbolic tangent squared left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis](images/c01-math-0016.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>tanh</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mrow><mi>tanh</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

Instead of using a hyperbolic tangent, one may prefer to use a function that goes from 0 to 1 in order to give the activation properties of a probability measure. The logistic function ![sigma left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> can be obtained by adding a bias to the tangent to raise it so it tends to 0 instead of tending to ![negative 1](images/c01-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> when ![z right-arrow infinity](images/c01-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math> and rescaling it so it tends to ![negative 1](images/c01-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>

(1.17)![one half left-parenthesis 1 plus hyperbolic tangent left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis right-parenthesis equals one half left-parenthesis 1 plus StartFraction e Superscript z Baseline minus e Superscript negative z Baseline Over e Superscript z Baseline plus e Superscript negative z Baseline EndFraction right-parenthesis equals StartFraction e Superscript z Baseline Over e Superscript z Baseline plus e Superscript negative z Baseline EndFraction equals StartFraction 1 Over 1 plus e Superscript minus 2 z Baseline EndFraction](images/c01-math-0017.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>tanh</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>z</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>z</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>z</mi></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>z</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>z</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></math> 

Since the constant multiplying the argument is arbitrary, it is often removed, and the logistic function has the expression

[(1.18)](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-disp-0018)![sigma left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over 1 plus e Superscript negative z Baseline EndFraction](images/c01-math-0018.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></math> 

The logistic function is represented in [Fig. 1.9](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0009)b. Its derivative has the expression

[(1.19)](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-disp-0019)![StartFraction d sigma left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis Over d z EndFraction equals sigma left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis left-parenthesis 1 minus sigma left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c01-math-0019.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></math> 

The differentiation of both sigmoid functions is left to the reader in Exercise 1.2.

The optimization criterion for the classifier ([1.14](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0014)) or its equivalent with the logistic function consists of minimizing the expectation of the mean square error (MSE) over the training dataset. This criterion, usually called minimum mean square error (MMSE), will provide a solution since it is a convex function of the error, thus having a single minimum. The criterion for the optimal set of parameters is

(1.20)![min Underscript bold w comma b Endscripts double-struck upper E left-bracket e Subscript i Superscript 2 Baseline right-bracket equals min double-struck upper E left-bracket left-parenthesis hyperbolic tangent left-parenthesis bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x Subscript i Baseline plus b right-parenthesis minus y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis squared right-bracket](images/c01-math-0020.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mrow><mi>min</mi><mspace width="0.05em"/></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></munder><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>min</mi><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>tanh</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced></math> 

The expectation cannot be computed, but, by virtue of the weak law of large numbers (WLLN), a sample average of the training errors tends in probability to the actual mean when the number of samples tends to infinity. Then, an adequate approximation to the previous criterion is

(1.21)![min Underscript bold w comma b Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts left-parenthesis hyperbolic tangent left-parenthesis bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x Subscript i Baseline plus b right-parenthesis minus y Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis squared](images/c01-math-0021.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mrow><mi>min</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></munder><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>tanh</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math> 

This expression, to be minimized with respect to the parameters, is a particular example of what is often referred to as a *cost function*. In order to derive the optimization, it is sufficient to compute the gradient of this cost function with respect to parameters ![bold w](images/c01-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math>

In this derivation, we made use of the definition ([1.14](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0014)) and the derivative of the hyperbolic tangent in [Eq. (1.16)](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0016). This is a way to solve the classification problem at hand. Nevertheless, there is a problem with this approach, as pointed out above. This problem is related to the fact that when the argument of the tangent has a high absolute value, the tangent tends to 1. When this happens, gradient ([1.23](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0023)) tends to zero, thus stalling the training. In [Section 1.5](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0017), we will revisit this problem, and we will propose a more justified solution that, among other properties, overcomes this issue.

An optimization algorithm consists of initially choosing arbitrary values for the parameters of the classifier and then iteratively modifying them in a direction opposite to the direction of the squared error gradient, with the purpose of approaching the values of the parameters to the point of minimum squared error. For this reason, the algorithms based on this strategy are called *gradient descent* algorithms (see e.g. (S. S. Haykin [2005](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0123))). The procedure is illustrated in [Fig. 1.10](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0010), and the update rule can be applied in batch mode

Once the update has been applied, it must be repeated until a criterion has been reached. Similarly, the update can be applied one sample at a time

(1.26)![bold w left-parenthesis k plus 1 right-parenthesis equals bold w left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis minus mu e Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis 1 minus f squared left-parenthesis bold x Subscript k Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis bold x Subscript k](images/c01-math-0026.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub></math> (1.27)![b left-parenthesis k plus 1 right-parenthesis equals b left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis minus mu e Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis 1 minus f squared left-parenthesis bold x Subscript k Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c01-math-0027.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where ![mu](images/c01-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> is a small scalar usually called *learning rate*, and it determines the length of the movement toward the minimum of the cost function relative to the gradient. Notice the similarity of these two expressions with the perceptron rule of Eqs. ([1.6](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0006)). The difference consists of that now the error is a continuous function, that can be differentiated, and that a new term relative to the activation function appears in these equations. This new term is precisely the reason why such an update rule is still not a good algorithm. Indeed, when the machine classifies the samples almost correctly, term ![left-parenthesis 1 minus f squared left-parenthesis bold x Subscript k Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></math> tends to zero, which may seem a good sign, but since the activation is squared, if a sample is misclassified and the corresponding activation saturates to 1 or ![negative 1](images/c01-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, this term tends to zero, which may stall the learning. Therefore, this criterion must be further modified in order to obtain an adequate criterion that does not suffer from this effect. A different approach to optimization and its relationship with the activation functions will be explained in [Sections 1.5.1](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0018) and [1.5.2](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0019).

![Figure 1.10 Illustration of the gradient descent procedure. The graph represents a cost function consisting of the expectation of a square error as a function of a parameter bold w. The optimum value bold w Superscript asterisk of the parameters is achieved when the cost function is the minimum. At this point, the gradient is zero. At iteration k, the value of the parameter is bold w Superscript k. The gradient nabla Subscript bold w Baseline double-struck upper E left-bracket e squared right-bracket of the cost function is computed, and then the parameter is modified in the direction opposite to the gradient, multiplied by a small constant mu. The operation must be repeated until the gradient is zero.](images/c01f010.png)

[**Figure 1.10**](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-fig-0010) Illustration of the gradient descent procedure. The graph represents a cost function consisting of the expectation of a square error as a function of a parameter ![bold w](images/c01-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math>. The optimum value ![bold w Superscript asterisk](images/c01-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></math> of the parameters is achieved when the cost function is the minimum. At this point, the gradient is zero. At iteration ![k](images/c01-i0100.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, the value of the parameter is ![bold w Superscript k](images/c01-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></math>. The gradient ![nabla Subscript bold w Baseline double-struck upper E left-bracket e squared right-bracket](images/c01-i0102.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mo>&#8711;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced></math> of the cost function is computed, and then the parameter is modified in the direction opposite to the gradient, multiplied by a small constant ![mu](images/c01-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math>. The operation must be repeated until the gradient is zero.

An equivalent expression of the update rule can be obtained with the use of a logistic activation. Note that if a logistic function is used, then the labels should be changed to ![y element-of StartSet 1 comma 0 EndSet](images/c01-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. A stronger justification for the use of these activations is provided in this chapter. The derivation of such rules is left to the reader as exercise 1.3.

 

### 1.2.4 The Least Mean Squares Algorithm

Notice that when the activation tends to 1, the gradient will stall. If a linear activation is used, that is, ![f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis equals bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x plus b](images/c01-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></math>, then the gradient becomes

(1.28)![bold w left-parenthesis k plus 1 right-parenthesis equals bold w left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis minus mu e Subscript k Baseline bold x Subscript k](images/c01-math-0028.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub></math> (1.29)![b left-parenthesis k plus 1 right-parenthesis equals b left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis minus mu e Subscript k](images/c01-math-0029.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> 

This algorithm is known as the least mean squares (LMS) algorithm, and it was first derived in Widrow and Hoff ([1960](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0371)).

 

## 1.3 Structure of a Neural Network

The perceptron unit in the structure presented before has a linear nature, that is, it can only classify problems that are linearly separable for data distributed in other ways, it would be impossible for such a structure to do a good job. The exclusive OR (XOR) problem in [Fig. 1.12](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0012), is a classic example that a linear perceptron cannot solve. In this example, the data has a label that is an XOR function of its coordinates. Therefore, the black dots are labeled as +1, and the white dots are labeled as 0.

It is clear that a linear function cannot classify the data. Nevertheless, it is possible to construct a nonlinear function with several perceptrons in two layers. The proposed structure to solve this problem is shown in [Fig. 1.13](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0013).

where we use the notation ![bold-italic sigma left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0118.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> to represent a vector of functions ![sigma left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0119.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> each one applied to the elements of a vector.

The layer of two neurons is often called a hidden layer, and its corresponding output is vector ![bold h](images/c01-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow></math>, which is a nonlinear transformation of the input. The vector is then linearly transformed using vector ![bold w](images/c01-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math>, and then the result is passed through another monotonically increasing activation function ![phi left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>

This is the simplest possible example of an NN, which applies a nonlinear transformation to the input in order to produce a nonlinear classification. But let us take a close look at how this simple NN with three neurons is able to solve the XOR problem in [Fig. 1.12](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0012). This is explained in [Example 1.3.1](#c01.xhtml#c01-fea-0008).

The previous example shows the bare minimum structure of an NN able to solve a nonlinear problem. As it can be seen, the parameters of the NN have been found painfully and after some heuristic considerations that cannot constitute a criterion to construct a learning algorithm similar to the perceptron rule or the MMSE introduced in [Sections 1.2.2](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0004) and [1.2.2](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0004).

Nevertheless, it is possible to have a much better solution to this problem. A better solution will provide a classification with a lower probability of error in an extended version of this problem, and the parameters should be obtained automatically by a learning algorithm from data. In order to achieve such a solution, we first need to introduce more about activation functions and a generalized algorithm to train an MLP, known as the BP algorithm, which will be introduced respectively in [Sections 1.3.1](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0012) and [1.5.3](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0025).

 

### 1.3.1 The Multilayer Perceptron

In the previous example, a two‐layer perceptron has been presented to demonstrate its capability to solve a nonlinear problem. The expressive capacity of an NN relies primarily on the use of nonlinear activations, and on the complexity of this network, or, in other words, in the number of layers and neurons or *nodes* in its layers. A generalized NN or MLP is then a structure with ![upper L plus 1](images/c01-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> layers, where layer ![l equals 0](images/c01-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> is the input ![bold x](images/c01-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> and, therefore, its number of nodes ![upper D 0 equals upper D](images/c01-i0150.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>D</mi></math> is equal to the dimension of input space. The network has ![upper L minus 1](images/c01-i0151.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> *hidden* layers with ![upper D Subscript l](images/c01-i0152.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></math> nodes that produce the column vector of outputs ![bold h Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis Baseline equals left-bracket h 1 Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis Baseline comma ellipsis comma h Subscript upper D Sub Subscript l Subscript Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis Baseline right-bracket Superscript down-tack](images/c01-i0153.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup></math>. The last layer is the output ![bold o equals left-bracket o 1 comma ellipsis comma o Subscript upper D Sub Subscript upper L Subscript Baseline right-bracket Superscript down-tack](images/c01-i0154.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup></math> of the MLP.

The layers are interconnected by edges. Each edge contains a weight ![w Subscript i comma j Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> that connects the output of node ![i](images/c01-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> of layer ![l minus 1](images/c01-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> to the input of node ![j](images/c01-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> in layer ![l](images/c01-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math>. The graphical representation of the MLP is shown in [Fig. 1.16](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0016), where biases ![b Subscript j Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>b</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> are not shown for simplicity.

Usually, the graphical representation of a multilayer perceptron is purely illustrative, and the information about its structure is given in the number of layers and the number of nodes in each layer. Nevertheless, sometimes one wants to represent a very dense MLP, in whose case, instead of drawing all nodes and connections or edges between nodes, a more compact drawing is used, as the one shown in [Fig. 1.17](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0017). The upper pane of the figure shows a traditional way of representing the MLP, while the lower one shows a more compact representation where the nodes are symbolized by boxes.

It is common to think of an MLP as a structure to process inputs in the form of vectors, but as a general matter of fact, an MLP can be used to process information organized as multidimensional arrays, particularly 2D or 3D arrays or matrices when the input data is an image. In these cases, the weight matrices become 3D or 4D arrays, and then it is also common to call them tensors. We do not use any of the properties of tensors in machine learning, and the use of this name for a multidimensional array of an NN is controversial; therefore, we will avoid the use of this term except when it is needed in order to be consistent with nomenclature in other scholarship or software.
