### 1.3.2 Multidimensional Array Multiplications

So far, matrix‐vector multiplications have been used as a basic operation to express the MLP operation, which, among other issues, constrains the MLP input to a vector of components. But, in general, it is possible to use different configurations as inputs. For example, an input may be a matrix representing an image, or a 3D matrix representing information in the space, as a 3D image. In order to construct an MLP with data organized in these structures, it is sufficient to vectorize or *flatten* the inputs, that is, reorganize the data in a vector with arbitrary order. Nevertheless, if the spatial information is important, this limits or heavily difficulties the types of operations to apply to the inputs, such as the convolution operation, as is seen in [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml). In general, it is more convenient not to flatten the input (though sometimes it will be done) and, instead of using matrices and vectors, use the more general concept of multidimensional arrays. Let us define, as an example, an array ![bold upper A element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper P times upper Q times upper R](images/c01-i0185.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msup></math> in three dimensions. It has entries ![i comma j comma k](images/c01-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></math> defined as

(1.45)![left-bracket bold upper A right-bracket Subscript i comma j comma k Baseline equals a Subscript i comma j comma k](images/c01-math-0045.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math> 

where ![1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper P](images/c01-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>P</mi></math>, ![1 less-than-or-equal-to j less-than-or-equal-to upper Q](images/c01-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>Q</mi></math>, ![1 less-than-or-equal-to k less-than-or-equal-to upper R](images/c01-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>R</mi></math>.

Assume two multidimensional arrays ![upper A](images/c01-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>, ![upper B](images/c01-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> with different dimensions and number of elements, but with a dimension with a common number ![upper P](images/c01-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> of elements. For example, take ![bold upper A element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper P times upper Q](images/c01-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>Q</mi></mrow></msup></math> and ![bold upper B element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper R times upper P times upper S](images/c01-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></msup></math>. The first one has two dimensions (a matrix) whose first dimension has ![upper P](images/c01-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> components and the second one is an array of three dimensions with ![upper P](images/c01-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> elements in its second dimension. The product between both arrays along the first dimension of ![bold upper A](images/c01-i0197.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi></mrow></math> and second dimension of ![bold upper B](images/c01-i0198.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi></mrow></math> is possible, which produces an array ![bold upper C](images/c01-i0199.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi></mrow></math> whose dimensions with components ![c Subscript j comma k comma l](images/c01-i0200.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></math>

[(1.46)](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-disp-0046)![c Subscript j comma k comma l Baseline equals left-bracket bold upper A dot bold upper B right-bracket Subscript j comma k comma l Baseline equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper P Endscripts a Subscript i comma j Baseline b Subscript k comma i comma l](images/c01-math-0046.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>P</mi></munderover><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></math> 

As a result, the common dimension disappears, and the new array has as many dimensions as the sum of the remaining ones. In this case, the first dimension of array ![bold upper A](images/c01-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi></mrow></math> and the second dimension of tensor ![bold upper B](images/c01-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi></mrow></math> disappear, so the remaining dimensions are ![upper Q times upper R times upper S](images/c01-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>. In general, the dimension across which the product is performed must be specified, but on occasions, there is only one common dimension, in which case the operation will not need such specification.

 

## 1.4 Activations

As seen before, activations play an important role in the MLP. The activations that are applied in the hidden nodes are necessary in order to endow the structure with nonlinear properties. But it also makes sense to use nonlinear activations in the output layer for a different purpose. The activations here play the role of probability estimation. The simplest example consists of using logistic activations at the output of a binary classifier, so the output approaches zero when the input sample is classified as belonging to class “0” and to one when the sample is classified as belonging to class “1.” With this, the intention is to use this output as an approximation of the probability that the class is 1 given the observation, i.e. ![p left-parenthesis y equals 1 vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0231.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. The usual activations for hidden and output layers are presented here, where the use of output activations as a probabilistic estimation is treated in [Section 1.5](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0017).

So far, we have presented the hyperbolic tangent and the logistic activation in Eqs. ([1.15](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0015)) and ([1.18](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0018)) that we reproduce here. If ![z equals bold w Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x plus b](images/c01-i0232.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></math> is the affine operation performed into any arbitrary neuron, the hyperbolic tangent is defined as

![hyperbolic tangent left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals StartFraction e Superscript z Baseline minus e Superscript negative z Baseline Over e Superscript z Baseline plus e Superscript negative z Baseline EndFraction](images/c01-math-0052.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>tanh</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>z</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>z</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></math> ![sigma left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals StartFraction 1 Over 1 plus e Superscript negative z Baseline EndFraction](images/c01-math-0053.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></math> 

Among them, the most used is the logistic activation, since it has an interpretation in terms of probability, which is important in some kinds of NNs as restricted Boltzmann machines, that are treated in [Chapter 7](#c07.xhtml). Nevertheless, these activations are not widely used in other NNs because they may produce training stalling (see Sub[section 1.2.3](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0007)). A more suitable activation for the hidden nodes of an MLP is a surprisingly simple one (Jarrett et al. [2009](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0160)), called rectified linear unit (ReLU). The expression of the ReLU is

(1.52)![phi Subscript upper R e upper L upper U Baseline left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals max left-parenthesis 0 comma z right-parenthesis](images/c01-math-0054.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>U</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>max</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

This activation is hardly nonlinear, but it has proven to be very powerful (Nair and Hinton [2010](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0239)) even in structures such as the above‐mentioned restricted Boltzmann machines. One can argue that this activation can also stop an algorithm since its derivative is always zero for negative inputs. An easy modification of this unit is the following:

(1.53)![phi Subscript upper M a x upper O u t Baseline left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals max left-parenthesis 0 comma z right-parenthesis plus a min 0 comma z](images/c01-math-0055.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>max</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>min</mi><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi></math> 

In this activation, the derivatives are 1 when ![z greater-than 0](images/c01-i0233.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>z</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and ![a](images/c01-i0234.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> when ![z less-than 0](images/c01-i0235.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>z</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, which fixes the issue. The value of ![a](images/c01-i0236.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> is supposed to be smaller than 1. This is usually referred to as a leaky ReLU.

Another activation, called maximum output (MaxOut), was presented in Ian Goodfellow et al. ([2013a](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0109)). In a traditional activation, each neuron is assigned a weight vector ![bold w](images/c01-i0237.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math> and a bias ![b](images/c01-i0238.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>. In a MaxOut, each neuron is assigned ![upper K](images/c01-i0239.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> vectors ![bold w Subscript k](images/c01-i0240.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub></math> and weights ![b Subscript k](images/c01-i0241.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>. The dot products between the input and all the vectors are computed, and the biases are added to each dot product. The MaxOut chooses the result with the maximum value as

(1.54)![phi left-parenthesis z right-parenthesis equals max left-parenthesis bold w 1 Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x plus b 1 comma ellipsis comma bold w Subscript upper K Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x plus b Subscript upper K Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c01-math-0056.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>max</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> 

The MaxOut activation can be seen as a generalization of the ReLU activation, which comes with the advantage that each neural network learns multiple functions of the same feature through the training of multiple weight vectors. Nevertheless, this has the disadvantage of an increased computational burden and the need to cross validate the number ![upper K](images/c01-i0242.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> of weight vectors.

 

## 1.5 Training a Multilayer Perceptron

The simple MMSE criterion has been applied to the solution of a linear problem in Section [1.2.3](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0007), in order to solve a problem that is not purely linearly separable. Then, the multilayer perceptron has been defined in Subsection 1.3.1, where a two‐layer structure has been applied to solve the classical XOR problem using the bare minimum structure with two nodes in the hidden layer. Nevertheless, this solution is purely ad hoc for this problem, and this cannot be generalized to a higher dimensional arbitrary problem. Nevertheless, a strategy similar to the algorithm applied to the linear perceptron can be generalized to the MLP. Also, we have seen different forms of activation for hidden nodes and activations adequate to binary and multiclass problems. In this section, we put everything together to construct a generalized set of training algorithms depending on the nature of the classification problem at hand. These algorithms fall under the umbrella of the so‐called BP algorithm. The general criterion to apply is called ML.

 

### 1.5.1 Maximum Likelihood Criterion

Assume a dataset ![StartSet bold x Subscript i Baseline comma y Subscript i Baseline EndSet](images/c01-i0243.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>, ![1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper N](images/c01-i0244.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>N</mi></math> consisting of ![upper N](images/c01-i0245.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> labeled patterns to be used for training purposes, where the labels are binary, that is, ![y Subscript i Baseline element-of StartSet 0 comma 1 EndSet](images/c01-i0246.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. In order to develop the training criterion, we assume further that a conditional probability of the labels over the samples ![p left-parenthesis bold y vertical-bar bold upper X right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0247.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> exists, where we defined ![bold y equals left-parenthesis y 1 comma ellipsis comma y Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript down-tack](images/c01-i0248.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mspace width="-0.15em"/><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup></math> as the sequence of labels corresponding to the training input patterns ![bold upper X equals left-parenthesis bold x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold x Subscript upper N Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0249.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></math>. An adequate way to perform a classification would be to know this probability. In this case, we just need to find the sequence ![bold y](images/c01-i0250.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math> of labels that maximizes this probability. Besides, it is reasonable to assume that the labels are conditionally independent, that is, for any pair ![bold x Subscript i Baseline comma bold y Subscript i Baseline](images/c01-i0251.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, we assume

[(1.55)](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-disp-0057)![p left-parenthesis y Subscript i Baseline vertical-bar bold x Subscript i Baseline comma bold x Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis equals p left-parenthesis y Subscript i Baseline vertical-bar bold x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis comma for-all j](images/c01-math-0057.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>j</mi></math> 

The second probability ![p left-parenthesis y Subscript i Baseline vertical-bar bold x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0252.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the probability of ![y Subscript i](images/c01-i0253.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> conditional to ![bold x Subscript i](images/c01-i0254.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>. If we had this probability, then we can easily make a decision: if the probability ![p left-parenthesis y Subscript i Baseline equals 1 vertical-bar bold x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0255.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is higher than 0.5, then we decide that ![y Subscript i Baseline equals 1](images/c01-i0256.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, or zero otherwise. The first probability is the probability of ![y Subscript i](images/c01-i0257.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> conditional to observations ![bold x Subscript i Baseline comma bold x Subscript j Baseline](images/c01-i0258.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub></math>. In principle, adding more observations may add more information to a better decision. While this may be true in specific scenarios, we will assume that all the information needed to make a decision on ![y Subscript i](images/c01-i0259.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is contained in ![bold x Subscript i](images/c01-i0260.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, and that adding a new observation does not change the probability, and this is what [Eq. (1.55)](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0057) means. Now, assume that we have two samples ![bold x 1](images/c01-i0261.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![bold x 2](images/c01-i0262.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math> and we want to compute the probability ![p left-parenthesis y 1 comma y 2 vertical-bar bold x 1 comma bold x 2 right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0263.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> of the sequence ![y 1 comma y 2](images/c01-i0264.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>. By using Bayes' rule, we get

stretchy="false">)</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

We have used here the assumption that ![y 1](images/c01-i0265.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> is independent of ![bold x 2](images/c01-i0266.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math> and ![y 2](images/c01-i0267.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> given the knowledge of ![bold x 1](images/c01-i0268.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and that ![y 2](images/c01-i0269.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> is independent of ![bold x 1](images/c01-i0270.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> given the knowledge of ![bold x 2](images/c01-i0271.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math>. It is worth noting that this does not mean that ![y 1](images/c01-i0272.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![y 2](images/c01-i0273.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> are independent, they are independent only if their respective patterns ![bold x 1](images/c01-i0274.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math>, ![bold x 2](images/c01-i0275.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math> are known. This can be easily generalizable as

[(1.57)](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-disp-0059)![p left-parenthesis bold y vertical-bar bold upper X right-parenthesis equals p left-parenthesis y 1 comma ellipsis comma y Subscript n Baseline vertical-bar bold x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold x Subscript upper N Baseline right-parenthesis equals product Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts p left-parenthesis y Subscript i Baseline vertical-bar bold x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c01-math-0059.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8719;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

If these patterns and their labels are known, that is, they are a set of training data, the above expression ([1.57](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0059)) is called a *likelihood*, and it has the property of being *factorizable* in elements ![p left-parenthesis y Subscript i Baseline comma bold x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0276.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

Provided that likelihood is constructed by a parametric function with a set of parameters ![bold-italic theta](images/c01-i0277.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></math> containing all weights and biases ![w Subscript i comma j Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis Baseline comma b Subscript j Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0278.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>b</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> of a learning machine, for example, an MLP, the training criterion for this MLP is to maximize this likelihood with respect to its parameters. Since the logarithm is a monotonically increasing function, maximizing the logarithm of the likelihood, or *log‐likelihood* is equivalent to maximizing [Eq. (1.57)](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0059). This is the ML criterion.

(1.58)![upper J Subscript upper M upper L Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic theta comma bold upper X comma bold y right-parenthesis equals log p left-parenthesis bold y vertical-bar bold upper X right-parenthesis](images/c01-math-0060.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

In many situations, an information‐theoretic interpretation of this cost function is used. For this purpose, we change the sign, and divide the equation by the number ![upper N](images/c01-i0279.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> of training data to obtain the so‐called negative log‐likelihood (NLL)

[(1.59)](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-disp-0061)![upper J Subscript upper M upper L Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic theta comma bold upper X comma bold y right-parenthesis equals minus StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction log p left-parenthesis bold y vertical-bar bold upper X right-parenthesis equals minus StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts log p left-parenthesis bold y Subscript i Baseline vertical-bar bold x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis almost-equals minus double-struck upper E Subscript bold x comma bold y Baseline log p left-parenthesis bold y vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c01-math-0061.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></msub><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

where ![bold-italic theta](images/c01-i0280.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></math> represents the set of parameters of an MLP that needs to be optimized by maximizing this cost function. The purpose of dividing the expression by ![upper N](images/c01-i0281.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> is to obtain the sample average of log probabilities ![minus StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript i Endscripts log p left-parenthesis bold y Subscript i Baseline vertical-bar bold x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0282.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, which is, by virtue of the WLLN (Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis [2000](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0034)), an approximation to the expectation of these logarithms. Assuming that the actual probabilities of ![bold y Subscript i](images/c01-i0283.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> are known, one can change this measure by ![minus double-struck upper E Subscript bold x comma bold y Baseline left-bracket p left-parenthesis bold y right-parenthesis log p left-parenthesis bold y vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis right-bracket](images/c01-i0284.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></msub><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></math>, which is, by definition, the cross‐entropy measure between the actual and the estimated probabilities (Cover and Thomas [2006](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0070)).

 

### 1.5.2 Activations and Likelihood Functions

Apart from the above interpretation in terms of Information Theory, the logarithm has a practical purpose, which will become apparent next, when we formulate the probabilities in terms of the output of an MLP, which is related to the chosen form for the output activations. Assume an MLP with a number of hidden layers and some activation functions for the hidden nodes. We take care here of the justification and interpretation of the choice of the activation function for the output layer. The first activation to be presented is the logistic one, which must be adequately constructed, and it is useful when the MLP is used for binary classification, so the output gives an estimation of the probability ![p left-parenthesis y equals 1 vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0285.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, that is, the probability that the label corresponding to input ![bold x](images/c01-i0286.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> is one, which is a Bernoulli distribution. Then we generalize this activation for the case where the classification neuron is multiclass, where the probability is a Multinoulli distribution. Finally, we present the activation used when the output is assumed to have a Gaussian distribution.

 

#### 1.5.2.1 Logistic Activation for Binary Classification

Here we assume that an MLP is used for binary classification ([Fig. 1.19](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0019)). Then, as mentioned before, the output is modeled as the probability of that ![y equals 1](images/c01-i0289.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, that is, the probability function is a Bernoulli mass function. We start by constructing an *unnormalized* log probability function as

(1.60)![log ModifyingAbove p With tilde left-parenthesis y vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis equals y z long right-arrow ModifyingAbove p With tilde left-parenthesis y vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis equals e Superscript y z](images/c01-math-0062.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>log</mi><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mi>z</mi><mo>&#x027F6;</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi>z</mi></mrow></msup></math> 

The probability is unnormalized because ![ModifyingAbove p With tilde left-parenthesis y equals 0 vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis plus ModifyingAbove p With tilde left-parenthesis y equals 1 vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis not-equals 1](images/c01-i0290.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, so this output does not have probability mass function properties. The way it works is the following: for ![y equals 1](images/c01-i0291.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, if the linear output ![z](images/c01-i0292.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> produced by the last layer of the MLP is positive, the product will be positive, producing a high value for the unnormalized probability, implying that the probability of 1 is high, but if ![z](images/c01-i0293.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> is negative, this implies that the probability of 1 is low since the unnormalized probability will be close to zero. In order to provide this function with probability mass function properties, we must construct a function for which ![p left-parenthesis y equals 0 vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis plus p left-parenthesis y equals 1 vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis equals 1](images/c01-i0294.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> as

The following example shows a fundamental difference between the use of the ML loss and the application of the MMSE loss.

 

#### 1.5.2.2 Softmax Activation for Multiclass Classification

In multiclass classification, it is common to construct structures whose output is vectorial, that is, the NN has an output consisting of a node per each one of the possible classes of the input patterns. These outputs are interpreted as the posterior probability of each one of the classes given the input. That is, if the number of possible classes is ![upper K](images/c01-i0322.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>, then one can denote a predictive posterior as ![p left-parenthesis y equals k vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c01-i0323.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, ![0 less-than-or-equal-to k less-than-or-equal-to upper K minus 1](images/c01-i0324.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. The linear component of the output is then written as

(1.69)![bold z equals bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis upper L right-parenthesis Baseline Superscript down-tack Baseline bold h Superscript left-parenthesis upper L minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c01-math-0071.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>

with

The *softmax* function is an activation consisting of the normalization of the above probability

[(1.72)](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-disp-0074)![p left-parenthesis y equals k vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis equals o Subscript k Baseline left-parenthesis bold h Superscript left-parenthesis upper L minus 1 right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis equals softmax left-parenthesis z Subscript k Baseline right-parenthesis equals StartFraction exp left-parenthesis z Subscript k Baseline right-parenthesis Over sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript upper K Endscripts exp left-parenthesis z Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis EndFraction](images/c01-math-0074.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mtext>softmax</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><mi>exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></math> 

This output has probability mass function properties, as the sum of outputs adds to 1. In order to construct a loss function, the common approach is to maximize the cross entropy between the outputs and the labels, which is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood. Since the output is a vector with ![upper K](images/c01-i0327.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> elements, we transform the scalar label ![y Subscript i Baseline equals k](images/c01-i0328.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></math> corresponding to training input ![bold x Subscript i](images/c01-i0329.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> into a binary vector ![bold y Subscript i Baseline equals left-bracket y Subscript 0 comma i Baseline comma ellipsis comma y Subscript upper K minus 1 comma i Baseline right-bracket Superscript down-tack](images/c01-i0330.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></math> where only element ![y Subscript k comma i Baseline equals 1](images/c01-i0331.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and the rest are zeros, which denotes that the class of the input pattern is ![k](images/c01-i0332.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>. This is often called one‐hot encoding.

We denote the real probability of that ![y Subscript i Baseline equals k](images/c01-i0333.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></math> as

The loss function obtained in [Eq. (1.64)](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0066) for binary classification can be also obtained by applying the cross entropy reasoning above. The corresponding proof is given in the following example.

### 1.5.3 The Backpropagation Algorithm

The BP algorithm seeks to optimize the parameters of the NN according to the ML criterion or a regularized criterion as summarized in [Section 2.3](#c02.xhtml#c02-sec-0007). The BP algorithm uses a gradient descent procedure, where the derivative of the cost function corresponding to each training sample is computed with respect to each one of the weights of the network, and then these weights are updated in the direction opposite to this gradient.

A gradient procedure applied to an NN is in principle cumbersome since the weights of each layer are connected to the next layer through nonlinear functions; however, the use of the chain rule of derivatives, extended to gradients, is applied to solve the problem in a generalized way that is simple and efficient to program.

The optimization of the NN, then, takes two steps. In the first one, the estimation cost function evaluated for a training sample is computed. This step is often called the forward step. Once the cost is computed, the backward step is applied to recursively compute the derivative of the error with respect to each weight, from the output layer to the input layer, and finally update the weights. The backward step optimizes the structure with respect to all parameters ![bold-italic theta colon StartSet w Subscript j comma k Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis Baseline comma b Subscript k Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis Baseline EndSet](images/c01-i0355.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>:</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>b</mi><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math> by

(1.68)](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0070), for multiclass classification in [Eq. (1.78)](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0080), and for multitask regression in [Eq. (1.85)](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0087). ### 1.5.4 Summary of the BP Algorithm

The BP algorithm derived above is formulated for a single input sample. The BP of a single error is depicted in [Fig. 1.23](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0023). In the figure, a training sample is applied to the input, and then the error ![delta](images/c01-i0409.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi></mrow></math> is computed. With it, the BP starts by updating the weights of the output layer with the product between the input to this layer and the error. The process continues with the error BP, which consists of transforming the error with the previous weight matrix and the derivatives of the activations, after which the update of the weights of this layer is applied.

Nevertheless, the gradient with respect to all weights must be computed and averaged for all samples in the batch of training data and then used to update the weights. A general BP algorithm can be summarized as follows. Assume a training set of data ![StartSet bold x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold x Subscript upper N Baseline EndSet](images/c01-i0410.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> with corresponding labels ![StartSet bold y 1 comma ellipsis comma bold y Subscript upper N Baseline EndSet](images/c01-i0411.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math>. The machine learning task can be a multiclass classification or a multitask regression. Here, without loss of generality, all data is used in a BP step, but later the concept of minibatch is discussed where the dataset is broken into training subsets, which generally improves the training results.

The first step will be the forward step, where all training data is applied to the NN, and all outputs are computed. In particular, we compute vectors ![bold z Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis Baseline comma bold h Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis l where the update term is always equal to the input to this layer (or the output of the previous one) times the error. The bias term has the same treatment, where it can be assumed that the input that goes through this parameter is a constant equal to 1. For the first layer, with ![l equals 1](images/c01-i0422.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, the input is ![bold h Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis Baseline equals bold x Subscript i](images/c01-i0423.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>.

This is the basic procedure for the training of an MLP. This procedure is nevertheless applied to optimize the NN using the ML criterion with any suitable likelihood function of the output. This procedure is illustrative of the strategy applied to the optimization of other structures, in particular, the convolutional NNs introduced in [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml) or the recurrent NNs introduced in [Chapter 5](#c05.xhtml).

 

## 1.6 Conclusion

The multilayer perceptron is the earliest form of deep learning that ever appeared, but it establishes the basics of the training procedures applied to any deep learning structure.

The concept of neuron is an idea that roughly reproduces the structure of a biological neuron, though the dynamics of an artificial neuron are very simplistic compared to the dynamics of a biological neuron. Nevertheless, this simple idea is able to implement powerful machine learning structures, as the multilayer perceptron summarized in this chapter. The first activation ever to be applied to a neuron is the sigmoid, but later it has been seen that simpler mathematical operations produce good results in an MLP. Namely, in present days, the most used nonlinear operation is the ReLU and its generalizations. The output layers usually contain activations that provide a probabilistic interpretation. While the first criterion to optimize an MLP is the MSE, we have seen that, when the output activation is a sigmoid, this criterion has points with vanishing gradient, which may make a gradient descent algorithm to stall.

In particular, we choose sigmoidal activations to represent the conditional probability of a training output given the corresponding input patterns, that is, its likelihood. We have seen likelihoods for binary outputs (Bernoulli) or multiclass outputs (Multinoulli) that lead to optimization criteria that do not show the risk of stalling in a point of vanishing gradient. Besides, in regression, we may use linear activations. The interpretation of these activations is given by the modeling of the regression error as a Gaussian distribution, which leads to a log‐likelihood that is estimated via these linear outputs.

The BP algorithm summarized here is a powerful way to implement the ML criterion in an MLP. The chain rule of calculus is used to derive a general procedure to implement a gradient descent algorithm to the weights of the MLP that computes an error term from the derivative of the cost function that is later transformed back through the MLP weights. This transformed error term is used to iteratively update the NN.

# 2  
Training Practicalities

 

## 2.1 Introduction

In this chapter, it is assumed that the reader is familiar with the fundamental, classic concepts of DL. Namely, [Chapter 1](#c01.xhtml) reviews the concept of neuron, the structure of a NN and associated functions like the ReLU, the softmax, the criteria used for the optimization of a NN, and the backpropagation algorithm, which should be connected with the concepts of gradient descent (GD) and overfitting, which is discussed below. Therefore, the reader is able to construct a basic learning machine and train it. Nevertheless, the training of a machine has certain particularities, among them, overfitting or local minima problems, low training speed, or others. These difficulties can be properly addressed by the use of additional training techniques that help to ease the learning process of a machine.

Under the above prerequisites, the present chapter is intended to introduce the reader to these techniques. First, the concept of generalization and overfitting is introduced, as overfitting is a phenomenon that is inherent to any learning machine, and it is particularly important in DL when the models to be trained have a large number of parameters. The overfitting is usually controlled by controlling the expressive capacity of the machine, which is achieved by the use of the so‐called regularization techniques.

First, it must be noticed that the gradient descent is initiated from an arbitrary point, that is, from arbitrary values of the parameters. It is obvious that not all initial values are adequate. This chapter presents the two main methods to properly initialize the NN parameters.

A common element in DL is the use of normalization techniques. They are necessary to have a set of features that are scaled in the same range of values. This makes the parameter optimization more efficient since normalization eases the machine from the burden of adapting its parameters to features of different scales. This would force the parameters associated with different features to converge to different scales associated with different dynamic ranges and average values, which, in turn, can lead to convergence difficulties.

Finally, it is common to modify the gradient descent procedure in order to speed it up through the use of features that modify the speed and direction of the parameter update vector with respect to the one produced by the gradient only.

 

## 2.2 Generalization and Overfitting

The whole purpose of training a learning machine is to achieve the best possible accuracy in a test sample, not previously seen by the training algorithm. If the training procedure is designed so it just minimizes a loss function over the training data, this may compromise the test performance. It is desired that the training dataset contains enough information about its structure, and this information is what one wants to transmit to the NN. Nevertheless, the information about the structure of the data is always limited, and this limitation becomes more important as the number of samples decreases. When the data does not contain enough information to represent its distribution, the difference between the performance of the NN during training and test may be significant. For a training dataset with a low number of data, the training error may be arbitrarily low if the complexity or the number of layers and nodes of the NN is sufficiently high. However, the test error rate will be high, as the NN will not be able to learn the distribution of the data. The difference between the training and test errors in an NN with sufficient complexity is called *overfitting*. The ability to obtain a sufficiently low error both in training and test is called *generalization* ability. Let us illustrate this in the following example.

Generalization bounds in NNs are treated in the works by Cao and Gu ([2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0052)), Hole ([1996](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0147)) among others. The last work provides, with a given probability, the bounds on the performance of NNs as a function of the NN complexity and the number of training samples. This number has a high impact in the generalization ability of an NN, and authors show that for an NN that is overly complex, the generalization bounds are good as long as the number of training samples is high enough.

 

### 2.2.1 Basic Weight Initializations

With the use of the BP algorithm, it is straightforward to code a procedure to train an MLP given a set of input data. The easiest way to program it consists of computing the gradient of the cost function with respect to the weight matrices for each one of the samples. The very first step of training consists of assigning initial values to the weights of the MLP. The techniques may slightly vary depending on the kind of activations used, but all of them assume implicitly that the optimal weights are distributed with a given probability that is centered around the origin.

If one initializes all weights to zero, the inputs to all activation functions will be zero. If the output layer contains sigmoidal activations modeling a Bernoulli or Multinoulli probability mass function, then the outputs will be uniform. For the case of a Bernoulli, the activation will show an output of 0.5, and for the case of a Multinoulli, the activations will be ![1 slash upper K](images/c02-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>K</mi></math>. The entropy of the output is then maximized, which can be interpreted as that initially the uncertainty of the NN is maximized. This may not work properly in the BP. Indeed, once the error term of the first layer is computed, it is back‐propagated to the previous layers. As a result, as the last layer has weights initialized to zero, the transformed error term will be simply zero and during the first update, only the last layer is updated, and all values of the weight matrix will be low. In the second iteration, only error terms of layer ![upper L](images/c02-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper L minus 1](images/c02-i0014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> will be different from zero, but the one for ![upper L minus 1](images/c02-i0015.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> will be low, thus producing a low update speed and possibly a local minimum solution.

In order to improve the results, it is advisable to start with random values in the weights. This may also pose problems to the training. If the values are too small, we may encounter the same difficulties as above, while if the values are too high, in these cases where the hidden activations are sigmoidal, all of them will be showing values close to 1 or to zero, and with derivatives close to zero, which will stall the training as well. While the problem is partially solved with the use of ReLU units, a more effective initialization can be applied that depends on the type of activation and the size of each layer (Mishkin and Matas [2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0231)). These are the activation aware initializations, namely the Xavier (Glorot and Yoshua Bengio [2010](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0103)) and He initializations (He et al. [2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0125)) described below.

 

### 2.2.2 Activation Aware Initializations

Xavier Glorot and Yoshua Bengio proposed in Glorot and Yoshua Bengio ([2010](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0103)) an optimal initialization for sigmoidal activations. This initialization consists of applying random values to the weights of layer ![l](images/c02-i0016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> distributed using a Gaussian distribution with standard deviation ![sigma equals StartFraction 1 Over StartRoot upper D Subscript l minus 1 Baseline EndRoot EndFraction](images/c02-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msqrt><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></math>, that is, the variance of the distribution is set as the number of nodes of the previous layer. This is commonly known as the Xavier initialization. They experimentally show that this simple initialization produces good results in NNs with logistic and hyperbolic tangent activations. Authors provide reasoning about the adequacy of their initialization, but they agree that many effects remain not understood. Nevertheless, He et al. ([2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0125)) show that this initialization does not produce adequate results when the used activations for the hidden layers are ReLU, since they are not symmetric. They proposed a modified initialization (known as He initialization) with standard deviation ![sigma equals StartRoot StartFraction 2 Over upper D Subscript l minus 1 Baseline EndFraction EndRoot](images/c02-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></math>. In their work, they test a NN with 30 layers and ReLU activations where their initialization results in convergence, but where the results with the Xavier initialization show a poor convergence. The reasons for this are not fully understood (Kumar [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0185)).

 

### 2.2.3 MiniBatch Gradient Descent

The standard gradient descent (GD) method, also called batch descent method and defined as the one that uses the whole data to compute the gradient, is quantitatively discussed against the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) (that uses one sample at a time) in Y. A. LeCun et al. ([2012](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0196)). The GD method has several advantages. First, under some assumptions, the convergence of the algorithm is properly understood. Also, the conjugate gradient approach (Shewchuk [1994](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0314)) can be used to accelerate the convergence.

Nevertheless, the cost function landscape does not usually present a single minimum, but it may have many local minima. A batch gradient descent will converge to the minimum, which is closer to the initial position of the weights, which precludes finding the optimal solution. On the contrary, the use of SGD translates into a poor (often called noisy) estimation of the gradient, so at every iteration, the gradient will point to a different direction that, on average, would be the same as the one computed by the batch method. This turns out to be advantageous because it tends to avoid local minima, and it has been shown to converge to better solutions.

Also, in some structures, if the convergence rate is high enough, the algorithm can be adaptive, this is, if the distribution of the data changes with time (i.e. it is nonstationary), an SGD may track these changes. The disadvantage of the SGD is also inherent to this noisy convergence. Due to this, the convergence is not consistent in variance, that is, while the expected solution of the SGD is the same as the one of the gradient descent if they converge to the same minimum, the SGD will have a variance in the solution that depends on the learning rate.

A natural solution that takes advantage of both methods is the use of mini batches (Møller [1993](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0233); Orr [1996](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0254)). This consists of computing the gradient with a fraction or mini‐batch of the data, then making an update, choosing another fraction, and repeating the process until convergence. This reduces the noise, which provides a better convergence, and it reduces the risk of local minima. Besides, conjugate descent or second‐order methods can be applied when using mini‐batches. The methods described below usually take advantage of mini‐batch training.

 

## 2.3 Regularization Techniques

Any model's overall performance depends on its ability to generalize any new input data from the problem domain. In the case of convolutional neural network (CNN) and other deep learning models, bias error, and variance significantly influence the model's quantitative performance. The bias error is an error from incorrect assumptions in the learning algorithm and performs poorly on a training dataset. The algorithm fails to capture the relevant relations between features and target outputs and causes underfitting due to high bias. On the other hand, variance is an error from sensitivity to small fluctuations in the training set. A high variance may result in modeling the training data's random noise and overfitting. In both these cases, the model does not perform well with new unseen test data. A proper bias‐variance trade‐off is necessary to develop an optimal model that achieves better generalization. Regularization is an essential technique in machine learning that can prevent the model from overfitting and underfitting by minimizing these two sources of error. We can address underfitting by changing the structure of the model so that it can fit more types of functions for mapping inputs to outputs. It is more common to have an overfit model since it is easier to identify and resolve an underfit model. An overfit model can be diagnosed by either training the network on more samples or changing the model's complexity. The structure and parameters of a model define its complexity. The complexity reduces when there is either a change in the number or the value of weights. The regularization techniques penalize the coefficients of the features so that it will result in a simpler network. For example, in some instances, the regularization coefficient is so high that some weight matrices are nearly equal to zero. Thus, it reduces the significance of each feature by keeping the same number of features.

 

### 2.3.1 ![upper L 1](images/c02-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![upper L 2](images/c02-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> Regularization

The most popular ways of regularization are ![upper L 2](images/c02-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> and ![upper L 1](images/c02-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>. The concept underlying regularization is that smaller weights result in simpler models, which helps to minimize overfitting. So, to produce a smaller weight matrix, these methods incorporate a regularization term and add it to the loss function. The ![upper L 2](images/c02-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> regularization works by adding a norm penalty ![double-vertical-bar bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis Baseline double-vertical-bar Subscript upper F Superscript 2](images/c02-i0024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math> to the parameters of each layer (Hoerl and Kennard [1970](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0145)). This corresponds to the sum of squares of all feature weights to the loss function. The regularization rate ![lamda](images/c02-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> is the hyperparameter (defined as non‐trainable parameter) that weighs the regularization term. The ![upper L 2](images/c02-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> approach pushes the weight to decrease but never to zero. This strategy works best when all input attributes impact the output and all the weights are the same size (A. Y. Ng [2004](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0246)).

In the case of ![upper L 2](images/c02-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> regularization, when our training algorithm tries to minimize the new loss function ![upper J left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, it will lower both the original loss function ![upper J Subscript upper M upper L Baseline left-parenthesis theta right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and the regularization term as

In linear estimators, this is known as also known as ridge regression (Shawe‐Taylor and Cristianini [2004](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0313); Hastie [2020](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0120)), and it is a form of Tikhonov regularization (see Tikhonov and Arsenin [1977](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0352)).

The ![upper L 1](images/c02-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> regularization, also known as least absolute shrinkage and selector operator (Lasso) regression (Tibshirani [1996](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0351)), uses another regularization term ![double-vertical-bar bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis Baseline double-vertical-bar Subscript 1](images/c02-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math>, which is the sum of the absolute values of the weight parameters in a weight matrix. Unlike ![upper L 2](images/c02-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> regularization, this approach assigns zero weight to irrelevant input features and nonzero weight to important input features.

Choosing an appropriate value for ![lamda](images/c02-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> is necessary to achieve the right balance between low complexity and high accuracy. If a high value of ![lamda](images/c02-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> is chosen, the solution will be simple, but it will not contain sufficient information from the training data to produce efficient predictions. When the value of ![lamda](images/c02-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> is too low, the solution becomes increasingly complicated. It retains too much information about the data specificities, and it will not make accurate predictions on new data.

 

### 2.3.2 Dropout

Dropout regularization is a method in which specific neurons are deactivated randomly with probability ![p](images/c02-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> during training (N. Srivastava et al. [2014](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0330)). These randomly picked neurons are dropped out and temporarily removed from the network for the current forward pass, and no weight updates are made on the backward pass. During dropout, the remaining neurons will search for alternative paths to pass the information and provide predictions for the missing neurons. As a result, the network learns separate internal representations, making it less sensitive to the specific weight of the neurons. A network of this type is more generic and helps to minimize overfitting. For example, in [Fig. 2.3](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0003)a, the NN is fully connected; hence, all the neurons are active. While using this model for training, some neurons tend to memorize the patterns within the training data. Hence, without dropout, the model does not generalize well to the test data. In [Fig. 2.3](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0003)b, dropout enhances the sparsity of the network. This drives neurons to extract robust features from training data and also aids in eliminating co‐adaptations across neurons, allowing each neuron to function more independently.

In this section, the dropout is formulated for the dense NNs presented in [Chapter 1](#c01.xhtml), but the formulation can be straightforwardly adapted for any structure, in particular for the convolutional models presented in [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml).

The training of a NN with dropout is performed the following way. At each layer, a vector ![bold r Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0038.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> with binary components ![r Subscript j Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis Baseline tilde upper B e r n o u l l i left-parenthesis p right-parenthesis](images/c02-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is drawn at random from a Bernoulli distribution. This vector acts as an inhibitor for the nodes such that the forward operation of this layer becomes
