(4.6)](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0008).

 

### 4.3.2 Backpropagation of a Convolution Layer

The BP when using convolutional layers is analogous to the BP presented in [Chapter 1](#c01.xhtml). Indeed, a convolution layer operation is identical to the operation of a dense layer except for the fact that the connectivity is sparse. This can be easily illustrated with a figure. Assume a simple convolution layer where the input data has dimensions ![upper M Subscript upper I Baseline equals 8](images/c04-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math> and ![upper N Subscript upper I Baseline equals 1](images/c04-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, so the input is a vector. There is only an input and an output channel, and the kernel is a vector of dimension ![upper M Subscript upper W Baseline equals 2](images/c04-i0110.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>W</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. The stride applied to the convolution is ![s equals 2](images/c04-i0111.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> and then a pooling with ![q equals 2](images/c04-i0112.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. Graphically, the operation can be drawn as the one in [Fig. 4.9](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0009).

The first layer of the figure represents the input, and the connections from the first one to the second one represent the convolutions between the input and the kernel. Note that the connection weights are repeated since they represent the elements of the convolution kernel. A convolution would generate an output of ![upper N Subscript upper I Baseline minus upper N Subscript upper W plus 1 plus 7](images/c04-i0117.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>W</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn></math> elements, but since a stride of 2 is applied, then the output of the convolution has ![left floor StartFraction upper M Subscript upper I Baseline plus p minus upper M Subscript w Baseline plus s Over s EndFraction right floor equals 4](images/c04-i0118.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="&#8970;" close="&#8971;" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mi>s</mi></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math> elements, and only 8 out of the 32 possible connections are present. The convolution operation can be computed as operation ![bold-script í’² Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis Baseline Superscript down-tack Baseline bold h Superscript left-parenthesis l minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0119.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-script">&#54450;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> where in this case ![bold-script í’² Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-script">&#54450;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> would be a matrix with the form

The convolution is applied with a stride ![s equals 2](images/c04-i0115.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, and then a pooling of two pixels (![q equals 2](images/c04-i0116.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>) is added.

The next layer represents the pooling, which takes two adjacent pixels and outputs one. The resulting output has two pixels. This connection is also sparse since only 4 out of 8 possible connections exist.

During the BP process, the objective is to approximate solutions that satisfy

where superindex ![l](images/c04-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> is the index for layer *k*, and the subindexes are the indexes of the elements of arrays ![bold upper W](images/c04-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold upper B](images/c04-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi></mrow></math> by applying a gradient descent procedure as explained in Section [1.5.3](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0025). The computation of the gradients in a convolutional layer is analogous. Let us consider convolutional layer ![l](images/c04-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> where the input is array ![bold upper H Subscript j Superscript left-parenthesis l minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0125.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> and the output is ![bold upper Z Subscript k Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> corresponding to input channel ![j](images/c04-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> and output channel ![k](images/c04-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>.

We can compute derivatives ([4.10](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0012)) for this particular case in a very straightforward way by taking into account that the convolution layer is a sparse version of a standard layer, so we can compute the convolution as a normal layer linear operation.

Assuming that a CNN has ![upper L Subscript upper C](images/c04-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>C</mi></msub></math> convolutional layers and ![upper L Subscript upper D](images/c04-i0130.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></math> dense layers, and by using the same reasonings as in [Section 1.5.3](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0025) we can arrive at an algorithm for the CNN BP. where in ![bold-italic phi Subscript f Baseline left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#981;</mi></mrow><mi>f</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> the subindex stands for *flattening*. This is the activation of the last convolutional layer, and therefore, this activation includes, besides the nonlinear function and the pooling, a flattening operation that maps all the pixels of the results of the convolutions into a vector, that is, then processed by the first dense layer. In other words, operation ![bold-italic phi Subscript f Baseline left-parenthesis bold upper Z Superscript left-parenthesis upper L Super Subscript upper C Superscript right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#981;</mi></mrow><mi>f</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Z</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfenced></math> produces output vector ![bold h Superscript left-parenthesis upper L Super Subscript upper C Superscript right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>.

In this expression, we see the output, which is generated after the activation of the linear operation performed by array ![bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis upper L Super Subscript upper C Superscript plus upper L Super Subscript upper D Superscript right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>, which is the set of parameters of the last dense layers and the activation output of the previous layer. The first dense layer is the one with an index ![upper L Subscript upper C Baseline plus 1](images/c04-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. Before that, the machine has convolutional layers with the arrays of kernels ![bold upper W Superscript l](images/c04-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mi>l</mi></msup></math>, ![l less-than-or-equal-to upper L Subscript upper C](images/c04-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>C</mi></msub></math>. ### 4.3.3 Forward Step in a CNN

Assume, for example, that a given batch of input samples ![bold upper X Subscript i Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper C Super Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis Superscript times upper D italic 1 Super Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis Superscript times upper D italic 2 Super Superscript left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0140.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#215;</mo><msubsup><mi>D</mi><mi>1</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#215;</mo><msubsup><mi>D</mi><mi>2</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></msup></math>, ![1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper N](images/c04-i0141.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>N</mi></math> and their corresponding labels ![bold y Subscript i](images/c04-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> are available for training purposes. Then, the forward step must be applied to the CNN for each one of these samples. In particular, all outputs of all layers for each one of the samples must be computed, i.e. we need to store outputs ![bold upper Z Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> and ![bold upper H Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> for all convolutional layers, and ![bold z Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>, ![bold h Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis l right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>, and ![bold o Subscript i](images/c04-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> for the dense layers and the output. Besides, all output errors ![bold-italic delta Subscript i Superscript left-parenthesis upper L Super Subscript upper C Superscript plus upper L Super Subscript upper D Superscript right-parenthesis Baseline equals bold o Subscript i Baseline minus bold y Subscript i](images/c04-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#948;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, which must be computed and stored.

The backward procedure is the same as in a standard NN, and it is described in Subsections [4.3.4](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0015) and [4.3.5](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0016).

To formulate the algorithm, it is necessary to backpropagate error ![bold-italic delta Superscript left-parenthesis upper L Super Subscript upper C Superscript plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0157.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#948;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> to ![bold upper Delta Superscript left-parenthesis upper L Super Subscript upper C Superscript right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0158.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#916;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>. This is straightforward if we remember that the last convolutional layer performs a pooling and then a flattening. Therefore, to backpropagate the error, it is necessary to undo the flattening and then undo the pooling (by filling with zeros the positions not selected by the pooling), to find an error ![bold upper Delta Superscript left-parenthesis upper L Super Subscript upper C Superscript plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0159.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#916;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> with the same dimensions as ![bold upper H Superscript left-parenthesis upper L Super Subscript upper C Superscript plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>. The pooling cannot be reversed, and therefore, to increase the dimensions to the same values as they were before the pooling, we just need to change the positions of ![bold upper Delta Superscript left-parenthesis upper L Super Subscript upper C Superscript plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#916;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> corresponding to the positions discarded by max‐pooling or to repeat the error values in the case that average pooling was applied. Then, the convolutional section BP applied over a batch of ![upper N](images/c04-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> samples is for all convolutional layers ![upper L Subscript upper C Baseline greater-than-or-equal-to l greater-than-or-equal-to 1](images/c04-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> as follows:

## 4.4 Extensions of the CNN

CNNs have revolutionized the field of computer vision, especially in the field of object recognition and other visual‐related applications. The ability of CNNs to extract hierarchical features from input data has made them quite popular, mainly in processing images. Researchers have explored different approaches to extend and enhance the traditional CNN architecture to tackle new challenges (M. Ajith and Calhoun [2023](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0007)), each time improving the model performance in specific domains.

We will be going over a spectrum of such extensions and will explore more about the advantages and disadvantages of these architectures. Throughout the section, we will provide an overview of the different kinds of CNNs that were inspired by traditional architecture for solving complex challenges associated with image classification problems. The ability of these structures to efficiently process information at multiscale levels, especially in extracting meaningful features also helped with improved the interpretability of the model results and the features extracted. This indeed proved to be useful in various domains/applications. These extensions continue to be popular in different domains such as medical imaging (A. R. Kurup et al. [2023](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0188); Maqsood et al. [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0219); Marcus et al. [2010](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0220); Byra et al. [2020](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0050)), object detection (Zhiqiang and Jun [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0397); M. Ajith and A. R. Kurup [2018](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0008); Duan et al. [2012](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0083)), natural language processing (Wróbel et al. [2020](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0377); Moriya and Shibata [2018](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0235)), or solar energy applications (M. Ajith and Manel Martínez‐Ramón [2023](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0011)).

 

### 4.4.1 AlexNet

AlexNet takes its name from Alex Krizhevsky, who introduced it in 2012 in collaboration with Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton (Alex Krizhevsky et al. [2012](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0182)). It was able to solve the problem of image classification on the ImageNet database consisting of 1000 different classes. Hence, this network was able to win the ImageNet ImageNet large scale visual recognition challenge (ILSVRC)‐2012 competition with the highest accuracy. Its structure is shown in [Fig. 4.12](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0012).

![Figure 4.12 Alexnet architecture.](images/c04f012.png)

[**Figure 4.12**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0012) Alexnet architecture.

The red–green–blue (RGB) images with dimensions ![224 times 224 times 3](images/c04-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>224</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>224</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> are passed through a set of 96 convolution kernels with dimensions ![11 times 11 times 3](images/c04-i0174.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>11</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> to produce 96 outputs. The convolutions include a stride of 4 pixels. Each element of the outputs is passed through a ReLU function. The dimensions of each one of the convolution outputs are ![left floor left-parenthesis 224 minus 11 plus 4 right-parenthesis slash 4 right floor equals 54](images/c04-i0175.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8970;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>224</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>&#8971;</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>54</mn></math>, but authors report dimensions of ![55 times 55](images/c04-i0176.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>55</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>55</mn></math>, which may be produced by padding of 3 pixels.

In the overall architecture, initially, an input image of size ![224 times 224 times 3](images/c04-i0177.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>224</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>224</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> is given to the first convolutional layer. This input is convolved using 96 kernels of size ![11 times 11 times 3](images/c04-i0178.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>11</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> and stride 4. The second convolutional layer on the other hand used 256 kernels of size ![5 times 5 times 48](images/c04-i0179.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>48</mn></math>. The following three convolutional layers are linked together without any pooling layers. The third and fourth convolutional layers have 384 kernels of size ![3 times 3 times 256](images/c04-i0180.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>256</mn></math> and ![3 times 3 times 192](images/c04-i0181.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>192</mn></math>, respectively. Finally, the fifth convolutional layer contains 256 kernels of size ![3 times 3 times 192](images/c04-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>192</mn></math>, and each of the FC layers has 4096 neurons.

The AlexNet paper introduced several novelties such as data augmentation, dropout, ReLU, overlapping pooling, and multi‐GPU training. Both data augmentation and dropout were developed to eliminate the overfitting problem. While performing data augmentation, the network was given different variations of the same image. This strategy is used while training the models to increase the heterogeneity of the available data without gathering new data. Specifically, they increased the size of the data by a factor of 2048 by extracting random patches from the images and altering the intensities of the RGB channels.

Dropout was another technique introduced by Geoffrey E. Hinton in 2012 for preventing overfitting (Geoffrey E. Hinton et al. [2012b](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0139)). In dropout, a neuron is dropped from the network with a predetermined probability (see Subsection 2.3.2). Every iteration uses a different network architecture, which forces each neuron to have more robust features. However, the number of iterations needed for the model's convergence is increased during dropout.

Previously, sigmoidal activation functions were the standard way of introducing nonlinearity to the CNN. But in AlexNet, the ReLU activation (see [Section 1.4](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0016)) was used for this purpose. The training time of ReLU‐based CNNs was faster than compared to tanh or logistic activation functions. Since they are saturating nonlinear functions, they have a compact range between ![negative 1](images/c04-i0183.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> or 0 and 1, whereas ReLU does not exhibit any restraints at its boundaries, thereby resulting in faster training.

Another unique feature of AlexNet is overlapping pooling so that the adjacent kernels over which the max is computed overlap each other. The traditional CNN used pooling layers without overlapping for downsampling the features. In AlexNet, the overlapping max‐pooling layers helped to reduce the error rates of the classifier and avoided overfitting. Moreover, AlexNet used the ImageNet dataset that had roughly 1.2 million training images. To avoid the memory issue and increase the training time, multiple GPUs were used for training this network.

 

### 4.4.2 VGG

The visual geometric group (VGG) is another classic CNN network named after the research group from Oxford University that developed the architecture for the network. This network was developed in the year 2014 by Karen Simonyan and Andrew Zisserman ([2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0320)). This network was the second place holder in the ILSVRC 2014 competition.

The main idea of the VGG nets was to see the effect of the depth of the convolutional network on the accuracy in large‐scale image recognition settings. Smaller convolutional filters were used in this network, which allowed the increased depth of the network by adding more weight layers.

The VGG architecture consists of a stack of convolutional layers through which the images are passed. The network uses convolutional filters of relatively smaller size and is significantly deeper in structure compared to previously developed structures using smaller convolutions (Ciresan et al. [2011](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0062)). The framework has five max‐pooling layers with a window size of ![2 times 2](images/c04-i0184.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>2</mn></math> and a stride of 2. The max‐pooling layers follow only a few convolutional layers and not all convolutional layers. The VGG architecture has three FC layers. The first two FC layers have 4096 nodes, the last one has 1000 nodes for each class, and the final layer uses a softmax activation.

The VGG framework was the first network to use a *preprocessing block* where the input size of the RGB images is cropped to 224 ![times](images/c04-i0185.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#215;</mo></mrow></math> 224 during training. The mean RGB value computed on the training set is subtracted from each pixel. Second, they use *smaller receptive fields* or kernels of ![3 times 3](images/c04-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> in the convolutional layers compared to the ones of ALexNets and their derivatives. The idea is that instead of using large receptive fields such as ![11 times 11](images/c04-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>11</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>11</mn></math> (Alex Krizhevsky et al. [2012](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0182)) and ![7 times 7](images/c04-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>7</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>7</mn></math> (Matthew D. Zeiler and Fergus [2014](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0389); Sermanet et al. [2013](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0311)), the same operation can be achieved by stacking the smaller ![3 times 3](images/c04-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> convolutional layers. The ![3 times 3](images/c04-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> layer stacked twice can be equally effective as that of a ![5 times 5](images/c04-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn></math> receptive field. Similarly, the ![7 times 7](images/c04-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>7</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>7</mn></math> receptive field can be replaced using 3 stacked ![3 times 3](images/c04-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> convolutional layers. In addition, the structure also incorporates ![1 times 1](images/c04-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> convolutions, which act as a linear transformation of the inputs. These units are then followed by ReLU activations (Alex Krizhevsky et al. [2012](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0182)) for introducing nonlinearity. The stride for convolutions is set to 1.

The spatial resolution is preserved while performing padding of inputs. This is done by padding using just 1 pixel for ![3 times 3](images/c04-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> convolutional layers. The depth of the network is another key feature. The depth of the structure is varied by adding more weight layers. There are six different versions based on the number of weight layers in the network. The initial version had 11 weight layers which were increased to 16 layers (VGG‐16) ([Fig. 4.13](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0013)) and lastly 19 layers (VGG‐19). VGG‐16 and VGG‐19 were the most popular ones. The configurations were varied mainly by adding the convolutional layers. The FC layer remained the same for all the different versions.

![Figure 4.13 VGG‐16 architecture.](images/c04f013.png)

[**Figure 4.13**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0013) VGG‐16 architecture.

 

### 4.4.3 Inception

The Inception‐v1/GoogLeNet is a CNN architecture with 22 layers and 5M parameters (Szegedy et al. [2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0339)). It was the winner of the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Competition in 2014. The previous CNN models were focused on going deeper to improve accuracy, but this compromised the computational cost of these networks. The Inception‐v1 network consists of recurring blocks of convolutional designs called Inception modules that make it wider. A naive inception module performs max‐pooling and ![1 times 1](images/c04-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, ![3 times 3](images/c04-i0197.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> and ![5 times 5](images/c04-i0198.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn></math> convolutions on the input. The final outputs are generated after passing them through the concatenation layer. But the ![3 times 3](images/c04-i0199.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> and ![5 times 5](images/c04-i0200.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn></math> convolutions were computationally expensive. Hence, dimensionality reduction was necessary, and it was achieved by incorporating ![1 times 1](images/c04-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> convolutions. The total number of layers utilized in the network's design is around 100, and a ReLU activation is used in all convolutions, including those inside the Inception modules. Toward the end of the architecture, the global average pooling layer replaced the FC layers, which further reduced the number of parameters and increased the top‐1 accuracy by 0.6%. Thus, the complexity of the model was reduced to a great extent without decreasing the speed and accuracy.

The Inception‐v1 contains the ![1 times 1](images/c04-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> convolutions that were first introduced in the Network In Network paper by Min Lin in 2013 (M. Lin et al. [2014a](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0202)). The ![1 times 1](images/c04-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> convolutional layer was used to decrease the number of parameters by reducing the number of channels. Its activation function also added nonlinearity to the model. For example, consider the following operations in which we convolve ![28 times 28 times 64](images/c04-i0204.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>28</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>28</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>64</mn></math> input feature maps with ![5 times 5 times 32](images/c04-i0205.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>32</mn></math> filters. Here the total no. of parameters ![equals left-parenthesis 28 times 28 times 32 right-parenthesis times left-parenthesis 5 times 5 times 64 right-parenthesis equals 40](images/c04-i0206.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>28</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>28</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>32</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>64</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn></math> million operations. Repeat the operations with the same input feature maps but with a ![1 times 1](images/c04-i0207.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> layer before the ![5 times 5](images/c04-i0208.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn></math> convolutional layer. The total no. of parameters ![equals left-parenthesis 28 times 28 times 16 right-parenthesis times left-parenthesis 1 times 1 times 32 right-parenthesis plus left-parenthesis 28 times 28 times 32 right-parenthesis times left-parenthesis 5 times 5 times 16 right-parenthesis equals 10](images/c04-i0209.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>28</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>28</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>16</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>32</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>28</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>28</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>32</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>16</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math> million operations. Hence, the use of ![1 times 1](images/c04-i0210.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> convolutions has reduced the number of operations by a factor of 4.

Additionally, the Inception‐v1 network introduced two auxiliary classifiers to prevent the vanishing gradient problem. An auxiliary loss was computed by applying a softmax activation at the output of the inception module, and this loss was added to the main network loss. Other variations of inception such as Inception‐v2 (Ioffe and Szegedy [2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0158)), Inception‐v3 ([Fig. 4.14](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0014)) (Szegedy et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0340)), and Inception‐v4 (Szegedy et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0341)) were introduced in the later years to curb the limitations of the initial version.

![Figure 4.14 Inception‐v3 architecture.](images/c04f014.png)

[**Figure 4.14**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0014) Inception‐v3 architecture.

 

### 4.4.4 ResNet

The residual neural network (ResNet) was a CNN architecture introduced in the year 2015 (He et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0126)). These structures were the winner of localization, ImageNet detection, segmentation, and detection in the 2015 common objects in context (COCO) and ILSVRC competitions. These structures were successful in providing great generalization performance on image recognition tasks. The idea of ResNet was to develop an efficient way to curb the huge problem of vanishing gradients (Yoshua Bengio et al. [1994](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0027); Glorot and Yoshua Bengio [2010](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0103)) associated with training deeper networks which indeed affects the convergence. Previously, this problem was addressed using normalized initialization (Y. A. LeCun et al. [2012](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0196); Glorot and Yoshua Bengio [2010](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0103); He et al. [2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0125)) and intermediate normalization layers (Ioffe and Szegedy [2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0158)). These techniques were able to make the networks with a significant number of layers converge using SGD and BP (Y. LeCun et al. [1989](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0194)). The convergence was achieved, but there was another problem called the *degradation* problem whereas the network depth increases, the accuracy starts getting saturated and degrades rapidly later on (He et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0126)). This resulted in higher training error after adding more layers to a deeper model compared to their shallower counterparts (He and J. Sun [2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0124)).

ResNet was the first network to introduce residual learning and skip connections skipping one or more weight layers to solve the degradation problem. The idea was that instead of jumping through the stacked layers try to fit a residual mapping. For example, if the original mapping before adding the skip connection was ![upper F Subscript l Baseline left-parenthesis x Subscript l minus i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0211.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, then after skipping connection it will fit ![upper G Subscript l Baseline left-parenthesis x Subscript l minus i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0212.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, i.e. the stacked nonlinear layers will fit another mapping ![upper F Subscript l Baseline left-parenthesis x Subscript l minus i Baseline right-parenthesis equals upper G Subscript l Baseline left-parenthesis x Subscript l minus i Baseline right-parenthesis minus x Subscript l minus i](images/c04-i0213.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>, where ![l](images/c04-i0214.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> is the layer index and ![i](images/c04-i0215.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> is the total number of layers skipped. The original mapping is hence transformed to ![upper F Subscript l Baseline left-parenthesis x Subscript l minus i Baseline right-parenthesis plus x Subscript l minus i](images/c04-i0216.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math>. This is shown in [Fig. 4.15](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0015) Using this technique, the optimization became simpler as it was easier to learn the residual mapping than the original underlying mapping. The connections are *identity mapping*, which is then added to the output of the stacked layers. These identity mappings do not add to the computational complexities, hence the number of parameters before and after remains the same. Through this concept, the structures were able to be successfully trained for 100s and 1000s of layers.

![Figure 4.15 Resnet‐34 architecture. Adapted from He, X. Zhang, et al., 2016 / IEEE.](images/c04f015.png)

[**Figure 4.15**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0015) Resnet‐34 architecture. Adapted from He, X. Zhang, et al., [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0126) / IEEE.

Other networks also used the shorter skip connections, in particular, gated shortcut connections such as highway network (R. K. Srivastava et al. [2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0331)) and long short term memory (LSTM) (Schmidhuber and Hochreiter [1997](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0305)). ResNets were very popular among them due to their capability of training very deep networks going up to 1001 layers, outperforming their shallower counterparts.

 

### 4.4.5 Xception

Xception was inspired by the concept of the Inception network introduced in [4.4.3](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0021). The Xception network was introduced by a Google researcher, Francois Chollet in 2017 (Chollet [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0060)), and it used the idea of depthwise separable convolutions by taking the concept of Inception to the extreme.

The Inception module introduced in Inception‐V3 made use of ![1 times 1](images/c04-i0217.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> convolutions to capture cross‐channel correlations, and the spatial correlations were learned using the regular ![3 times 3](images/c04-i0218.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> or ![5 times 5](images/c04-i0219.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn></math> operations as shown in Fig.  [4.16](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0016). This idea of the Inception module can be reformed to have the input passed through ![1 times 1](images/c04-i0220.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> convolution followed by just one particular size convolution for example: of ![3 times 3](images/c04-i0221.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> as shown in Fig.  [4.17](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0017).

![Figure 4.16 Inception module as in Inception‐V3.](images/c04f016.png)

[**Figure 4.16**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0016) Inception module as in Inception‐V3.

![Figure 4.17 “Extreme” version of the Inception Module as described in \[?\].](images/c04f017.png)

[**Figure 4.17**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0017) “Extreme” version of the Inception Module as described in \[?\].

This version can be considered the “extreme version” of Inception. This version of the Inception module is close to the depthwise separable convolution operation. The concept of depthwise separable convolutions was introduced in Sifre and Mallat ([2014](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0319)) in 2014. These operations were also incorporated into programming frameworks such as TensorFlow in 2016 (Abadi et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0001)). Depthwise separable convolution has two parts: depthwise convolution followed by pointwise convolution. Depthwise convolution performs spatial convolutions independently on each of the channels of the input. Pointwise convolution performs a ![1 times 1](images/c04-i0222.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> convolutional operation. This operation helps with projecting the output to a new channel space.

The Xception architecture shown in [Fig. 4.18](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0018) consists of 36 convolutional layers organized into 14 different modules. The stacked linear layers make use of depthwise separable convolutions. These modules include residual connections around them which are linear. The convolutional base is followed by a layer dedicated to logistic regression. The experiments were also evaluated for a configuration where a FC layer was also introduced ahead of a logistic regression layer. The number of parameters was nearly the same for both Inception V3 and Xception. The comparison between the models was done using two image classification setups: the famous single‐labeled 1000‐class classification on the ImageNet dataset and the 17000‐class test for performing multilabel classification on the JFT dataset. The JFT dataset was an internal Google dataset first introduced in (Geoffrey E. Hinton et al. [2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0141)). The dataset contains 350 million images with labels corresponding to 17000 classes. For both datasets, different optimization configuration was set. In both cases, the Xception architecture showed significant improvement in performance with a higher margin for the JFT dataset.

 

### 4.4.6 MobileNet

MobileNets (Howard et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0151)) represent a class of efficient CNN models specifically designed for mobile and embedded vision applications. The first version of MobileNets was introduced by Google in 2017. These models leverage a novel convolutional layer called depthwise separable convolution, which was later adopted in advanced Inception models. This approach significantly reduces computational demands and model size compared to other well‐known CNN architectures. MobileNets are characterized by their compactness, speed, and efficiency, and they find utility across a diverse range of applications, including object detection, fine‐grain classification, face attribute analysis, and large‐scale geo‐localization. The key features of MobileNets are

![Figure 4.18 Xception architecture.](images/c04f018.png)

[**Figure 4.18**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0018) Xception architecture.

 

#### 4.4.6.1 Depthwise Separable Convolutions

The MobileNet model utilizes a convolution technique known as depth‐wise separable convolutions. This method breaks down a standard convolution operation into two distinct steps: a depthwise convolution and a pointwise convolution with a ![1 times 1](images/c04-i0223.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> kernel. The depthwise convolution applies a single filter to each input channel, and then the pointwise convolution employs a ![1 times 1](images/c04-i0224.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> convolution to combine the results of the depthwise convolution (refer to [Fig. 4.19](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0019)). In contrast, a standard convolution carries out filtering and combining inputs in a single step. Depthwise separable convolutions effectively divide this process into two separate layers: one for filtering and another for merging inputs. This factorization technique brings about significant advantages, notably reducing computational demands and the overall size of the model.

![Figure 4.19 MobileNet architecture.](images/c04f019.png)

[**Figure 4.19**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0019) MobileNet architecture.

 

#### 4.4.6.2 Width Multiplier

The width multiplier parameter which is represented as ![alpha](images/c04-i0225.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> was introduced to achieve an even smaller and faster MobileNet model. The purpose of this width multiplier ![alpha](images/c04-i0226.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> was to uniformly reduce the network's width at each layer. For any given layer and width multiplier ![alpha](images/c04-i0227.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>, the number of input channels ![upper M](images/c04-i0228.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> becomes ![alpha upper M](images/c04-i0229.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>M</mi></math>, and the number of output channels ![upper N](images/c04-i0230.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> becomes ![alpha upper N](images/c04-i0231.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>N</mi></math>. The width multiplier takes values in the range (0, 1\], with typical settings being 1, 0.75, 0.5, and 0.25. When ![alpha](images/c04-i0232.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> equals 1, it represents the baseline MobileNet, and for ![alpha less-than 1](images/c04-i0233.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, it corresponds to reduced MobileNets. The width multiplier has the effect of quadratically reducing computational cost and the number of parameters by approximately ![alpha squared](images/c04-i0234.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math>.

 

#### 4.4.6.3 Resolution Multiplier

The resolution multiplier ![gamma](images/c04-i0235.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> serves as an additional parameter used to reduce the computational demands of MobileNets. It is applied uniformly to shrink both the input image and the internal representation of each layer. In practical terms, ![gamma](images/c04-i0236.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> is initially set according to the desired input resolution, allowing for flexible adjustments based on the level of computational efficiency you aim to achieve. The resolution multiplier ![gamma](images/c04-i0237.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> falls within the range of (0, 1\], which results in the input resolution of the network being set to values such as 224, 192, 160, or 128. When ![gamma](images/c04-i0238.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> is equal to 1, it corresponds to the standard MobileNet, while ![gamma](images/c04-i0239.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> values less than 1 represent MobileNets with reduced computational requirements. The resolution multiplier has the effect of reducing computational cost by a factor of ![gamma squared](images/c04-i0240.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math>.

MobileNets represent a computationally efficient CNN architecture, making them suitable for resource‐constrained devices. These models are known for their compact size, making them easy to deploy on devices with limited memory and storage capacity. Users can fine‐tune width multiplier, and resolution multiplier parameters to balance computational cost and model performance, making MobileNets adaptable to various scenarios. However, their compactness may limit their capacity for complex tasks, and aggressive parameter reductions can lead to trade‐offs in model size versus performance. Nonetheless, MobileNet remains a compelling choice for achieving efficient deep learning inference on mobile platforms.

 

### 4.4.7 DenseNet

DenseNet was developed by Cornell Uni, Tsinghua Uni, and Facebook Research in 2017 for visual object recognition (G. Huang et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0154)). In most CNN architectures, due to the depth of the network, the information flow from input to output is disrupted and the model experiences the vanishing gradient problem. DenseNets were created to exploit the full potential of deep CNNs by applying feature reuse. Despite being similar to ResNets, the DenseNets improve accuracy by concatenating the feature maps from various layers. The mathematical formulation is shown in the below equation:

![Figure 4.20 DenseNet architecture.](images/c04f020.png)

[**Figure 4.20**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0020) DenseNet architecture.

(4.18)![f Superscript l Baseline equals upper F Superscript l Baseline left-parenthesis left-bracket f Superscript 0 Baseline comma f Superscript 1 Baseline comma f squared comma period period period period period f Superscript l minus 1 Baseline right-bracket right-parenthesis](images/c04-math-0021.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>f</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mspace width="0.1em"/><msup><mi>f</mi><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mspace width="0.2em"/><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

where ![upper F Subscript l](images/c04-i0241.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></math> corresponds to the function that concatenates the output feature maps of the previous layers. This function can be a combination of operations such as batch normalization, ReLU, pooling, or convolution. The feature maps of all preceding layers, i.e. ![f Superscript 0 Baseline comma f Superscript 1 Baseline comma f squared comma period period period period period f Superscript l minus 1](images/c04-i0242.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>f</mi><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mspace width="0.2em"/><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> are sent into the ![l](images/c04-i0243.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math>th layer ![f Superscript l](images/c04-i0244.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>f</mi><mi>l</mi></msup></math>.

The key features of DenseNet are (see [Fig. 4.20](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0020)):

*   **Dense blocks**: DenseNets are composed of several dense blocks with ![n](images/c04-i0245.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> dense layers. Each dense layer is made up of ![1 times 1](images/c04-i0246.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and ![3 times 3](images/c04-i0247.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> convolutions. The dense layer receives input from the preceding feature maps, which are then passed on to the subsequent layers. The number of filters in the convolutional layers changes with each dense block, while the size of the feature maps stays constant. Transition layers are the layers that exist between dense blocks. If a dense block comprises ![m](images/c04-i0248.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> feature maps, the transition layer creates ![theta m](images/c04-i0249.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>m</mi></math> output feature maps, where ![0 less-than theta less-than-or-equal-to 1](images/c04-i0250.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. As a result, it aids in reducing the number of feature maps and improving the model's compactness.
*   **Growth rate**: The number of parameters and model complexity are determined by the initial number of feature maps. If each function ![upper F Superscript l](images/c04-i0251.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>F</mi><mi>l</mi></msup></math> generates ![k](images/c04-i0252.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> feature maps, the ![l](images/c04-i0253.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math>th layer must have ![k Superscript 0 Baseline plus k times left-parenthesis l minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0254.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>k</mi><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> input feature maps, where ![k Superscript 0](images/c04-i0255.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>k</mi><mn>0</mn></msup></math> is the number of channels in the input layer. Here ![k](images/c04-i0256.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is the hyperparameter which denotes the growth rate. This means that for each layer added, we add ![k](images/c04-i0257.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> additional feature maps to the overall number of feature maps and hence the total number of parameters. The feature maps may be viewed as the network's overall state. The authors have used a ![k](images/c04-i0258.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> value of 32 for all the experiments. These 32 feature maps are concatenated and fed as input to the next layer. Consequently, the growth rate governs how much new information each layer contributes to the overall system.
    
    The main advantages of DenseNets include the requirement of fewer parameters for creating compact models that deliver state‐of‐the‐art performances. Additionally, the network is also parameter efficient; a 250‐layer model has just 15.3M parameters; and it outperforms models with more than 30M parameters, such as FractalNet and Wide ResNets. DenseNets can also extend to hundreds of layers while posing no optimization challenges. This structure produces constant improvements in accuracy as the number of parameters increases, with no indications of performance deterioration or overfitting. Furthermore, DenseNets require significantly fewer parameters and less computation to achieve state‐of‐the‐art performance.
    

 

### 4.4.8 EfficientNet

EfficientNet was the latest model introduced by Tan and Q. Le ([2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0343)) in this series of image classification CNN architectures. EfficientNets were able to efficiently scale up ResNet and MobileNets using a compound coefficient scaling model as shown in [Fig. 4.21](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0021). The results were evaluated on different state‐of‐the‐art datasets. The common practice of model scaling was focused on increasing the number of layers depthwise or width‐wise. Another approach was to introduce only high‐resolution images as inputs for improved performance. But, in both these cases the requirement of manual tuning becomes huge. The idea of EfficientNet was to scale up the CNNs using a more structured approach without compromising efficiency and performance.

The models analyzed the effect of scaling each of the dimensions in the network with respect to a fixed resource constraint. The baseline network was evaluated under the same condition for different scaling options which gave the scaling coefficient. The scaling coefficient is further used to scale up the model size and also to keep the computational cost minimal.

The base model plays a key role in determining the effectiveness of the model scaling approach. Additionally, using the neural architecture search approach (Wistuba et al. [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0373)) using the AutoML mobile neural architecture search (MNAS) (Tan et al. [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0344)) framework, a new base network was developed. The resulting model was similar to MNasNET and MobileNetV2 in structure but was larger in terms of higher FLOPs. The baseline model was scaled up using the compound coefficient scaling approach to obtain the family of EfficientNet models. The scaling approach was able to give an improvement in performance with respect to ResNet, DenseNet, Inception, etc. Hence, the EfficientNet family of models gave a good performance and model efficiency.

![Figure 4.21 EfficientNet architecture.](images/c04f021.png)

[**Figure 4.21**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0021) EfficientNet architecture.

 

### 4.4.9 Transfer Learning for CNN Extensions

Most of the above‐mentioned CNN extensions are heavy models and hence training them from scratch can be computationally expensive. Therefore, these models are trained commonly in a computationally simpler way using *Transfer Learning*. Transfer learning is an approach that uses the principle idea of helping machine learning algorithms to improve the performance in the domain of interest by borrowing labeled data or extracting knowledge from related domains (Pan [2014](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0256)). Transfer learning can be defined as a machine learning technique that incorporates additional information apart from the knowledge gained from the training data which may be from one or more related domains. The approach focuses on the idea of reusing previously learned knowledge (Pan and Q. Yang [2009](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0257)) and transferring the knowledge across domains (Zhuang et al. [2020](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0400)).

In real‐world scenarios, we can find many examples of transfer learning. For example, knowledge gained from playing the ukelele might help you with learning other instruments such as guitar and piano. A person having some musical background can learn musical instruments faster compared to someone who is not familiar with the background. In such a case, a person learning knowledge from a particular background is extending it or transferring it to learn a related task. Similarly, in machine learning, we can leverage the knowledge gained in one domain to be shared and applied in a related domain of interest. Now, in machine learning, this can be viewed as the train data and target data being in two different subdomains, with them being linked by a common higher‐level domain which gives a foundation on how the subdomains are related (K. Weiss et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0367)).

This kind of knowledge engineering using transfer learning is beneficial when it comes to fields where the data gets outdated frequently or fields where the data availability is low. The lack of sufficient training data poses difficulty in training such models efficiently. In such cases, the reuse of training data or extracted knowledge in related domains can be of great use for improving the performance of the system. The transfer learning idea has been implemented across different domains such as for object detection problems (M. Ajith and A. R. Kurup [2018](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0008)), in image classification (M. Ajith and Manel Martínez‐Ramón [2021](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0010), [2023](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0011)), text classification (Harel and Mannor [2010](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0119)), in medical fields (A. Kurup et al. [2020](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0187)), image segmentation, and sentiment classification (C. Wang and Mahadevan [2011](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0363)).

There are two different types of transfer learning: Homogeneous and heterogeneous (Pan [2014](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0256)). Homogenous transfer learning directly correlates to a big data environment. The idea is to avoid the collection of more data samples and use the available resources from a domain to build predictive models for other target domains. Homogeneous transfer learning has overlapping feature space across both the source domain and target domain, and even the label spaces between the categories/tasks will be identical. Further, the homogeneous approaches can be subcategorized as instance‐based, feature‐based, relational‐based, and parameter‐based. These subcategories are based on the type of transfer of the model. As for heterogeneous transfer learning, the feature spaces are also heterogeneous, and they come from different domains with the labels being nonidentical.

The heterogeneous transfer learning problems are solved using two main approaches: symmetric transformations and asymmetric transformations. In the case of symmetric transformation, both the source and target domains are separately transformed into a common latent feature space. The asymmetrical transformation aims at transforming the source and target instances of the same class without having context feature bias (K. Weiss et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0367)). In most of the heterogeneous scenarios, an initial assumption is made that the source and target instances are coming from the same domain and do not have any difference in distributions.

Now let us look into an example of transfer learning using the CNN extension. The example here depicts a homogeneous transfer learning approach where we are using a pretrained model learned on a larger dataset (ImageNet dataset) sharing a similar feature space as that of the training inputs to adapt to a new dataset. For using the CNN architecture for transfer learning, we remove the top layers of the model and freeze the rest of the layers which constitute the base model. The base model uses the pretrained weights obtained from the model trained on the large ImageNet database which has previously learned knowledge. This knowledge is transferred using a transfer learning approach to learn features that could help classification in the new dataset.

 

### 4.4.10 Comparisons Among CNN Extensions

The advent of AlexNet, which included the ReLU activation layer, started the emergence of deep learning in image classification in 2012. The use of a CNN in image classification improved the accuracy while minimizing the need to manually feature engineer each image. Following AlexNet, various CNN architectures were developed with more characteristics to efficiently categorize images. The accuracy of an algorithm for a classification task is the measure of the number of accurate predictions divided by the total number of data points. Now, in the case of the top‐1 accuracy, you check if the predicted class with the highest probability is the same as the actual label. In the case of the top‐5 accuracy, you check if the target label is one of your top 5 predictions, i.e. the ones with the highest probabilities. For example, consider a sentiment analysis machine learning classification task with seven classes such as anger, surprise, sadness, happiness, neutral, fear, and disgust. Let the image containing fear emotion be present during the test, and the output predictions of the classification model have the probabilities such as anger – 0.4, sadness – 0.2, fear – 0.3, happiness – 0.04, disgust – 0.03, neutral – 0.01, and surprise – 0.02. Here it can be seen while using top‐1 accuracy, the output is counted as incorrect since it predicted anger. While using top‐5 accuracy, the output is correct, as fear is among the top‐5 predictions. Hence, in a classification problem with *k* possible labels, every classifier has 100% top‐*k* accuracy. In the ImageNet classification problem, top‐1, and top‐5 accuracies are important units for evaluating the performance of the various models (see [Fig. 4.26](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0026) and [Fig. 4.27](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0027)). In 2012, AlexNet competed in the ImageNet challenge and easily outperformed all prior nondeep learning‐based models. It was trained on a GTX580 GPU with 3GB of RAM. In the ImageNet large scale visual recognition challenge (ILSRVC), it achieved a top‐5 accuracy of 84.6%. In 2014, the VGG network was introduced that used a deeper structure with much smaller filters. The Visual Geometry Group at Oxford University proposed two new designs, VGG‐16 and VGG‐19, with the key distinction being that VGG‐16 utilized 16 convolutions while VGG‐19 used 19. The authors believed that the extra layers enhanced the robustness of the model and allowed it to learn more complex features. As a result of the new layers, the number of parameters increases from 138 to 143M. So these structures are computationally expensive with 138M total parameters and each image having a memory of 96MB, which is significantly larger than a normal image. Furthermore, in the 2014 ILSVRC competition, VGG‐16 was the runner‐up with a top 5 accuracy rate of 91.90%. The Google researchers proposed a novel architecture called the GoogLeNet network, also known as the Inception‐v1 architecture, in 2014. With a top 5 accuracy rate of 93.3%, the authors won the ImageNet competition. The basic idea behind the GoogLeNet architecture was to employ several convolution layers in the same block to go not only deeper but also wider; these blocks are known as Inception blocks. The existence of an inception module allows the network to gather several aspect ratios of the same image by employing the convolution layers in parallel. The biggest disadvantage of this network is the computational power required to train it with a large number of deep and wide layers. Following the popularity of Inception‐v1, the authors released subsequent versions such as Inception‐v2 and Inception‐v3 in the subsequent years. Among these networks, Inception‐v1 and Inception‐v3 are the most popular architectures. Six convolution layers are utilized in the Inception‐v1 inception blocks, whereas seven convolution layers are used in the Inception‐v3 inception blocks. The computational cost of Inception‐v3 which is 42 layers deep is just roughly 2.5 times that of Inception‐v1. Finally, the Inception‐v3 has also achieved a top 5 error rate of 3.58% and finished first runner up at the ILSVRC 2015.

![Figure 4.26 Comparison of top 1% and top 5% accuracy of different CNN architectures for image classification.](images/c04f026.png)

[**Figure 4.26**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0026) Comparison of top 1% and top 5% accuracy of different CNN architectures for image classification.

![Figure 4.27 Comparison of top 1% accuracy, number of parameters and operations (G‐Flops) different CNN architectures for image classification.](images/c04f027.png)

[**Figure 4.27**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0027) Comparison of top 1% accuracy, number of parameters and operations (G‐Flops) different CNN architectures for image classification.

The ResNet, which stands for residual network, was also developed in 2015, and its key advantage is the use of residual connections, which allows for the usage of a large number of layers. Moreover, increasing the network's depth rather than its width results in fewer parameters. Hence, to be fully trained, this network requires huge datasets, resulting in a computationally expensive training process. There are several ResNet architectural versions, which have the same principle but with a variable number of layers. Also, ResNet won the 2015 ILSVRC and COCO competitions with a top five accuracy rate of 94.4%.

In 2017, DenseNet was developed after being inspired by ResNet. However, instead of residual connections, the authors proposed using dense blocks. The DenseNet architecture maximizes the residual mechanism by densely connecting each layer to its succeeding layers. As a result, feature and gradient transmission is more effective, and the network is easier to train. DenseNet utilized fewer parameters and achieved a top 5 accuracy rate of 93.2% on the ILSVRC competition. The information loss is minimized between the deep layers due to the presence of connections between all layers. It also minimizes vanishing gradients and helps in feature reuse. However, this structure requires a very large dataset to achieve a good performance. Later in 2017, the Inception‐v3 architecture inspired the Xception network, and the fundamental concept was to replace the inception module with depthwise separable convolutions. The Xception model outperformed the VGG‐16, ResNet‐152, and Inception‐v3 architectures, with a top 5 accuracy rate of 94.50% on the ILSVRC challenge. In comparison with Inception, Xception has fewer parameters and is faster. As a result, the main advantage of this network is that even though it has a deep structure it utilizes a minimum number of parameters. This makes it computationally efficient in comparison to other deep networks.

In 2017, a group of Google researchers introduced MobileNetV1. MobileNets, and Xception share similar concepts but have different advantages. Xception has high precision, whereas MobileNets is a lightweight model that strikes the balance between model compression and accuracy. Later in 2018, MobileNetV2 was presented as an improvement to V1 followed by other versions in upcoming years. The key differences between the MobileNetV2 architecture and the V1 design are that the former uses residual connections and the expand/projection layers. The MobileNetV2 has fewer parameters than the v1 and scored slightly higher on the classification test. The top‐5 accuracy for MobileNetV1 on ImageNet is 89.9%, compared to 91.9% for VGG‐16. Hence, the MobileNets can be used to replace the VGGNet‐16 that is widely used as a feature extractor for otherNNs for an instant 10 speedup. Furthermore, MobileNets also offers a huge speed boost as it uses only 4.2M learned parameters in comparison to VGG‐16 which uses 138M parameters.

In 2019, Google released a research paper on EfficientNet, a new family of CNNs. Instead of laborious manual tweaking, these CNNs provide a more principled way for scaling up a CNN to improve accuracy and efficiency. To enhance accuracy, typical techniques strive to increase the depth and scale the width of the networks. However, the majority of deeper networks suffer from vanishing gradients and are difficult to train. Although strategies such as batch normalization and skip connections are useful in tackling this problem, empirical investigations show that accuracy decreases as network depth increases. Increasing width, on the other hand, hinders the network from learning complicated characteristics, resulting in diminishing accuracy. Unlike traditional techniques, EfficientNets evenly scales each dimension with a given set of scaling coefficients, exceeding the state‐of‐the‐art accuracy. The initial architecture was EfficientNet‐B0, which achieved 93.5% top‐5 accuracy with only 5.3M parameters, while the most recent version, EfficientNet‐B7, achieves state‐of‐the‐art 97.1% top‐5 accuracy on ImageNet while being significantly smaller and quicker. EfficientNets were evaluated on eight commonly used transfer learning datasets to further evaluate their performance, and they obtained state‐of‐the‐art accuracy in 5 out of the 8 datasets.

 

## 4.5 Conclusion

This chapter provides an overview of the CNN. This structure, which has been proven to be very successful in image processing, is inspired in what is believed to be the structure of the visual cortex of mammals, and the successive layers of the network extract features that are at the initial states local ones, but that become also global in deeper stages.

The nature of the CNN is sparse, this is, the convolutions can be seen as sparse matrix multiplications between the inputs and the convolution kernels. This fact, among other properties, makes the CNN less computationally complex than a fully connected neural network with similar depth.

The training process consisting of forward and BP is explained in detail, and the derivation is done by using the basic equation of the MLP BP together with the representation of the convolution as sparse matrix multiplication, to prove that this backpropagation is formally very similar to the one of the MLP.

Finally, popular models derived from CNN are presented, and the chapter is concluded by summarizing the advantages and trade‐offs of CNN.
