# 5  
Recurrent Neural Networks

 

## 5.1 Introduction

The NNs, including CNNs, use predetermined input and output sizes and a feedforward mechanism for the information flow. However, sequential data requires a mechanism to retain past information to predict future values due to the dependencies between the data points. For these problems, a class of networks known as recurrent neural network (RNN) is frequently utilized.

The RNN was introduced in the decade of 1980 by various scholars. The work by Rumelhart et al. ([1986](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0295)) introduces the backpropagation algorithm for both FFNNs and RNNs, where the RNNs are introduced with an application to learn sequences of alphanumeric characters. The first applications of RNN were in head tracking for virtual reality (Saad et al. [1999](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0296)), financial time‐series prediction (Giles et al. [1997](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0101)), music synthesis (Liang et al. [1999](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0200)) and electric load forecast (Costa et al. [1999](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0069)), among others (Medsker and L. Jain [2001](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0224)).

While they are inspired in the FFNN, they can deal with variable‐length sequential data. In as way, one can think of the comparison between a CNN and an RNN by noticing that a CNN has a finite time (or space) response, while an RNN has an infinite time response as a consequence of its recurrent nature.

They have a high‐dimensional hidden state with nonlinearities that give them the ability to recall and process previous information. The RNN takes an input, modifies its hidden state, and produces a prediction at every timestep. The high‐dimensional hidden state of the RNN allows it to integrate data over several timesteps and utilize it to generate precise predictions. RNNs take advantage of current prediction to provide the future one, and this mechanism is commonly known as a recurrence. Let us assume that we have an input word “apple,” and it is first fed into an FFNN. The network processes the word by considering a single character at a time and predictions are made for the character that comes after “l.” This task becomes impossible for the model since it does not have any memory about the previous characters “a,” “p,” “p,” and “l.” RNNs on the other hand memorize the previous inputs due to their internal memory. Hence, they are commonly used for sequential data like speech (Lim et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0201)), text (Sutskever et al. [2011](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0335)), audio (Feng et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0092)), video (Güera and Delp [2018](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0116)), weather (Alemany et al. [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0013)), and financial data (Tino et al. [2001](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0354)).

There are several variants of RNN, including long short‐term memory (LSTM) networks and gated recurrent unit (GRU). These variants introduce additional gates and memory cells that help the network to better propagate information over longer periods of time. Overall, the architecture of an RNN is defined by the number of units in the network, the type of units used, and the connections between the units.

 

## 5.2 RNN Architecture

Probably the earliest RNN to be incepted, before the works of Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams, is the Hopfield Network, introduced in 1982 by John Hopfield ([1982](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0149)), but in this paper, the author acknowledges that his structure was first introduced in 1974 by W. A. Little ([1974](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0206)) in order to model the existence of persistent states in the brain. Hopfield's work is the first one that incorporates the idea of recurrence in artificial neural networks. This network has a set of neurons with binary threshold outputs that are bidirectionally connected to each other ([Fig. 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0001)). The Hopfield network was used in system optimization problems as the classic traveling salesman problem (Hopfield and Tank [1985](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0150)). Continuous state Hopfield networks were used to model the human memory (Amit and Amit [1989](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0016)). See [Section 7.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0002) for more details about the Hopfield network.

 

### 5.2.1 Structure of the Basic RNN

The first RNN of interest for sequence modeling that can be trained using the backpropagation algorithm as described in Rumelhart et al. ([1986](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0295)) is the so‐called Elman network, introduced by J. L. Elman in 1990 (Elman [1990](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0088)), which follows a similar structure introduced by M. Jordan ([1986](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0164)).

An Elman RNN block consists of a single unit in the network, along with the input and output connections for that unit. The structure is represented in [Fig. 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0002). At time instant ![t](images/c05-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, the unit receives an input ![bold x Subscript t](images/c05-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> as well as a feedback consisting of the hidden state ![bold h Subscript t minus 1](images/c05-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> computed from the previous time step. The unit processes this input and produces a new hidden state ![bold h Subscript t](images/c05-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> whose nonlinear activation is a hyperbolic tangent. The RNN then computes linear transformation ![bold z Subscript t](images/c05-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> of the hidden state ![bold h Subscript t](images/c05-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. This is followed by a nonlinear activation that produces output ![bold o Subscript t Baseline equals left-bracket o Subscript 0 comma t Baseline comma ellipsis comma o Subscript upper K minus 1 comma t Baseline right-bracket Superscript down-tack](images/c05-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup></math>, which is usually a softmax activation when the RNN is used for multiclass classification among ![upper K](images/c05-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> classes. This process is repeated at each time step in the sequence, allowing the RNN to process sequential data.

After this, the resulting vector is passed through the nonlinear activation (hyperbolic tangent) to produce state vector ![bold h Subscript t](images/c05-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. This vector is then delayed with delay T, which can be thought of as a first in first out (FIFO) memory of one element, where when ![bold h Subscript t](images/c05-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is introduced, the previous value ![bold h Subscript t minus 1](images/c05-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> is extracted. The state ![bold h Subscript t minus 1](images/c05-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> is then transformed with ![bold upper W Subscript h h](images/c05-i0024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></math> and added to the transformed input. State ![bold h Subscript t](images/c05-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is also transformed with matrix ![bold upper W Subscript h o](images/c05-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub></math> and bias vector ![bold b 0](images/c05-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math> and then passed through the softmax activation to produce the output.

Thus, a standard RNN predicts the output sequence ![bold o 1 comma ellipsis comma bold o Subscript upper T Baseline](images/c05-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow><mi>T</mi></msub></math> from a given a sequential input ![bold x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold x Subscript upper T Baseline](images/c05-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>T</mi></msub></math> by passing it through multiple hidden states ![bold h 1 comma ellipsis comma bold h Subscript upper T Baseline](images/c05-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>T</mi></msub></math>. The expressions for the output and hidden states are

The computation of the hidden states and output states in the forward pass of the RNN is done by repeating these operations.

The three matrices ![bold upper W Subscript x h](images/c05-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></math>, ![bold upper W Subscript h h](images/c05-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></math>, and ![bold upper W Subscript h o](images/c05-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub></math> together with the bias vectors ![bold b Subscript h](images/c05-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow><mi>h</mi></msub></math> and ![bold b 0](images/c05-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math> perform respectively the affine transformation from the input to the hidden state, the transformation from the hidden state ![bold h Subscript t minus 1](images/c05-i0038.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> to ![bold h Subscript t](images/c05-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> and from the hidden state to the output.

The recurrent nature of the network is shown in [Eq. (5.1)](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0001), where one can see that the hidden state ![bold h Subscript t](images/c05-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> contains information for input ![bold x Subscript t](images/c05-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, but it also retains information coming from the previous inputs, carried by previous state ![bold h Subscript t minus 1](images/c05-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>. It is straightforward to see that for any set of non‐null parameters, this structure has an infinite‐time impulse response, this is, assuming a nonzero input ![bold x 1](images/c05-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> followed by an infinite sequence of null vectors ![bold x Subscript t Baseline equals bold-italic 0](images/c05-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn mathvariant="bold-italic">0</mn></math>, recursive [Eq. (5.1)](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0001) produces an varying input ![bold h Subscript t](images/c05-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> for an indefinite time. In a feedforward array, such a sequence will produce a constant response for ![t greater-than 1](images/c05-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>.

The interpretation of the function of the three weight matrices is straightforward. Input matrix ![bold upper W Subscript x h](images/c05-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></math> is in charge of the extraction of features from the input at instant ![t](images/c05-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, while output matrix ![bold upper W Subscript h o](images/c05-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub></math> is used to interpret the hidden state ![bold h Subscript t](images/c05-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> in terms of the task at hand, this is, to infer a classification or regression from the hidden state. Therefore, the only recurrent matrix is ![bold upper W Subscript h h](images/c05-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></math>, which is the one designated to store the information of the sequence that relates past instants of time to the classification or regression at hand.

 

### 5.2.2 Input–Output Configurations

The RNN learn from sequences of inputs, which can be configured in several ways, depending on the particular task to solve. These structures are used in many sequence learning problems such as in NLP and speech recognition. RNNs can be categorized input different types based on the number of inputs and outputs being processed it. It is to be noted that these types can both be extended to univariate and multivariate models based on the application at hand.

An RNN is said to be *Single Input–Single Output* when the structure is constructed so the input is a single pattern or element of a sequence, and the output is also an element corresponding to the response of the input. These structures represent the traditional Vanilla Neural network architecture. These models are also known as *One‐to‐One* RNN.

*Single input–multiple output* architectures are commonly known as *One‐to‐many* RNN. They receive one input and generate multiple outputs. An example of a One‐to‐many RNN would be an Image captioning model where the input is a single image and the output is a sequence of words or sentences describing the image.

The *Multiple inputs–Single Output* configuration learns from multiple input nodes and gives only one output. They are more commonly known as *Many‐to‐One* RNN. An example of this category of RNN would be an architecture that takes a sequence of words as input to detect the sentiment of the text in the form of a label such as positive or negative. Another example would be predicting a ![n](images/c05-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>th sample using a sequence of past ![n minus 1](images/c05-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> samples. These models can be used to provide an overall label or summary of a sequence of inputs.

Last, the *Multiple input–multiple outputs* RNN use multiple inputs to produce multiple outputs. They are more commonly known as *Many‐to‐Many* RNN. Many‐to‐many RNNs are often used where both the input and output sequences are in the form of a sequence. For example, this approach can be used in forecasting problems to predict ![n](images/c05-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> future samples from past ![m](images/c05-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> samples. In this scenario, both the input and output data are sequence data. Similarly, another example would be translating a sequence of words from one language to another word by word which also uses sequence data as input and output. The number of input samples can be the same as that of the output samples ![m equals n](images/c05-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></math>, There can also be cases where the input and output samples are not equal. This often happens in translation problems where the translation of a sentence in one language can be shorter or longer compared to that of the output language.

 

## 5.3 Training an RNN

Dynamic visualization of the RNN is shown in [Fig. 5.4](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0004) where the structure is unrolled over the input sequence. The corresponding compact representation is in [Figs. 5.5](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0005) and [5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0006). Here every neuron in the hidden layer receives input from both the most recent hidden states and the current input vector at each time step. This representation is useful to illustrate the training process, where each time instant here can be seen as a layer of a neural network, similar to the FFNN, with two main differences with respect to these structures. First, the RNN produces an output at each layer. Namely, in the layer corresponding to instant ![t](images/c05-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, the structure produces output ![bold o Subscript t](images/c05-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. Also, weights ![bold upper W Subscript x h](images/c05-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></math>, ![bold upper W Subscript h h](images/c05-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></math>, ![bold upper W Subscript h o](images/c05-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub></math>, ![bold b Subscript h](images/c05-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow><mi>h</mi></msub></math> and ![bold b 0](images/c05-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math> are the same in each layer, while in an FFNN the weights are different and they have different dimensions.

By observing these fundamental differences, a backpropagation algorithm based on the same principles as the ones applied for FFNN in [Chapter 1](#c01.xhtml) and CNN in [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml) can be applied to this type of neural network. Here, the backpropagation through the layers of [Fig. 5.4](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0004) is actually performed from the last time instant to the first one, and for this reason, this algorithm is known as backpropagation through time (BPTT) (R. J. Williams and Zipser [1995](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0372)).

Assume that the RNN is designed to classify among ![upper K](images/c05-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> classes of data and a training sequence ![bold x Subscript t Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper D](images/c05-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>D</mi></msup></math>, ![bold y Subscript t Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper K](images/c05-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>K</mi></msup></math>, ![1 less-than-or-equal-to t less-than-or-equal-to upper T](images/c05-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>T</mi></math> is available. We must then maximize the cross entropy between the labels and the outputs or, equivalently, the output likelihood. This is, the cost function to optimize is

Parameter ![bold-italic theta equals StartSet bold upper W Subscript x h Baseline comma bold upper W Subscript h h Baseline comma bold upper W Subscript h o Baseline EndSet](images/c05-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></math> symbolizes the set of all trainable parameters of the RNN.

The BPTT algorithm is now derived by computing the derivative of the cost function with respect to each parameter at each time instant.

It should be noticed that there is a peculiarity in the training of these structures that comes from their recurrent nature. We must consider that the hidden state ![bold h Subscript t](images/c05-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> at every instant depends on the states ![bold h Subscript t prime](images/c05-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msub></math>, ![t prime less-than t](images/c05-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>t</mi></math>. mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfenced></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

The first term of the right side of [Eq. (5.10)](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0010) is the expression of the error backpropagated from the output at instant ![t](images/c05-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> through the output weights ![bold upper W Subscript h o](images/c05-i0102.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub></math>. The error backpropagated from the next time instant is the second term, which contains the output error at instant ![t plus 1](images/c05-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> backpropagated to the network at instant ![t](images/c05-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> through the hidden weights ![bold upper W Subscript h h](images/c05-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></math>.

This is a recursive gradient, where ![bold upper W Subscript h h](images/c05-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></math> appears again inside the gradient with respect to ![bold h Subscript t plus 1](images/c05-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and, as a result when the full recursion is computed, this matrix appears raised to the power ![upper T minus t](images/c05-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi></math>. This can produce difficulties in learning long‐term dependencies, as we will see in [Section 5.4](#c05.xhtml#c05-sec-0011).

### 5.3.2 Gradient with Respect to the Input Weights

By inspection of [Fig. 5.5](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0005), if we undo the path from ![bold o Subscript t](images/c05-i0118.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, the error term ![bold-italic delta Subscript t](images/c05-i0119.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#948;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> at this point must be first backpropagated through ![bold upper W Subscript h o](images/c05-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub></math> in order to reach ![bold upper W Subscript x h](images/c05-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></math> at input ![bold x Subscript t](images/c05-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, but then, it has to be repeatedly backpropagated through ![bold upper W Subscript h h](images/c05-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></math> in order to reach the input matrix at each one of the inputs ![bold x Subscript t minus t prime](images/c05-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msub></math>.

If we compute directly the gradient with respect to the weights, the chain rule must be used as follows. First, the gradient ![nabla Subscript bold h Sub Subscript t Baseline upper J Subscript upper M upper L](images/c05-i0125.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mo>&#8711;</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msub><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub></math> of the cost function is computed with respect to ![bold h Subscript t](images/c05-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, which is done in [Eq. (5.10)](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0010). After, we need to compute the derivatives of the components of ![bold h Subscript t](images/c05-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> with respect to each component of ![bold z Subscript t Superscript left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>, which will give the derivative of the hyperbolic tangent activation. The final element of the chain is the gradient of ![bold z Subscript t Superscript left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> with respect to ![bold upper W Subscript x h](images/c05-i0130.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></math>, which gives vector ![bold x Subscript t](images/c05-i0131.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. The product of these elements has to be written in the right order so the gradient has the same dimensions as matrix ![bold upper W Subscript x h](images/c05-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></math>. The result is

In this expression, we find Jacobian ![StartFraction delta bold h Subscript t Baseline Over delta bold z Subscript t Superscript left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis Baseline EndFraction](images/c05-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfrac></math> with elements ![StartFraction d h Subscript i comma t Baseline Over d z Subscript j comma t Superscript left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis Baseline EndFraction](images/c05-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfrac></math>. Since the state ![bold h Subscript t](images/c05-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is an elementwise hyperbolic tangent operation, these elements are zero if ![i not-equals j](images/c05-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>j</mi></math> and otherwise, ![StartFraction d h Subscript i comma t Baseline Over d z Subscript i comma t Superscript left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis Baseline EndFraction equals hyperbolic tangent prime left-parenthesis z Subscript i comma t Superscript left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi>tanh</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Therefore, this Jacobian is a diagonal matrix containing these elements.

A similar result can be found for the biases

[(5.17)](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-disp-0017)![nabla Subscript bold b Sub Subscript h Subscript Baseline upper J Subscript upper M upper L Baseline equals sigma-summation Underscript t equals 1 Overscript upper T Endscripts diag left-parenthesis hyperbolic tangent prime left-parenthesis bold z Subscript t Superscript left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis left-parenthesis nabla Subscript bold h Sub Subscript t Subscript Baseline upper J Subscript upper M upper L Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05-math-0017.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mo>&#8711;</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></msub><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><mtext>diag</mtext><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mrow><mi>tanh</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>&#8711;</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msub><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> 

The above equations have the same form as any previously computed gradient, this is it is the product of the input sample ![bold x Subscript t](images/c05-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> as a column vector times a vector representing the backpropagated error, which, in this case, it is embedded in the (recursive) gradient with respect to the hidden state. This is, the error backpropagated to the input can be written as ![diag left-parenthesis hyperbolic tangent prime left-parenthesis bold z Subscript t Superscript left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis left-parenthesis nabla Subscript bold h Sub Subscript t Subscript Baseline upper J Subscript upper M upper L Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0139.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>diag</mtext><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mrow><mi>tanh</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>&#8711;</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msub><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfenced></math>.

 

### 5.3.3 Gradient with Respect to the Hidden State Weights

For this set of weights, the backpropagation of the error at instant ![t](images/c05-i0140.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> goes from the output ![bold o Subscript t](images/c05-i0141.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> in [Fig. 5.5](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0005), it is transformed with output weights ![bold upper W Subscript h o](images/c05-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub></math>, and this error is used to update ![bold upper W Subscript h h](images/c05-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></math> with the input to these weights, which is ![bold h Subscript t minus 1](images/c05-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>. The backpropagation in time then goes to the previous time instant, which requires another transformation of the error with the hidden state matrix.

In order to see this, we can just compute the gradient of the cost function as in [Section 5.3.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-sec-0007).

Algebraically, the only difference is that the gradient of ![bold z Subscript t Superscript left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> is computed now with respect to the hidden weights, and the result is the input to these weights, i.e. ![bold h Subscript t minus 1](images/c05-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, This, inside the summation along time, is the BPTT.

Finally, one may assume that weights ![bold b Subscript h](images/c05-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow><mi>h</mi></msub></math> belong to the hidden layers. For these biases, the backpropagated error (without multiplying it times an input) is applied as an update. If we remove ![bold h Subscript t minus 1](images/c05-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> from ([5.18](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0018)), we obtain the same result as in [Eq. (5.17)](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0017).

 

### 5.3.4 Summary of the Backpropagation Through Time in an RNN

All the above elements of the training can be summarized as follows in order to describe the backpropagation procedure in an RNN. Assuming a labeled training batch consisting of a sequence with ![upper T](images/c05-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> samples, the first step is to compute the output errors ![bold-italic delta Subscript t](images/c05-i0150.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#948;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, ![1 less-than-or-equal-to t less-than-or-equal-to upper T](images/c05-i0151.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>T</mi></math>. These errors are then used to update the output weights with Eqs. ([5.13](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0013)) and ([5.15](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0015)).

(5.19)![StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column bold upper W Subscript h o 2nd Column left-arrow bold upper W Subscript h o Baseline minus mu sigma-summation Underscript t equals 1 Overscript upper T Endscripts bold h Subscript t Baseline bold-italic delta Subscript t Superscript down-tack Baseline 2nd Row 1st Column bold b Subscript o 2nd Column left-arrow bold b Subscript o Baseline minus mu sigma-summation Underscript t equals 1 Overscript upper T Endscripts bold-italic delta Subscript t EndLayout](images/c05-math-0019.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable><mtr><mtd class="array"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd class="array"><mo>&#8592;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#948;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="array"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow><mi>o</mi></msub></mtd><mtd class="array"><mo>&#8592;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow><mi>o</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#948;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

With the output errors, the gradient of the cost function with respect to the hidden states is computed recursively through time as

(5.20)![nabla Subscript bold h Sub Subscript upper T Baseline upper J Subscript upper M upper L Baseline equals bold upper W Subscript h o Baseline bold-italic delta Subscript upper T](images/c05-math-0020.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mo>&#8711;</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow></msub><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#948;</mi></mrow><mi>T</mi></msub></math> 

for the last time instant, and

[(5.21)](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-disp-0021)![nabla Subscript bold h Sub Subscript t Subscript Baseline upper J Subscript upper M upper L Baseline equals bold upper W Subscript h o Baseline bold-italic delta Subscript t Baseline plus bold upper W Subscript h h Baseline diag left-parenthesis hyperbolic tangent prime left-parenthesis bold z Subscript t plus 1 Superscript left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis left-parenthesis nabla Subscript bold h Sub Subscript t plus 1 Subscript Baseline upper J Subscript upper M upper L Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05-math-0021.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mo>&#8711;</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msub><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>o</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#948;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mtext>diag</mtext><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mrow><mi>tanh</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>&#8711;</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> 

for the previous instants. Then, these gradients are used to update the rest of the weights. For the input weights, with Eqs. ([5.16](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0016)) and ([5.17](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0017)) we obtain the updates

## 5.4 Long‐Term Dependencies: Vanishing and Exploding Gradients

The RNN structure is intended to infer an output sequence from input sequences by learning about the input sequences across time. This property follows from the structure of the RNN, which is of an infinite impulse response nature. As a comparison, an FFNN has a finite response, this is, if a test pattern is presented at the input, it will produce a given output and, when another pattern is presented at the input, the output will be produced in a way that is independent of the previous input. Therefore, the FFNN does not keep any information on past inputs. The RNN, contrary to the FFNN, keeps information on past inputs, and therefore the output is a function that depends on the history of the input sequence. The structure extracts the information from the input sequence through time to perform a task as recognition or prediction. Nevertheless, when the information needed to perform the task at hand spans a long time, the RNN has difficulties capturing this information (Yoshua Bengio et al. [1994](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0027); Allen‐Zhu et al. [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0014); Pascanu et al. [2013](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0260); A. H. Ribeiro et al. [2020](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0286)). The problem is rooted both in the internal structure of the RNN and in the gradient‐based training that has been presented in [Section 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-sec-0005).

The phenomena that make the preservation of long‐term dependencies difficult in an RNN are called the exploding and vanishing problems. The explanation of these phenomena is relatively simple if we take into account the equations of the training recursion or BPTT. Particularly, it has been stated that this procedure implies the recursive computation of the Jacobian in [Eq. (5.9)](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0009). By using it in the recursion in [Eq. (5.21)](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0021), it is straightforward to see that this recursion simplicity includes the product of Jacobians (Salehinejad et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0302)):

where ![bold upper Q Subscript h h](images/c05-i0167.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![bold-italic upper Lamda Subscript h h](images/c05-i0168.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#923;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></math> are respectively the eigenvector matrix and the diagonal matrix containing the eigenvalues of the decomposition. When ![t much-less-than upper T](images/c05-i0169.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8810;</mo><mi>T</mi></math> two possible problems arise. The first one appears when one eigenvalue is less than 1. In this case, ![lamda Subscript h h comma d Superscript upper T minus t](images/c05-i0170.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> tends to zero. This is known as the vanishing gradient phenomenon. The opposite problem appears when one eigenvalue is higher than 1, and in this case, its power diverges. This is the so‐called exploding gradient problem. Notice that this product of Jacobians multiplies the error backpropagated to the instant ![upper T minus t](images/c05-i0171.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi></math>. If the vanishing gradient phenomenon dominates, that translates into the RNN neglecting or excluding the information carried in sample ![bold x Subscript upper T minus t](images/c05-i0172.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></math> and hidden state ![bold h Subscript upper T minus t minus 1](images/c05-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> from the training. Therefore, if there is a dependency on this or previous samples for the classification of the sequence at instant ![upper T](images/c05-i0174.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>, this will not be stored in the hidden state weights or the input weights. If the exploding gradient phenomenon dominates, then the backpropagation will simply diverge.

Yosua Bengio and co‐workers proposed in 1994 in his paper (Yoshua Bengio et al. [1994](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0027)) solutions to thevanishing and exploding gradient phenomena for the RNNs to be able to learn long‐term dependencies. Rather than changing the structure of the RNN, they considered the fact that this problem originated from the gradient descent procedure inside the BPTT. The first alternative presented consisted of using simulated annealing (S. Kirkpatrick et al. [1983](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0176); Corana et al. [1987](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0066)). Roughly speaking, the algorithm performs a random search by assigning a random value to the parameters and then accepting or rejecting them based on a criterion consisting of computing the output error with respect to these parameters. The process is repeated for a set of random values. After that, new random values are generated around the chosen ones, they are accepted or rejected, and the process starts over. The generation of random points has a variance that decreases with time, simulating an annealing process that cools down with time. While the process can show good results, it is naturally very slow compared to other methods. Multi‐grid random search is also proposed, which is a process similar to the simulated annealing but generating points around the best point only.

Another proposed algorithm is based on pseudo‐Newton approximations of the cost function (Becker and Cun [1988](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0025)). Essentially, for a given value of the weights, a second‐order approximation of the surface of the cost function can be constructed with the gradient and the Hessian (or an approximation of it). Then, it is easy to find analytically the optimum value of this approximation, which is taken as a new point to start over the algorithm until convergence.

While these solutions and others also proposed may solve the problem, other structures have been proposed further that tackle directly solutions to capture long‐term dependencies such as the long short‐term memory network, that will be introduced in [Section 5.7](#c05.xhtml#c05-sec-0015).

 

## 5.5 Deep RNN

The deep recursive neural network (DRNN) is a natural extension of the RNN to endow it with higher expressive capacity. While there are several ways to extend an RNN, the easiest one is to stack multiple recurrent hidden layers (Pascanu et al. [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0261)) as in [Figs. 5.10](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0010) and [5.11](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0011), This structure is called a stacked RNN. A different structure that is also a deep RNN is the so‐called deep‐transition RNN, which, instead of using a linear layer to compute the transition between hidden states, uses a fully connected (FC) neural network. These networks have been used in music prediction and language modeling among others.

## 5.6 Bidirectional RNN

The RNN presented so far is intended to infer some latent variable ![bold y Subscript t](images/c05-i0175.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> from input samples ![1 less-than-or-equal-to t less-than-or-equal-to t](images/c05-i0176.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>t</mi></math> of a given sequence and the present sample, this is, from the past and the present. In signal processing, this approach is often called causal, since the present and the future are modeled with dependencies on the past. Nevertheless, when the whole sequence is available, the inference of the latent variable at instant ![t](images/c05-i0177.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> can be modeled as dependent on samples of the next instants. This is sometimes called anti‐causal modeling.

The bidirectinal recursive neural network (BRNN) (Schuster and Paliwal [1997](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0308)) was introduced to make causal and anti‐causal inferences in sequences. The BRNN has been used in handwritten recognition (Liwicki et al. [2007](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0211)), translation (Sundermeyer et al. [2014](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0334)), and part‐of‐speech detection, among others.

The BRNN ([Fig. 5.14](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0014)) has the following forward and backward state equations:

## 5.7 Long Short‐Term Memory Networks

The long short‐term memory network (LSTM) is a variation of RNNs that can handle long‐term connections and that was first introduced by Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber in 1997 (Schmidhuber and Hochreiter [1997](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0305)). Ideally, RNNs are capable of handling any kind of long‐term as well as short‐term dependencies present in the input sequences. For instance, in the case of short‐term connections, only the most recent information needs to be examined to perform the current task. In this situation, RNNs can store activation representations of current inputs utilizing their feedback connections. However learning to store information over long time intervals by recurrent backpropagation, on the other hand, consumes time, owing to decreasing error backflow. The gradients in time tend to explode or vanish in traditional BPTT (R. J. Williams and Zipser [1995](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0372); Paul J. Werbos [1988](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0370)) or Real‐Time Recurrent Learning (Robinson and Fallside [1987](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0290)). As the gradients grow smaller and approach zero, the weights stay constant and cause vanishing gradients. But when gradients explode, the weights fluctuate and result in the divergence of the gradient descent algorithm. Hence, Hochreiter and Schmidhuber designed LSTM to tackle the problems posed by standard RNNs.

First, it is worth noticing that these phenomena of vanishing and exploding gradients can be avoided if [Eq. (5.28)](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0028) remains constant. The LSTM passes an internal state from one time instant to the next one, with unit gain and without using any nonlinear function. This ensures that the gradient can be propagated without exploding or vanishing. In the original LSTM paper by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber this mechanism is called constant error carousel (CEC). Later, in equivalent depictions of the LSTM structure, this mechanism has been called internal state ![bold c Subscript t](images/c05-i0178.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> (see, e.g. (A. Zhang et al. [2021](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0395))).

 

### 5.7.1 LSTM Gates

The LSTM unit is a cell whose inputs are the internal state ![bold c Subscript t minus 1](images/c05-i0179.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, the hidden state ![bold h Subscript t minus 1](images/c05-i0180.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, and the present input pattern ![bold x Subscript t](images/c05-i0181.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. The LSTM unit computes the values of three gates, usually called forgetting gate ![bold f Subscript t](images/c05-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">f</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, input gate ![bold i Subscript t](images/c05-i0183.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">i</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, and output gate ![bold o Subscript t](images/c05-i0184.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow><mi>o</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

From the above expressions, it is clear that these gates can be seen as three neural network layers in a parallel configuration ([Fig. 5.15](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0015)), but usually it is more convenient, for the sake of simplicity, to represent them in a compact fashion as in [Fig. 5.16](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0016).

The input node ![bold c overTilde Subscript t](images/c05-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is also computed as a function of the previous hidden state ![bold h Subscript t minus 1](images/c05-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and the input pattern ![bold x Subscript t](images/c05-i0197.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, but its corresponding activation is a hyperbolic tangent ([Fig. 5.17](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0017)), i.e.

[(5.33)](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-disp-0033)![bold c overTilde Subscript t Baseline equals hyperbolic tangent left-parenthesis bold upper W Subscript x c Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x Subscript i Baseline plus bold upper W Subscript h c Baseline bold h Subscript t minus 1 Baseline plus bold b Subscript c Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05-math-0033.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>tanh</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msubsup><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></math>  

### 5.7.2 LSTM Internal State

The above gates and the input node are used in the LSTM unit to compute the so‐called internal state ![bold c Subscript t](images/c05-i0199.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. This state is first multiplied elementwise by the forgetting gate ![bold f Subscript t](images/c05-i0200.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">f</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. This operation is intended to attenuate or erase components of the previous internal state ![bold c Subscript t minus 1](images/c05-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> when it is necessary. Therefore, the forgetting gate is trained so it can forget the internal state as a function of the previous hidden state and the current input. After this operation, the previous internal state is used to compute the present one. The operation is done in two steps. First, an update of the previous current state is computed by elementwise multiplication of the input node ![bold c overTilde Subscript t](images/c05-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> and the input gate ![bold i Subscript t](images/c05-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">i</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. Essentially, ![bold c overTilde Subscript t](images/c05-i0204.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is used to update the previous internal state to obtain the new one. The input gate is therefore trained to determine what fraction of each component of the input node is necessary for the update. The full expression of the forgetting and update operations shown in [Fig. 5.18](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0018) is

![Figure 5.15 The full structure of the LSTM gates. They are four NN layers placed in parallel, where, in the figure, the weights bold upper W Subscript h f and bold upper W Subscript x f that map the previous hidden state bold h Subscript t minus 1 and the input pattern bold x Subscript t into the forgetting gate bold f Subscript t are shown. This representation is never used in the LSTM. Instead, the more compact representation in Fig. 5.19 is commonly used.](images/c05f015.png)

[**Figure 5.15**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0015) The full structure of the LSTM gates. They are four NN layers placed in parallel, where, in the figure, the weights ![bold upper W Subscript h f](images/c05-i0185.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![bold upper W Subscript x f](images/c05-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub></math> that map the previous hidden state ![bold h Subscript t minus 1](images/c05-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> and the input pattern ![bold x Subscript t](images/c05-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> into the forgetting gate ![bold f Subscript t](images/c05-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">f</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> are shown. This representation is never used in the LSTM. Instead, the more compact representation in [Fig. 5.19](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0019) is commonly used.

![Figure 5.16 Compact representation of the three LSTM gates. The first one (bold f Subscript t) is trained to partially or totally forget the previous internal state if forgetting is necessary. The second one (bold i Subscript t) determines how much of the input must be taken into account in order to modify the internal state. The third one (bold o Subscript t) constitutes the output, and it will modulate the internal state bold c Subscript t to compute state bold h Subscript t.](images/c05f016.png)

[**Figure 5.16**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0016) Compact representation of the three LSTM gates. The first one (![bold f Subscript t](images/c05-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">f</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>) is trained to partially or totally forget the previous internal state if forgetting is necessary. The second one (![bold i Subscript t](images/c05-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">i</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>) determines how much of the input must be taken into account in order to modify the internal state. The third one (![bold o Subscript t](images/c05-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>) constitutes the output, and it will modulate the internal state ![bold c Subscript t](images/c05-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> to compute state ![bold h Subscript t](images/c05-i0194.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>.

![Figure 5.17 The LSTM gates and input node bold c overTilde Subscript t.](images/c05f017.png)

[**Figure 5.17**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0017) The LSTM gates and input node ![bold c overTilde Subscript t](images/c05-i0198.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>.

[(5.34)](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-disp-0034)![bold c Subscript t Baseline equals bold c Subscript t minus 1 Baseline circled-dot bold f Subscript t Baseline plus bold c overTilde Subscript i Baseline circled-dot bold i Subscript t](images/c05-math-0034.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8857;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">f</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8857;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">i</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> 

Here it is worth noticing the equivalence of the structure in [Fig. 5.18](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0018) with the unit gain self‐feedback described as constant error carousel (CEC) in the original paper by Schmidhuber and Hochreiter ([1997](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0305)). Indeed, the backpropagation of the error through the internal state line is done without transformation through any nonlinear function derivative or weight matrix, therefore avoiding the phenomena of vanishing or exploding gradients.

 

### 5.7.3 Hidden State and Output of the LSTM

The full structure of the LSTM cell is depicted in [Fig. 5.19](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0019). The output of the LSTM is the gate ![bold o Subscript t](images/c05-i0210.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. This output must be normalized in order to produce a softmax output, which will be used for the classification and to compute the error for the backpropagation, but this gate is also used to modulate the hidden state, and this is why the activations are sigmoids, which ensures that each element of the output gate ranges from 0 to 1. The computation of the hidden state is done as

![Figure 5.18 The forgetting gate bold f Subscript t is elementwise multiplied with the internal state at the previous instant bold c Subscript t minus 1. If the outputs of the forgetting gate are low, this means that this gate is applying a forgetting factor to the internal state. At the same time, input gate bold i Subscript t elementwise multiplies input node bold c overTilde Subscript t, and the product is added to the previous internal state to produce the new internal state bold c Subscript t.](images/c05f018.png)

[**Figure 5.18**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0018) The forgetting gate ![bold f Subscript t](images/c05-i0205.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">f</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is elementwise multiplied with the internal state at the previous instant ![bold c Subscript t minus 1](images/c05-i0206.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>. If the outputs of the forgetting gate are low, this means that this gate is applying a forgetting factor to the internal state. At the same time, input gate ![bold i Subscript t](images/c05-i0207.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">i</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> elementwise multiplies input node ![bold c overTilde Subscript t](images/c05-i0208.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, and the product is added to the previous internal state to produce the new internal state ![bold c Subscript t](images/c05-i0209.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>.

![Figure 5.19 The hidden state bold h Subscript t is constructed with the internal state bold c Subscript t modulated by the output state. This figure represents the full structure of the LSTM.](images/c05f019.png)

[**Figure 5.19**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0019) The hidden state ![bold h Subscript t](images/c05-i0211.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is constructed with the internal state ![bold c Subscript t](images/c05-i0212.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> modulated by the output state. This figure represents the full structure of the LSTM.

[(5.35)](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-disp-0035)![bold h Subscript t Baseline equals hyperbolic tangent left-parenthesis bold c Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis circled-dot bold o Subscript t](images/c05-math-0035.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>tanh</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8857;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> 

Notice that the internal state is not bounded by a nonlinear operation in order to avoid vanishing effects. Therefore, the hidden state ![bold h Subscript t](images/c05-i0213.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is constructed by simply bounding the values of the internal state between ![negative 1](images/c05-i0214.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and ![plus 1](images/c05-i0215.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> with a hyperbolic tangent activation. Then, the output of this activation is elementwise multiplied by the output gate. If an element of the output gate is close to 1, then the corresponding element of the hidden state is kept and transmitted to the next stage. But if an element of the output gate is close to zero, the corresponding element of the hidden state is inhibited. To interpret this, we must notice that when element ![k](images/c05-i0216.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> of the output gate is low, that means that the class of input ![bold x Subscript t](images/c05-i0217.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is probably not ![k](images/c05-i0218.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, i.e. ![p left-parenthesis y Subscript t Baseline equals k vertical-bar bold x Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis almost-equals 0](images/c05-i0219.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8776;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. Therefore, we drop the corresponding component of the hidden state so it does not influence the next cells with respect to the current time instant.

 

### 5.7.4 LSTM Backpropagation

The backpropagation in an LSTM is similar to the one that was derived for the Elman RNN in [Section 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-sec-0005). Here we assume that the output of the LSTM is its hidden state, but it is common to use this state in an FC structure in order to perform a given task, in which case the backpropagation can be extended straightforwardly. The cost function in our case is to be expressed as a function of the hidden states, and therefore ![bold-italic delta Subscript t](images/c05-i0220.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#948;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is

[(5.36)](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-disp-0036)![bold-italic delta Subscript t Baseline equals bold-italic f left-parenthesis bold h Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis minus bold y Subscript t](images/c05-math-0036.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#948;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> 

The hidden state depends on the elementwise product of the output state ![bold o Subscript t](images/c05-i0221.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">o</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> and the internal state passed through the hyperbolic tangent activation, as defined in [Eq. (5.35)](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0035). By applying the chain rule, the gradient of the cost function with respect to the output gate is
