### 5.7.5 Machine Translation with LSTM

A translation machine consists of a structure where the inputs are sequences of different lengths in a given *input language* (e.g. English):

> *Spring begins today*.

and whose outputs are sentences of a different length in a *target language* (e.g. French):

![Figure 5.22 (a) shows the training loss curve for LSTM model over 1000 epochs. (b) shows the comparison between the actual time series and the prediction performed by the LSTM.](images/c05f022.png)

[**Figure 5.22**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0022) (a) shows the training loss curve for LSTM model over 1000 epochs. (b) shows the comparison between the actual time series and the prediction performed by the LSTM.

> *Le printemps commence aujourd'hui*.

At first sight, large feedforward structures like CNN may seem like a good idea since they can have a great number of parameters, necessary to store the complexities of both the source and the target language. It is noteworthy that for each language, a translator must have available more than ![1 0 Superscript 5](images/c05-i0238.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>5</mn></msup></math> words of each language. To this first complexity, we must add the language structure complexities. As a result, actual translation machines may need many millions of parameters. But to these difficulties, another one must be added, and it is the fact that the sequences to be translated have arbitrary lengths, and the same sentence can have two different lengths in two different languages, as is the case of the example above. While deep feedforward structures have been successfully used in language, in particular for speech processing (see e.g. the works by Geoffrey E. Hinton et al. ([2012c](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0140)) in acoustic modeling or (George E. Dahl et al. [2011](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0072)) in speech recognition), these structures are tremendously limited in their use for translation due to the fact that the input and output dimensions are fixed.

Coding a sentence with arbitrary length into a vector of fixed dimensionality, nevertheless, is possible with the use of RNN, through the use of its hidden state. One of the first successful variable length machine translation schemes is given by Sutskever et al. ([2014](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0337)) while working at Google, Inc. The main idea of the translation strategy is depicted in [Fig. 5.23](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0023). The structure consists of two sections. In the figure, the upper section is the so‐called encoder, and it is in charge of encoding or compressing a sequence of words into a hidden state. The lower section is another RNN, and it uses the hidden state as an input in order to translate the sentence.

![Figure 5.23 Sequence to sequence translation with LSTM. The upper sequence codes the English sentence “spring begins.” into state bold h 4. The lower sequence uses this state to sequentially translate the sentence into the French sentence “le primtemps commence.”](images/c05f023.png)

[**Figure 5.23**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0023) Sequence to sequence translation with LSTM. The upper sequence codes the English sentence “spring begins.” into state ![bold h 4](images/c05-i0239.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mn>4</mn></msub></math>. The lower sequence uses this state to sequentially translate the sentence into the French sentence “le primtemps commence.”

The first step for sequence‐to‐sequence translation consists of creating a word embedding, this is, a dictionary of tokens, this is, a corpus of words for each language, where each word is associated with a token. A token is a vector of integers representing each one of the words. The corpus may also contain signs such as stops, commas, and the beginning of sequence (\_BOS) and end of sequence (\_EOS) tokens.

Assuming that word embeddings are available for both languages, the methodology works as follows. An RNN (for example the Elman RNN or an LSTM) is initialized with the token corresponding to the first word of the sequence (spring). The recurrent block is then fed back with the current state and the next word (begins). The process is iterated until the \_EOS is found, indicating that the recursion can be finished. The final state ![bold h Subscript upper T](images/c05-i0240.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>T</mi></msub></math> of the encoding machine is then used in the decoder RNN for the translation. This state is concatenated with the \_BOS token. The hidden state ![bold h prime 1](images/c05-i0241.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math> of the decoder RNN is then used as the input of an FC structure with as many softmax outputs as words in the target dictionary to predict the token of the first word of the translated sequence. The hidden state, together with the internal state ![bold c prime 1](images/c05-i0242.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>, and the predicted token are fed back into the RNN to predict the next token. When the recursion predicts the \_EOS token, the translation is finished. In the paper by Sutskever et al. ([2014](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0337)), a deep LSTM is used. Such a structure simply stacks several LSTM blocks, so the state of each one is fed back into itself and at the same time, it is used as an input to the next one. These structures have been successful in speech recognition tasks (Graves et al. [2013](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0114); Sak et al. [2014](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0297)).

The FC output estimates the probability of each word in the dictionary, and this output is used to optimize the structure according to a ML criterion. In particular, the criterion is intended to maximize the translation log‐likelihood

[(5.47)](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-disp-0047)![upper J Subscript upper M upper L Baseline equals StartFraction 1 Over StartAbsoluteValue upper S EndAbsoluteValue EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript upper T comma upper S Endscripts log p left-parenthesis upper T vertical-bar upper S right-parenthesis](images/c05-math-0047.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></mfrac><munder><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></munder><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where ![StartAbsoluteValue dot EndAbsoluteValue](images/c05-i0243.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math> denotes the cardinality of the source sequence ![s](images/c05-i0244.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper T](images/c05-i0245.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> is the target sequence. Equivalently, one can minimize the NLL of the sequence, which is equal to the previous expression with a minus sign. Accounting for the length of the sequence is important here, as it will be discussed in [Section 5.7.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-sec-0022).

 

### 5.7.6 Beam Search in Sequence to Sequence Translation

In the sequence‐to‐sequence translation method described above, each token of the target sequence is decided through the observation of the probability of each token in the dictionary estimated by a FC layer whose output has thousands of elements, corresponding to the number of words in the target dictionary.

This practically guarantees that at each iteration, a subset of words will have a high probability, thus adding uncertainty to the prediction. In order to reduce the uncertainty, each iteration is repeated with a subset (or beam) of ![k](images/c05-i0246.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> tokens with the highest probability. The procedure creates a tree of decisions whose paths have associated probabilities that can be computed and then the decision is taken according to them.

The procedure is illustrated as follows. Assume a dictionary with only three tokens ![bold y 1](images/c05-i0252.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math>, ![bold y 2](images/c05-i0253.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, ![bold y 3](images/c05-i0254.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub></math>, and \_EOS. In the *greedy search* illustrated in [Fig. 5.24](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0024), at each iteration a token is chosen according to the maximum probability criterion, which is then introduced in the next iteration to compute a new set of probabilities. According to all estimated probabilities, the obtained sequence is ![bold y 1 comma bold y 2 comma bold y 3](images/c05-i0255.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub></math>, \_EOS. But notice that in the first iteration, token ![bold y 3](images/c05-i0256.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub></math> has a significant probability and, therefore, it is worth trying the evolution of the tree starting with this. This is the principle of the beam search.

![Figure 5.24 Greedy search in sequence‐to‐sequence translation. The dictionary has tokens bold y 1, bold y 2, bold y 3, and \_EOS. After the first iteration of the decoder, the FC layer outputs the probabilities 0.5, 0.3, 0.2, and 0.0, and therefore token bold y 1 is used in the next iteration, where bold y 2 obtains the highest probability. The procedure is repeated until token \_EOS is chosen, as it has the maximum probability.](images/c05f024.png)

[**Figure 5.24**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0024) Greedy search in sequence‐to‐sequence translation. The dictionary has tokens ![bold y 1](images/c05-i0247.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math>, ![bold y 2](images/c05-i0248.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, ![bold y 3](images/c05-i0249.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub></math>, and \_EOS. After the first iteration of the decoder, the FC layer outputs the probabilities 0.5, 0.3, 0.2, and 0.0, and therefore token ![bold y 1](images/c05-i0250.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> is used in the next iteration, where ![bold y 2](images/c05-i0251.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math> obtains the highest probability. The procedure is repeated until token \_EOS is chosen, as it has the maximum probability.

![Figure 5.25 Beam search with k equals 2 in a dictionary with four tokens.](images/c05f025.png)

[**Figure 5.25**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0025) Beam search with ![k equals 2](images/c05-i0257.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> in a dictionary with four tokens.

In a beam search, at each iteration, the ![k](images/c05-i0258.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> tokens with the highest probability are chosen and then sequentially used as input for the next iteration. This produces ![k](images/c05-i0259.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> possible outcomes of the FC output, which creates ![k](images/c05-i0260.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> possible paths. In the example of [Fig. 5.25](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0025), a beam search with ![k equals 2](images/c05-i0261.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> is applied. During the first recursion of the decoder, the FC layer outputs four probabilities, of which ![bold y 1](images/c05-i0262.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![bold y 3](images/c05-i0263.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub></math> have the highest probabilities. Them, both tokens are tested as inputs for the next recursion, which creates two sets of probabilities. If ![bold y 1](images/c05-i0264.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> is used, then ![bold y 2](images/c05-i0265.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math> and ![bold y 3](images/c05-i0266.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub></math> have the highest probability. If ![bold y 3](images/c05-i0267.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub></math> are used, ![bold y 3](images/c05-i0268.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msub></math> and \_EOS are the most probable. This creates more possible paths in the next iteration, where 4 tokens are tested. Each time that \_EOS is found among the ![k](images/c05-i0269.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> most probable tokens, the corresponding path is finished. After all paths are finished, the log‐likelihoods or the NLL of the paths is computed, and the path with the lowest NLL is chosen.

[Table 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0001) summarizes the (unfinished) process of [Fig. 5.25](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0025). Among all the finished paths, all except the one with the lowest NLL are discarded. The search must be continued for all the remaining paths. Notice that since the sequences have different lengths, here it is very important to divide the log probabilities in [Eq. (5.47)](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0047) by the sequence length. Of course, this translation example is not realistic, because two of the non‐discarded sequences have a word repeated two and three times, which, in natural languages is very very very unlikely.

Once all paths are finished, the final translation will be the sequence with the lowest NLL or, in other words, the translation with the highest probability.

Sutskever et al. ([2014](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0337)) describe the experimental setup as follows. They used the WMT 2014 English–French translation dataset (Bojar et al. [2014](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0045)), with 12 million sentences, 284 million French words, and 304 million English words, with a dictionary containing 160.000 English words and 80.000 French words. The source language was English. The out‐of‐dictionary words were changed by a UNK (unknown) token, and the translations were produced by beam search. The authors noticed that the results improved slightly when the source sentences were reversed.

The tested structures were single and deep LSTMs with hidden states of 1000 cells. The word embeddings had dimension 1000 (this is, the tokens were coded in vectors of length 1000), and the output of the FC structure was a softmax of dimension 80.0000. The parameters of the LSTM were initialized at random with a uniform distribution between ![minus](images/c05-i0280.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></math>0.08 and 0.08, and the optimization algorithm was a momentum gradient descent with ![mu equals 0.7](images/c05-i0281.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.7</mn></math>. The gradient descent was applied in batches of 128 sequences. Also, in order to avoid any possible exploding gradients, the training included a hard limit constraint in the norm of the weights. The evaluation metrics were the bilingual evaluation understudy (BLEU) (see [Table 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-tbl-0002)).

![Table 5.1  Probabilities of the tokens across finished and unfinished paths in Fig. 5.25 and NLL of each one of the paths.](images/c05-i0270.png)

## 5.8 Gated Recurrent Units

The traditional RNNs suffer from the vanishing gradient problem, which can make it difficult to propagate important information from the past to the present, leading to a loss of context and meaning. The GRU (Cho et al. [2014a](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0057)) is a new type of RNN that uses a gating mechanism to update or forget information from the past selectively was proposed to address these issues. The GRU is intended to find a compromise between the ease of use and interpretability of classic RNNs and the complexity of more sophisticated designs such as LSTMs. It was found to be more effective on several benchmark datasets for machine translation. The performance comparison of GRU to that of LSTMs showed that it is faster to train, and it uses less memory. GRU outperformed traditional RNNs and is competitive with LSTMs while processing datasets with longer sequences.

GRUs solve the vanishing gradient problem using two gates namely the update gate and reset gate. These gates decide what information to retain or discard through to the output. The update gate determines both how much information to retain from the previous hidden state and how much information to use in the current hidden state. The reset gate functions much like the forgetting gate of an LSTM. This gate determines how much of the previous hidden state to discard and how much information to consider when updating the current hidden state.

In a GRU, the hidden state of instant ![t minus 1](images/c05-i0282.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> is concatenated with current input ![bold x Subscript t](images/c05-i0283.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> and passed through two dense layers with sigmoid activation ([Fig. 5.27](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0027)) that constitute the reset ![bold r Subscript t](images/c05-i0284.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> and update ![bold u Subscript t](images/c05-i0285.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> gates, with expressions

## 5.9 Conclusion

The RNN models, originally inspired in the Hopfield network, are the first structures able to process sequential models with arbitrary length. Indeed, the previously introduced deep structures are designed to process inputs with fixed dimensions, and, hence, their use for sequences is limited.

The Elman RNN is the first recursive structure, introduced to make predictions based on the information stored in the hidden layer conveyed by the past elements of the sequence. The training of the RNN is carried out by the backpropagation of the error. The particularity of the RNN is that the error is backpropagated from the current output at each time instant to the present input and to all the past inputs, and this is why this optimization is called backpropagation through time. The RNN has many variants, among them the bidirectional RNN is used in those cases where at a time instant, elements of posterior time instants in the sequence are available. This is particularly interesting in translation or text prediction. Deep structures consisting of stacking several RNN or others, as RNN with hidden states based on FC neural networks exist.

A main drawback of the RNN consists of the vanishing and exploding gradients phenomena, that in particular preclude the retention of information from remote samples, or long‐term information. This is due to the fact that the backpropagation contains a term that is a function of the ![t](images/c05-i0292.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>th power of the hidden matrix weight. The LSTM is a recursive neural network introduced to solve this problem by the propagation of an internal state that is not processed by the matrix. The GRU was introduced later to produce similar results with a lower computational complexity.

The RNN has played a prominent role in tasks related to signal processing and language modeling, such as translation, part of speech detection, financial time series, energy load forecast, and others.

# 6  
Attention Networks and Transformers

 

## 6.1 Introduction

Attention mechanisms are a natural step in the evolution of the way in which AI is understood and designed, in an attempt to imitate the function of the biological neural tissue (see e.g. (Lotter et al. [2020](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0212))). The first versions of deep learning (DL) mechanisms were inspired by the structure of the brain tissue, and later, researchers tried to reproduce the function of the memory. Starting in the first years of the 21st century, major investigations focused on human behavior, which produced an explosion of advanced and very complex AI structures.

The inception of the first neural network mechanisms can be seen as an attempt to mimic the structure of a biological neuron, through the introduction of the perceptron by Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts in 1948 and first implemented by Frank Rosenblatt ([1958](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0293)).

Yan LeCun, in the 1980s, featured a quantum leap in the development of machine learning‐based AI for image processing. In order to find the inspiration for that work, we need to go back to 1959, when David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel first described the visual cortex in cats. A neural network structure that imitated the cortex model, constructed with artificial neurons, the first functional image recognition machine, was the CNN, first introduced by LeCun in 1989. CNN structures, which somehow modeled biological vision (Kriegeskorte [2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0180)). These approaches roughly simulated the structure of the brain tissue in a simplified fashion (Kuzovkin et al. [2018](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0189); De Cesarei et al. [2021](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0074)). This neural network was successful in character recognition to handwritten digits with unprecedented accuracy. This was the first one of a series of models with increasing complexity that ended with some very successful image recognition structures around 2012. Several CNNs were published that had outstanding accuracy in classifying images among 1000 different classes, and they were trained which huge image databases.

The previous approaches roughly simulated the structure of the brain tissue in a simplified fashion and worked for visual recognition. But what about language model (LM)s? At practically the same time, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) were first introduced as a model that went away from such a merely structural conceptualization to take an approach based on the function of the brain, in particular, to reproduce the persistence of the memory (Bitzer and Kiebel [2012](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0042); Güçlü and Van Gerven [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0115); Hallez et al. [2023](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0118)), and they were first applied by John Hopfield in 1982 to solve optimization problems. In 1997, alternative recurrent models, already introduced by Jeff Elman in 1972 and later improved.

An even more sophisticated path toward the evolution of AI was opened when researchers started to devise mechanisms to emulate human behavior through attention mechanisms. Interestingly, the use of these mechanisms gave rise to the first machines that could likely pass the Turing test (Pinar Saygin et al. [2000](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0264)). The first released attention‐based chatbot released by Google Inc., developed in 2017 and named language model for dialogue applications (LaMDA) (Thoppilan et al. [2020](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0350)) created a significant amount of controversy when Blake Lemoine, one of the engineers of the team that developed the chatbot, suggested that the machine may present signs that imitate consciousness (Tiku [2022](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0353)), something that was widely misinterpreted as him claiming that the machine was actually sentient. He was doing a study related to gender, ethnicity, and religious biases. In the course of his experiments, he asked what religion the machine would be if it was an officiant in Israel. The machine responded “The only true one: the Jedi religion.” That triggered in him a feeling that the machine was perceiving that the question was tricky, and deflected with irony. Lemoine concluded that if the machine was not able to pass the Turing test, we can say that it is not sentient, but if it passed, then we cannot discard it.

Blaise Agüera y Arcas, an AI research leader at Google denied that claim. But this opened a debate that escalated later. In March 2023, MLRI researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky wrote in Time Magazine “Progress in AI capabilities is running vastly, vastly ahead of progress in AI alignment or even progress in understanding what the hell is going on inside those systems. If we actually do this, we are all going to die.”

In May of this year, Geoffrey Hinton, the godfather of AI resigned from Google in order to “freely speak out about the risks of AI.” He claimed that a part of him now regrets his life's work (C. Metz [2023](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0227)). He thinks that the computer models that we have now may be better than the human brain for certain tasks, and the idea of artificial superintelligence may come very soon.

Yoshua Bengio, a second father of AI, is more specific: AI can pass the Turing test, and they can fool us into thinking that they are human beings: which can destabilize democracy through disinformation since AI is basically in the hands of anyone. An AI can achieve levels of complexity similar to those of the human brain without the limitations of the human brain, so one of these machines can be smarter than we are. A machine could act in a way that we could not, and it could, for example, misuse legislation by finding loopholes more efficiently that the smartest lawyer. Bengio claims a regulatory body for these and many more, maybe unknown, issues of AI. He signed, with Hinton and many other scientists, a letter claiming a pause in the AI experiments.

Max Tegmark, another of the authors of the letter, an MIT researcher in AI wrote an article in Time Magazine (Tegmark [2023](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0347)) that warns of the risk of extinction due to the AI. He wrote “Before superintelligence and its human extinction threat, AI can have many other side effects worthy of concern, ranging from bias and discrimination to privacy loss, mass surveillance, job displacement, growing inequality, cyberattacks, lethal autonomous weapon proliferation, humans getting ‘hacked’, human enfeeblement and loss of meaning, non‐transparency, mental health problems (from harassment, social media addiction, social isolation, dehumanization of social interactions) and threats to democracy\[…\].”

The debate is open and, beyond educated apocalyptic claims, it is a natural consequence of the great and previously unseen power of AI nowadays in general and, in particular, of attention mechanisms.

 

## 6.2 Attention Mechanisms

Attention is a core human brain functioning mechanism and is a complex cognitive function (Rensink [2000](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0282); Corbetta and Shulman [2002](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0067)). One important property of the human learning mechanism is the ability to concentrate on information in parts and not as an entirety. This capability of human learning is called attention. For example, while perceiving things visually humans tend to focus on certain parts or aspects of the scene, and this part is identified by them to find similarities with other scenes having the same component. Humans tend to learn to focus on an individual aspect rather than the scene as a whole (Niu et al. [2021](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0250)). Therefore, humans process information by selecting high‐value features from a huge information source with the help of limited resources for processing information. With this kind of approach, humans learn more accurately and efficiently over time. This type of learning in humans is referred to as an attention mechanism as they focus or attend to certain specific information out of massive information.

Attention in machine learning refers to giving importance and priority to certain pieces of input data while disregarding the rest to replicate the cognitive attention mechanism. It enabled researchers to develop algorithms that can distinguish between input components that are crucial for solving an issue and those that are not. According to research, adding an attention layer to several types of deep learning neural networks increases their performance (Bahdanau et al. [2014](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0021)). The attention model has been utilized successfully in practice to address a variety of real‐world issues in the fields of natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision, including language translation (Z. Lin et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0204)), document classification (Z. Yang et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0383)), image captioning (K. Xu et al. [2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0381)), and image synthesis (S. E. Reed et al. [2016a](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0280)). For instance, in tasks involving machine translation, only selected words may be useful for predicting the subsequent word. While in an image‐captioning problem, certain areas of the input image are more useful for generating the caption. Attention models integrate the idea of relevance by assisting the model to constantly focus on only those portions of the input that aid in effectively finishing the task.

 

### 6.2.1 The Nadaraya–Watson Attention Mechanism

In 1964, Nadaraya and Watson proposed a regression model (Nadaraya [1964](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0238); Watson [1964](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0366)) that may be considered an initial foundation of attention mechanisms in deep learning. It is a non‐parametric regression approach that computes the conditional probability of a target variable given a set of features or predictor variables, with no assumptions about the actual data distribution. Given ![n](images/c06-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> training data with features and their associated target values ![left-parenthesis bold x 1 comma bold y 1 right-parenthesis comma left-parenthesis bold x 2 comma bold y 2 right-parenthesis comma ellipsis comma left-parenthesis bold x Subscript n Baseline comma bold y Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, for a new instance ![bold x Subscript j](images/c06-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub></math> (this instance is usually called a *query* in this context), we want to estimate the target value ![ModifyingAbove bold y With Ì‚ Subscript j](images/c06-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub></math>. A naive regression model may simply estimate the median or average value of the target variable for all observations without taking into account the relationship with the features. The expression for this model can be defined as:

(6.1)![ModifyingAbove bold y With Ì‚ Subscript j Baseline equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts bold y Subscript i](images/c06-math-0001.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> 

On the other hand, the Nadaraya–Watson model assigns weights for every observation and aggregates the weighted responses to determine the regression function at a specific point. The weights represent the significance of each of the training feature samples to the query ![bold x](images/c06-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>. Thus the Nadaraya–Watson model is able to capture more complicated and non‐linear interactions between features and target variables than the naive approach. The target variable ![ModifyingAbove bold y With Ì‚](images/c06-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math> may be estimated in this case as

[(6.2)](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-disp-0002)![ModifyingAbove bold y With Ì‚ Subscript j Baseline equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts alpha Subscript i comma j Baseline bold y Subscript i](images/c06-math-0002.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> 

Coefficients ![alpha Subscript i comma j](images/c06-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> are referred to as the *attention coefficients*, and they are computed as

[(6.3)](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-disp-0003)![alpha Subscript i comma j Baseline equals StartStartFraction upper K left-parenthesis StartFraction bold x Subscript j Baseline minus bold x Subscript i Baseline Over h EndFraction right-parenthesis OverOver sigma-summation Underscript k equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts upper K left-parenthesis StartFraction bold x Subscript j Baseline minus bold x Subscript k Baseline Over h EndFraction right-parenthesis EndEndFraction](images/c06-math-0003.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></math> 

where ![upper K left-parenthesis dot right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is a kernel function, or a positive definite function that is used to measure the similarity between samples ![bold x Subscript i](images/c06-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![bold x](images/c06-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>. By virtue of the Mercer's Theorem (Aizerman [1964](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0006)), positive definite functions are equivalent to dot products of mappings of vectors ![bold x Subscript i Baseline comma bold x Subscript j Baseline](images/c06-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub></math> into a higher dimension Hilbert space. The kernels used in the Nadaraya and Watson regression papers were radial basis functions as the square exponential kernel, (sometimes called Gaussian kernel) the Epanechnikov Epanechnikov ([1969](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0090)) kernel, the triangular kernel, and others, this is, functions that are circularly symmetric around the origin and monotonically decreasing when the distance ![StartAbsoluteValue bold x Subscript i Baseline minus bold x EndAbsoluteValue](images/c06-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math> increases. Therefore, parameter ![h](images/c06-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> establishes the width of the kernel that controls the bias‐variance tradeoff of the regression (Geman et al. [1992](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0098)).

Essentially, the weighting function in the Nadaraya–Watson regression model and the attention mechanism in the current deep learning models have a conceptual similarity. These models aim to give more priority to specific regions of the input while making a prediction. Nevertheless, there exist some significant differences between the two models. For instance, in the Nadaraya–Watson model, the weights are determined based on the distance between the test point and the training samples. However, the weights in the attention mechanism are learned by the model during training and frequently rely on the content of the input sequence.

![Figure 6.1 (a) Attention matrix represents the attention weights between the training data and the queries. (b) Nadaraya–Watson regression model.](images/c06f001.png)

[**Figure 6.1**](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-fig-0001) (a) Attention matrix represents the attention weights between the training data and the queries. (b) Nadaraya–Watson regression model.

 

### 6.2.2 The Bahdanau Attention Mechanism

The sequence‐to‐sequence translation machine presented in [Section 5.7.5](#c05.xhtml#c05-sec-0021) based on an encoder–decoder architecture constructed with recurrent networks may have a major limitation due to the fact that the source sequence is entirely coded in a single hidden state ![bold h](images/c06-i0024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow></math>. The encoder–decoder architecture is efficient for tasks where the source sequence is small. However, when the sequence is long, it becomes challenging for the encoder–decoder to store all the contextual information as a single fixed‐length vector. By coupling the attention mechanism with the traditional encoder–decoder framework, the decoder can selectively focus on relevant parts of the input sequence when generating each output token. This enables the model to overcome the limitation of the fixed‐length context vector and improves its performance in tasks with longer input sequences. Consider the given source and target sentences in a machine translation task from English to German:

*   **Source (English)**: “How does the bird fly?”
*   **Target (German)**: “Wie fliegt der Vogel?”

The word “How” in the source sequence is linked to the word “Wie” in the target sequence. Moreover, “bird” corresponds to “Vogel,” and “fly” translates to “fliegt” in German. Instead of analyzing the entire sequence, the focus shifts to specific sections that influence the prediction in the target sentence. The word “does” is given less importance, resulting in its hidden states in the context vector computation containing less information compared to terms like “bird” and “flight.”

This limitation can be overcome with the use of attention mechanisms. The power of attention mechanisms relies on the fact that these mechanisms only attend to the parts of the input sequence that are important for the prediction of the next word. These are the parts of the sentence that are then used to modify the state before producing the next prediction. This is essentially the idea that gave rise to the transformers.

The attention mechanisms were developed by Bahdanau and his team for sequence‐to‐sequence modeling tasks (Bahdanau et al. [2014](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0021)). It is a type of neural network architecture that is commonly used for applications that involve processing sequences of data, not only for machine translation (Neubig [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0245)) but also for speech recognition (Prabhavalkar et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0268)), and text summarization (Shi et al. [2021](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0315)).

![Figure 6.2 The Bahdanau attention mechanism. ¶ Source: Adapted from Bahdanau et al. (2014). At instant t, the decoder is fed with a linear combination bold c Subscript t of the forward section of the encoder recurrent network. The elements of the linear combination are attention coefficients that use the present decoder state and the forward states of the encoder.](images/c06f002.png)

[**Figure 6.2**](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-fig-0002) The Bahdanau attention mechanism. ¶ Source: Adapted from Bahdanau et al. ([2014](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0021)). At instant ![t](images/c06-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, the decoder is fed with a linear combination ![bold c Subscript t](images/c06-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> of the forward section of the encoder recurrent network. ### 6.2.3 Attention Pooling

In [Sections 6.2.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-sec-0003) and [6.2.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-sec-0005) we have seen different examples. In this section, a more formal definition of attention is derived, and all the concepts previously introduced are redefined for clarity.

Assume that a database is available where each entry ![i](images/c06-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> has two fields, namely a key ![bold k Subscript i](images/c06-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">k</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and a value ![bold v Subscript i](images/c06-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>. In order to retrieve values of interest, a query ![bold q](images/c06-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></mrow></math> is constructed and compared to all the keys in the database. A classic query would be, for example, a sentence written in SQL (a language used to construct queries in databases) that establishes a set of conditions. For example, in a people database, get all entries whose name is “Óscar García.” The result will retrieve the data (value) corresponding exclusively to the people with this name (used as a key). An approximate search will extend the results to those people whose name is “Oscar Garcia” (without the tildes) or “Óscar Garci,” people with longer names (“Óscar Gómez García”), or people with typos or alphabet code errors in their names (“&#243;scar Garc&#237;ia”). The approximate search can establish a score that denotes the degree of similarity between the query and the key. This is the idea of an attention mechanism, applied to any type of data.

Now assume a set of queries, keys, and values that have a representation as vectors constructed with real numbers, and that the result of the query is to be reconstructed as a linear combination of the retrieved values in a way formally equal to the Nadaraya–Watson regression in [Eq. (6.2)](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0002). The result of the query can be written as

[(6.9)](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-disp-0009)![bold z equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts alpha left-parenthesis bold q comma bold k Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis bold v Subscript i](images/c06-math-0009.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mi>&#945;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">k</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> 

where ![alpha left-parenthesis bold q comma bold k Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">k</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is the so‐called *attention score* between query ![bold q](images/c06-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></mrow></math> and key ![bold k Subscript i](images/c06-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">k</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, and its value is high if the similarity between both is high. Equation ([6.9](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0009)) is called an *attention pooling*. Representation ![bold z](images/c06-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow></math> is a result of the attention of the query toward all keys. The attention scores must satisfy a couple of properties, namely

(6.10)![StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column Blank 2nd Column 0 less-than-or-equal-to alpha left-parenthesis bold q comma bold k Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to 1 2nd Row 1st Column Blank 2nd Column sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts alpha left-parenthesis bold q comma bold k Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis equals 1 EndLayout](images/c06-math-0010.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable class="lmatrix"><mtr><mtd></mtd><mtd class="array"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">k</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd></mtd><mtd class="array"><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mi>&#945;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">k</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

This is, the linear combination in [Eq. (6.9)](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0009) must be convex. The scores must satisfy the properties of a probability mass function, something that is satisfied with the use of a softmax function. Therefore, in order to construct an attention pooling, an appropriate nonnegative function ![f left-parenthesis bold q comma bold k Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">k</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> that measures similarity between the query and the keys must be found and then all the similarity outputs must be processed with a softmax function to construct the set of scores as depicted in [Fig. 6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0004).

![Figure 6.4 Attention mechanism.](images/c06f004.png)

[**Figure 6.4**](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-fig-0004) Attention mechanism.

The dot product between vectors is an adequate similarity function. For a collection of vectors over a hypersphere of radius ![r](images/c06-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>, the dot product between two vectors is minimal (![minus r squared](images/c06-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>) if both vectors have opposite directions and it is maximal (![r squared](images/c06-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>) if both vectors are equal. But since the function must be not nonnegative, one can use the exponential of the negative dot product, which is then a nonnegative function. If the query ![bold q](images/c06-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></mrow></math> and the keys ![bold k Subscript i](images/c06-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">k</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> have a Euclidian norm that is approximately constant, then the softmax operation applied to these exponentials is

[(6.11)](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-disp-0011)![alpha left-parenthesis bold k Subscript i Baseline comma bold q right-parenthesis equals StartFraction exp left-parenthesis upper D Superscript 1 slash 2 Baseline bold q Superscript down-tack Baseline bold upper M bold k Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis Over sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts exp left-parenthesis upper D Superscript 1 slash 2 Baseline bold q Superscript down-tack Baseline bold upper M bold k Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis EndFraction](images/c06-math-0011.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#945;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">k</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">k</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mi>exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">k</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfrac></math> 

where the dot product is normalized with the length ![upper D](images/c06-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> of the query and key vectors and matrix ![bold upper M](images/c06-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi></mrow></math> is needed when the query and the key do not have the same dimension in order to map them into a common space. In this case, the operation is called a scaled dot product.

 

### 6.2.4 Representation by Self‐Attention

The idea of attention pooling can be implemented for machine learning. Assuming a sequence of ![upper N](images/c06-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> elements ![bold x 1 comma ellipsis comma bold x Subscript upper N Baseline](images/c06-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>N</mi></msub></math>, a representation of the entire sequence can be constructed as a function of the attention ![alpha Subscript i comma j Baseline equals alpha left-parenthesis bold k Subscript i Baseline comma bold q Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">k</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> of each one of the patterns over all the sequence. Representation

(6.12)![bold z Subscript j Baseline equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts alpha Subscript i comma j Baseline bold v Subscript i](images/c06-math-0012.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><msub><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> 

will then contain information on local and global relationships between elements of the sequence according to a similarity criterion, to be used for a given task.

In self‐attention, the queries, keys, and values are all represented by the elements of the sequence. Assuming that the dot product‐based attention in [Eq. (6.11)](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0011) is used to compute the attention coefficient between elements ![bold x Subscript i](images/c06-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![bold x Subscript j](images/c06-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub></math>, one of the elements will be playing the role of the query and the other will be the key. But this attention mechanism is very simple, and it is essentially a function of the angle between both vectors. If we want to make this comparison more powerful, we can transform the query and the key with a parameter matrix with arbitrary coefficients. The similarity criterion is then driven by the values of these two matrices, which need to have the same dimensions for the dot product to work. The value can also be mapped in a given space by a matrix. The queries, keys, and values are then transformed as ![bold q Subscript i Baseline equals bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis q right-parenthesis down-tack Baseline bold x Subscript i](images/c06-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, ![bold k Subscript i Baseline equals bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis down-tack Baseline bold x Subscript i](images/c06-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">k</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, and ![bold v Subscript i Baseline equals bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis v right-parenthesis down-tack Baseline bold x Subscript i](images/c06-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>. Matrices ![bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis q right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> and ![bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> must have the same size, while matrix ![bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis v right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> has arbitrary size. This structure is built this way for the parameters in the matrices to be easily trainable.

If matrix ![bold upper A](images/c06-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi></mrow></math> is constructed with entries ![alpha Subscript i comma j](images/c06-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> corresponding to the attention coefficients, and matrix ![bold upper X](images/c06-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></mrow></math> contains column vectors ![bold x Subscript i](images/c06-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> then the representation of all input data through the attention mechanism can be written as

### 6.2.5 Training the Self‐Attention Parameters

The parameter matrices that transform the data into queries, keys, and values are trainable by using the standard backpropagation method, according to, for example, to the ML criterion and a given task. For example, if a sequence ![bold x Subscript i](images/c06-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, ![1 less-than-or-equal-to i less-than-or-equal-to upper N](images/c06-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>N</mi></math> is available, the attention mechanism will produce a representation ![bold z Subscript i](images/c06-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>. This representation can be passed through a FC layer to perform a given pattern recognition task. In this simple structure, we only have three layers (see [Fig. 6.5](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0005)).

![Figure 6.5 Representation bold z Subscript j of a single element bold x Subscript j through dot product attention over a sequence of upper N elements processed through a dense layer with weights bold upper W to illustrate the backpropagation procedure. The output error is backpropagated to the output bold z Subscript j to update parameters bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis v right-parenthesis and then to the output of the softmax function in order to update bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis and bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis q right-parenthesis. The process must be repeated for all elements of the sequence.](images/c06f005.png)

[**Figure 6.5**](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-fig-0005) Representation ![bold z Subscript j](images/c06-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub></math> of a single element ![bold x Subscript j](images/c06-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub></math> through dot product attention over a sequence of ![upper N](images/c06-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> elements processed through a dense layer with weights ![bold upper W](images/c06-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow></math> to illustrate the backpropagation procedure. The output error is backpropagated to the output ![bold z Subscript j](images/c06-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub></math> to update parameters ![bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis v right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> and then to the output of the softmax function in order to update ![bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math> and ![bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis q right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>. The process must be repeated for all elements of the sequence.

The output of the fully connected layer will give an error ![bold-italic delta Subscript j](images/c06-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#948;</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub></math>, one error vector per element of the sequence. ### 6.2.6 Multi‐head Attention

The actual power of attention mechanisms consists of constructing representations that are a function of a diversity of attention modules. Each one of these modules is called an attention head, and a representation that combines different attention mechanisms is called a multi‐head attention mechanism.

![Figure 6.6 Multi‐head attention.](images/c06f006.png)

[**Figure 6.6**](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-fig-0006) Multi‐head attention.

The mechanism is illustrated in [Fig. 6.6](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0006), where a single query ![bold q Subscript j](images/c06-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub></math> is represented with the keys and values corresponding to element ![i](images/c06-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> of the sequence, to produce the scalar component ![z Subscript i comma j](images/c06-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> of the representation. In a self‐attention mechanism, the query is represented by element ![bold x Subscript j](images/c06-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub></math> of the sequence itself, and the key and value are represented by element ![bold x Subscript i](images/c06-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>. These values are linearly transformed ![upper S](images/c06-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math> times by arrays ![bold upper W Subscript s Superscript left-parenthesis q right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>, ![bold upper W Subscript s Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0110.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>, ![bold upper W Subscript s Superscript left-parenthesis v right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0111.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>. produces a vector ![bold h Subscript i comma j comma s](images/c06-i0112.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></math> which is a nonlinear operation of query ![j](images/c06-i0113.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> with key and value ![i](images/c06-i0114.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, to produce the attention element ![s](images/c06-i0115.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>, with the form

### 6.2.7 Positional Encoding

In machine‐to‐machine translation and other NLP applications, the position of each word relative to the sequence that is to be processed is fundamental for the meaning of the sentence. The same has to be said of the possible applications of attention mechanisms to other types of data, namely images or sequences of images, where the images are chinked into patches and introduced in an attention machine. The position of each patch inside the image is fundamental to interpreting the image and extracting knowledge from it.

Therefore, the elements of the sequences used as inputs must contain information about their position that can be used by these attention mechanisms. The concept of positional encoding was introduced with this purpose in Vaswani et al. ([2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0359)) for sequence translation. The authors point out that their model does not contain any recurrence or any convolutional operation that can take advantage of the positions from a structural point of view. In other words, if we introduce a sequence into a recurrent structure or a convolutional structure, it will produce an output. If we change the order of the elements, the output will be different. In an attention mechanism, the output will be the same, but with a different order. This is, the attention mechanism does not inherently capture the particularities of a different position of the sequences.

This inconvenience can be overcome by *injecting* positional information to each one of the elements by simply adding a positional vector to each element. This vector has to have the same length as the elements of the sequence. This idea was originally introduced by Gehring et al. ([2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0097)). Given a sequence of elements ![bold x overTilde Subscript i Baseline element-of double-struck upper R Superscript upper D](images/c06-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>D</mi></msup></math>, with components ![x overTilde Subscript i comma j](images/c06-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math>, subindex ![i](images/c06-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> represents the position of the element inside the sequence and ![j](images/c06-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> the position of each scalar inside each vector. Then, a positional encoding is applied as
