An immediate way of extending the RBM to the DL area is to construct a machine that stacks a series of RBM structures. Such models are known as a deep Boltzmann machine (DBM) (R. Salakhutdinov and G. Hinton [2009](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0299)). The advantage of this structure is that the training can be done layer‐wise since all layers are conditionally independent of each other given the previous and following layers. A DBN has the same structure, except that it is partially directed, which can be trained using a form of greedy layer‐wise algorithm.

 

## 7.3 Deep Belief Networks

The DBN (Geoffrey E. Hinton et al. [2006](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0136); Geoffrey E. Hinton [2007](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0132)) were the first nonconvolutional model that could be successfully trained when constructed as deep structures. Indeed, the existing deep models before the DBN were very hard to train since they posed many practical difficulties, and therefore, Kernel machines and the support vector machine (SVM) (see, e.g. Schölkopf and Sung ([1997](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0306)) and Smola et al. ([1998](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0321)) or Gaussian process (GP) (Rasmussen and C. K. I. Williams [2005](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0277))) were the most popular learning machines at that time (I. Goodfellow et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0111)).

In a DBN, the structure is constructed as a stack of RBM. This is because the structure has several layers of hidden units with no connections between nodes of the same layer. The hidden units are binary, but the input and output layers can have a continuous representation.

 

### 7.3.1 Training a DBN

The training of a DBM proposed by Hinton is simply to apply the contrastive divergence sequentially to each one of the layers starting from the input one (see e.g. (Yoshua Bengio et al. [2006](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0028))). It is proven that using this procedure, when a new layer is added, a bound on the training likelihood is increased (Geoffrey E. Hinton et al. [2006](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0136)). When it is necessary to fine‐tune it with labeled training data. For example, in Geoffrey E. Hinton et al. ([1995](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0135)), the wake‐sleep algorithm is proposed. After the fine‐tuning of the structure, a gradient descent can be applied with respect some criterion to continue training the model. For example, if the structure is to be used in supervised learning, the likelihood with respect to a set of desired outputs ![y Subscript k](images/c07-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> corresponding to training samples ![bold x Subscript k](images/c07-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub></math> can be used Kurup et al. ([2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0186)).

 

## 7.4 Autoencoders

An AE is an NN designed to compress input data into a meaningful representation and reconstruct it as closely as possible to the original data. Geoffrey Hinton and the parallel distributed processing (PDP) research group first introduced AEs in (Rumelhart [1986](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0295)). They aimed to solve the challenge of *backpropagation without a teacher* by utilizing the input data as a guide to the learning process. In a traditional supervised learning scenario, the labels provide the correct answers for training. AEs use unsupervised learning, where the model learns from the input data without explicit labels.

Over the past decade, starting around 2006, AEs have regained prominence within the framework of the deep architecture paradigm (Geoffrey E. Hinton et al. [2006](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0136); Geoffrey E. Hinton and R. R. Salakhutdinov [2006](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0133); Yoshua Bengio et al. [2007](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0029); Erhan et al. [2010](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0091)). During this time AEs, notably in the form of RBMs, were arranged hierarchically and trained in an unsupervised manner from the bottom up. Afterward, the process involved a supervised learning phase to train the top layer and refine the architecture. These architectures demonstrated exceptional performance on various classification and regression challenges.

AEs are *generative* models that can be used in many applications due to their ability to learn representations. These learned representations can be assumed to have useful properties which was translated to its many variants. A few of the common applications using AE architecture or its variants include facial recognition (Geoffrey E. Hinton et al. [2011](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0137); A. R. Kurup et al. [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0186)), compression, denoising, feature reduction, clustering, anomaly detection and image processing (Ye et al. [2018](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0384); Bando et al. [2018](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0022); Bevilacqua et al. [2008](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0037)).

 

### 7.4.1 Autoencoder Framework

An AE neural network represents an unsupervised learning algorithm that employs backpropagation, with the target values set to replicate the input data. The basic configuration of an AE is shown in [Fig. 7.4](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0004). It consists of three layers: the input layer, the hidden layer, and the output layer. The input layer, together with the hidden layers, serves as the encoder, while the hidden layer in conjunction with the output layers functions as the decoder. The AE operates by taking an input vector, ![bold x element-of upper R Subscript d](images/c07-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>, and initially transforming it into a hidden representation, ![bold h element-of upper R Subscript d](images/c07-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>, through a mapping function defined as:

![Figure 7.4 A fundamental view of the AE architecture, illustrating its encoder‐decoder structure.](images/c07f004.png)

[**Figure 7.4**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0004) A fundamental view of the AE architecture, illustrating its encoder‐decoder structure.

[(7.14)](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-disp-0014)![bold h equals sigma left-parenthesis bold upper W Superscript down-tack Baseline bold x plus bold b right-parenthesis](images/c07-math-0014.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

Here ![bold x](images/c07-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> represents input data and ![bold h](images/c07-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow></math> signifies latent variables within the information bottleneck (IB). The concept of IB (Tishby et al. [2000](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0355)), posits that it can extract essential information by compressing the data flow in the network. These compressed pieces of information are known as latent variables or representations. *Latent variables* are unobservable random variables extracted from the distribution, offering abstract insights into data topology and distribution. The equation ![f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis equals bold h](images/c07-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></math> forms the encoder part of the network. Conversely, to reconstruct the input, the decoder takes latent variables from the bottleneck and constructs a reverse mapping function, denoted as ![f prime left-parenthesis bold h right-parenthesis equals bold x prime](images/c07-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> which is defined as:

[(7.15)](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-disp-0015)![bold x prime equals sigma left-parenthesis bold upper W prime bold h plus bold b prime right-parenthesis](images/c07-math-0015.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

For example, consider an input image sized at ![28 times 28](images/c07-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>28</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>28</mn></math>. This image needs to be flattened before it can be fed into a neural network. When flattened, the representation becomes a vector of 784 elements, which is then inputted into the *encoder*. The output of the encoder is directed toward the bottleneck's latent space to create a compact representation. For instance, having 8, 16, or any other chosen number of nodes in the latent space indicates the effective reduction of a 784‐sized image into a more compact dimension. Subsequently, the *decoder* network endeavors to reconstruct the original ![28 times 28](images/c07-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>28</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>28</mn></math> input image from this compressed state within the bottleneck. After the image is reconstructed, a comparison is made between the reconstructed image and the original image. This involves calculating the difference and determining the loss.

The training process of an AE involves optimizing the model parameters ![left-parenthesis bold upper W comma bold upper W prime comma bold b comma](images/c07-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi><mo>,</mo></math> and ![bold b prime right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> to minimize the reconstruction error between the input data ![bold x](images/c07-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> and the reconstructed output ![bold x prime](images/c07-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>. This optimization is performed using an optimizer such as SGD and involves employing loss functions such as MSE or binary *cross‐entropy*, especially in binary scenarios. Consequently, this type of network is trained in an unsupervised manner with the objective of reproducing its input at the output layer.

The MSE is computed as the sum of squared differences between the individual data points:

The cross‐entropy error, represented as ![upper J Subscript upper C upper E Baseline left-parenthesis bold x comma bold x prime right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>E</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, is computed as a measure of dissimilarity between the input data ![bold x](images/c07-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> and the reconstructed output ![bold x prime](images/c07-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>. This error is quantified by evaluating the negative sum over all data points from 1 to ![upper N](images/c07-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> of a logarithmic expression. Specifically, it calculates the negative log‐likelihood of the reconstruction.

In recent years, the deep learning literature has witnessed the emergence of various AE architectures, each particularly designed to tackle specific challenges and tasks. Among the notable variants of AEs, the undercomplete AE stands out for its focus on acquiring compact and informative representations through constraints on the hidden layer's size, which encourages feature selection and compression. The denoising AE has been engineered to robustly learn meaningful features, even in the presence of noisy or corrupted input data, making it invaluable for noise reduction and data denoising tasks.

Meanwhile, convolutional AEs are proficient in handling structured data like images, utilizing convolutional layers to capture spatial hierarchies. This enables their use in applications such as image reconstruction, generation, and feature learning. Sparse AEs, another noteworthy variant, emphasizes the importance of sparsity in the learned representations. By promoting sparse activations in the hidden layer, these AEs encourage the selection of only the most essential features, enhancing interpretability and reducing redundancy. Lastly, variational autoencoders (VAEs) introduce probabilistic encoding, enabling AEs to effectively model data distributions and generate diverse samples.

## 7.5 Undercomplete Autoencoder

Undercomplete AE is the simplest architecture in the family of AEs. In general, AEs are unsupervised learning approaches where the neural network is trained to generate the copy of input at the output end (Buongiorno et al. [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0049)). In AE, the hidden layer ![bold h](images/c07-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow></math> generates a latent representation of the input data ![bold x](images/c07-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>. This latent representation is used to reconstruct the copy of the data. The encoder part generates the codes which gives a higher‐level representation of the data that needs to be reconstructed by the decoder layer. The number of layers in the encoder defines how well the input data is coded. In other words, the encoder layers need to approximate the data well so that it can reconstructed properly by the decoder.

An important factor in the level of compression that is achieved includes the input size and the size of the latent code. The AEs can be constructed in such a manner that either the size of the code is greater, smaller, or equal to that of the size of the input. When the size of the code is greater than the size of the input, such networks are called overcomplete AE. When the size of code and input are equal, they are complete AE. In undercomplete AEs, the latent code generated is a compressed representation of input, i.e. the size of code is lesser compared to that of the size of the input (see [Fig. 7.8](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0008)) (Thies and Alimohammad [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0348)). The idea behind undercomplete AE is to train a network that reconstructs the data using a smaller representation. This type of network focuses on learning the most significant features of the training data. Applications that commonly rely on these models include *compression* (Thies and Alimohammad [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0348)), image denoising (Dodda et al. [2022](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0078)), and anomaly detection (Sreenatha and Mallikarjuna [2023](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0329)).

The training criterion of undercomplete autoencoders is the same as that of the AE in general, i.e. using the train data to minimize the MSE which corresponds to the difference between actual input ![bold x](images/c07-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> and reconstructed output ![bold x prime](images/c07-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>. In general, the loss function corresponds to the following:

where the first term corresponds to the standard MSE, the second term is the weight regularization and the third term is for sparsity regularization. ![c 1](images/c07-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![c 2](images/c07-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> are the scaling factors to adjust the weight of each of the terms in the function. These regularization functions can be as simple as that of ![upper L 1](images/c07-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>, and ![upper L 0](images/c07-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> norms. These regularization techniques help with the generalization capabilities of the model.

 

## 7.6 Sparse Autoencoder

The basic architecture of autoencoders tries to approximate identity function since the ultimate aim of such models is to reconstruct the input. This might seem like a trivial solution. However, if we implement certain constraints to the network, i.e. by limiting a certain number of hidden units, we can learn interesting details as well as structures of the data (A. Ng et al. [2011](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0247); H. Lee et al. [2007](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0198)).

Consider we have an input size of ![n equals 100](images/c07-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></math> and we are trying to reconstruct this input using 50 hidden units. In this scenario, if the input features are Gaussian independently and identically distributed (i.i.d.), meaning there is no correlation between the input samples, the task of reconstruction might be difficult. However, if we have an input with some features that are correlated to each other, then we can assume that the neural network might be able to identify a few of those correlations in the data. This means the network can learn those correlations to reconstruct the input.

The above example points to a scenario where we have a lesser number of hidden units compared to the input. What if the number of hidden units is large? In such a case, the argument would be to impose certain constraints on the network. We can introduce **sparsity** constraint over the hidden units. This would enable the AE to learn the structure of data even with a large number of hidden units. Sparse autoencoder (SAE) shown in [Fig. 7.9](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0009) limits the constraints by penalizing activations within the layers using a sparsity parameter. This means that the network will be limited to certain specific attributes or features associated with the input. Given an observation, the model will try to encode and decode using only a smaller number of neurons at a time. The idea of sparse penalty term was inspired by sparse coding introduced in Olshausen and Field ([1996](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0253)).

Within the network, assuming sigmoid activation, a neuron can either be in an “active” state (outputs value close to 1) or an “inactive” state (outputs value close to 0). If we call the activation of ![i Superscript normal t normal h](images/c07-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi></mrow></msup></math> hidden unit as ![bold h Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for a given input ![bold x](images/c07-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>. The average activation of the hidden unit *i* (over the entire training set) which corresponds to the sparse penalty term (Jun Deng et al. [2013](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0076)) is given by

(7.19)![ModifyingAbove rho Subscript i Baseline With Ì‚ equals StartFraction 1 Over upper N EndFraction sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript upper N Endscripts bold h Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis bold x Subscript j Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-math-0019.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

where ![upper N](images/c07-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> corresponds to the number of input examples. Now this average activation of the hidden unit ![i](images/c07-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> can be approximately enforced to a parameter called *sparsity parameter* or sparsity level, ![rho](images/c07-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math>.

(7.20)![ModifyingAbove rho Subscript i Baseline With Ì‚ equals rho](images/c07-math-0020.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>&#961;</mi></math> ![Figure 7.9 SAE architecture. Node activations vary depending on the inputs. Therefore, not always the same nodes become inactive. ¶ Source: https://towardsdatascience.com/Medium.](images/c07f009.png)

[**Figure 7.9**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0009) SAE architecture. Node activations vary depending on the inputs. Therefore, not always the same nodes become inactive. ¶ Source: [https://towardsdatascience.com/Medium](https://towardsdatascience.com/Medium).

The sparsity parameter value is generally close to 0, for example, ![rho equals 0.05](images/c07-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></math>. This would push the hidden state activation to a near 0 value, making the hidden layer mostly “inactive” (W. Sun et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0332)). This sparsity parameter is now added to the objective function to penalize ![rho Subscript i](images/c07-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> in case it deviates significantly from ![rho](images/c07-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math>. This can be expressed using the penalty term:

(7.21)![upper P Subscript p e n a l t y Baseline equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper D Subscript l Baseline Endscripts bold-italic upper K bold-italic upper L left-parenthesis rho StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue rho Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-math-0021.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></munderover><mstyle mathvariant="bold-italic"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">K</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">L</mi></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

where ![upper D Subscript l](images/c07-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></math> is the number of neurons present in the hidden layer ![l](images/c07-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math>. ![bold-italic upper K bold-italic upper L left-parenthesis rho parallel-to rho Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mstyle mathvariant="bold-italic"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">K</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">L</mi></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>&#8741;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> corresponds to the KL divergence (Kullback and Leibler [1951](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0184)) given by:

(7.22)![bold-italic upper K bold-italic upper L left-parenthesis rho StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue rho Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis equals rho log StartFraction rho Over rho Subscript i Baseline EndFraction plus left-parenthesis 1 minus rho right-parenthesis log StartFraction 1 minus rho Over 1 minus rho Subscript i Baseline EndFraction](images/c07-math-0022.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mstyle mathvariant="bold-italic"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">K</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">L</mi></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mi>log</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>log</mi><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></math> 

The above approach makes sure that when ![rho equals rho Subscript i](images/c07-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, then the ![bold-italic upper K bold-italic upper L left-parenthesis rho StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue rho Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis equals 0](images/c07-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mstyle mathvariant="bold-italic"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">K</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">L</mi></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. Otherwise, when ![rho Subscript j](images/c07-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub></math> diverges from ![rho](images/c07-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math>, the ![bold-italic upper K bold-italic upper L left-parenthesis rho StartAbsoluteValue EndAbsoluteValue rho Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mstyle mathvariant="bold-italic"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">K</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">L</mi></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> increases monotonically. Hence, this acts like a sparsity constraint. Now, the overall cost function can be written as:

(7.23)![upper J Subscript s p Baseline left-parenthesis bold upper W comma bold b right-parenthesis equals upper J left-parenthesis bold upper W comma bold b right-parenthesis plus lamda sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript upper D Subscript l Baseline Endscripts bold-italic upper K bold-italic upper L left-parenthesis rho parallel-to rho Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-math-0023.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></munderover><mstyle mathvariant="bold-italic"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">K</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">L</mi></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>&#8741;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

where ![lamda](images/c07-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> is the weight of the sparsity penalty term. Note that the ![upper J Subscript s p Baseline left-parenthesis bold upper W comma bold b right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is directly related to parameters ![bold upper W](images/c07-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold b](images/c07-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow></math> and we need to minimize the cost function to obtain the two parameters. Again, the SGD approach is used to train this type of architecture, and the ![bold upper W](images/c07-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold b](images/c07-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow></math> get updated at each iteration. The forward pass computes the average activation ![rho Subscript i](images/c07-i0100.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> to obtain the sparse error. The BP helps with updating the weight and bias parameters. Using this approach the (SAE) learns the feature representations relevant for the reconstruction of input data.

 

## 7.7 Denoising Autoencoders

So far we have looked into AE models that have identical input and output as the main goal was to reconstruct the input and learn representations of it that would be relevant for reconstruction. Also, we looked into models that can perform this reconstruction using different strategies by modifying the number of layers or by putting a constraint on the hidden units. There can be applications where we need the AE model that learns generalizable coding to recreate the original data even if we pass corrupted data. *Denoising* is such an application where the input is noisy or corrupted data, while the expectation from the model is to provide a noiseless output.

Denoising autoencoder (DAE) (Vincent et al. [2008](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0360)) changes the reconstruction criterion for a more interesting and challenging objective of cleaning partially corrupted data, i.e. *denoising*. The assumption made for implementing this criteria is that: firstly, the higher‐level representation is expected to be robust and stable even under corruptions of input. Secondly, the denoising task helps with extracting useful features associated with the structure of input data and is a type of constraint that helps the model learn better. This would help the model to capture a better high‐level representation of the data (Vincent et al. [2010](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0361)).

 

### 7.7.1 Denoising Autoencoder Algorithm

Denoising autoencoder (DAE) is a variation of the traditional AE. As described before, the idea behind DAE is to retrieve the original clean input using the corrupted version of it (Ferles et al. [2018](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0093)). The first step in this approach is to corrupt the input data using a stochastic mapping given by:

(7.24)![ModifyingAbove bold x With Ì‚ tilde bold upper Q Superscript left-parenthesis d right-parenthesis Baseline left-parenthesis ModifyingAbove bold x With Ì‚ vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c07-math-0024.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>&#8764;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

where ![ModifyingAbove bold x With Ì‚](images/c07-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math> is the corrupted version of input ![bold x](images/c07-i0102.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>. Similar to [Eq. (7.14)](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0014), the input ![ModifyingAbove bold x With Ì‚](images/c07-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math> is encoded to a hidden representation given by:

(7.25)![bold h equals bold-italic sigma left-parenthesis bold upper W Superscript down-tack Baseline ModifyingAbove bold x With Ì‚ plus bold b right-parenthesis](images/c07-math-0025.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

where instead of the original input we pass the noisy input ![ModifyingAbove bold x With Ì‚](images/c07-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math>. Note that the parameters in the encoder part are the ![bold upper W Superscript down-tack](images/c07-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup></math> and ![bold b](images/c07-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow></math>. Further, the reconstruction is obtained similar to [Eq. (7.15)](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0015) given by:

(7.26)![bold x prime equals bold-italic sigma left-parenthesis bold upper W bold h plus bold b prime right-parenthesis](images/c07-math-0026.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

and the parameters associated with the decoder portion include ![bold upper W](images/c07-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold b prime](images/c07-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math>. Both sets of encoder and decoder parameters are trained to minimize the average reconstruction error on the training dataset. This means the idea is to have the ![bold x prime](images/c07-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> to be as close to the uncorrupted ![bold x](images/c07-i0110.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> as possible. Now, the main difference in the case of denoising is that the ![bold x prime](images/c07-i0111.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> is a deterministic function of ![ModifyingAbove bold x With Ì‚](images/c07-i0112.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math> rather than ![bold x](images/c07-i0113.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> as in AE. The loss function is either the cross‐entropy loss (![e Subscript c e Baseline left-parenthesis bold x comma bold x prime right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0114.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>) when using sigmoid combined with affine transformation in the decoder or the MSE loss (![e Subscript m s e Baseline left-parenthesis bold x comma bold x prime right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0115.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>) in case of just affine decoder. The parameters are initialized randomly, followed by optimization using stochastic gradient descent.

![Figure 7.10 The DAE architecture. ¶ Source: Adapted from Vincent et al. (2010).](images/c07f010.png)

[**Figure 7.10**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0010) The DAE architecture. ¶ Source: Adapted from Vincent et al. ([2010](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0361)).

It is to be noted that the same reconstruction error is being minimized between the clean ![bold x](images/c07-i0116.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> and reconstructed ![bold x prime](images/c07-i0117.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> which corresponds to maximization of the lower bound on mutual information between the reconstruction ![bold x prime](images/c07-i0118.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> and the clean noiseless version ![bold x](images/c07-i0119.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>. The main difference now is that ![bold x prime](images/c07-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup></math> is obtained using the deterministic mapping to the corrupted input ![ModifyingAbove bold x With bold Ì‚](images/c07-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mo mathvariant="bold">&#770;</mo></mover></mstyle></math> shown in [Fig. 7.10](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0010). This allows the model to learn the hidden representation through far more clever mapping than just identity mapping. This indeed aids with extracting useful features to aid the denoising application.

 

## 7.8 Convolutional Autoencoder

Convolutional autoencoder (CAE) combines the concept of CNNs introduced in [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml) and Autoencoder framework. Since CNNs are best known for their ability to model image data, (CAE) can be used for applications such as image compression (Akyazi and Ebrahimi [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0012); Cheng et al. [2018](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0055)), image denoising (Gondara [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0107)), anomaly detection (M. Ribeiro et al. [2018](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0285); Chow et al. [2020](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0061); Shen Yan et al. [2023](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0382)), etc.

Autoencoders pose the main limitation of not being able to capture the two‐dimensional details in an image or video frame sequences (Masci et al. [2011](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0221)). This can introduce redundancy in the network parameters which may de‐emphasize the local information associated with the images. Most of the successful object recognition models (Lowe [1999](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0213); Serre et al. [2005](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0312)) had the ability to extract localized scale‐invariant features that occurred repeatedly across the input. The concept of CAE was first introduced in Masci et al. ([2011](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0221)). Unlike the conventional AE, in CAE, the weights are shared across all the locations in input. This helps in preserving the spatial locality which is similar to CNN. In CAE, the latent representation is in the form of image patches. Hence, the linear combination of these image patches is used for reconstruction.

As for the CAE architecture, the concept is similar to the one described in [Section 7.4.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0010). Consider a single channel input ![bold x](images/c07-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>. Similar to [Eq. (7.14)](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0014), the latent representation of the ![k](images/c07-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>th feature map corresponding to input ![bold x](images/c07-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> is given by the following equation:

(7.27)![bold h Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline equals bold-italic sigma left-parenthesis bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline asterisk bold x plus bold b Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c07-math-0027.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#42;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

where the bias is broadcast across the whole map, ![sigma](images/c07-i0125.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> is the activation function and ![asterisk](images/c07-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></math> stands for the two‐dimensional convolutional operation between the weights of ![k Superscript normal t normal h](images/c07-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi></mrow></msup></math> feature map (![bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>) and the input. For each latent map, only a single bias is used. This is done to make sure that each filter specializes in features of the entire input as having different bias values per pixel might introduce many degrees of freedom. The reconstruction part is performed using the following equation:

Similar to the standard neural networks, the backpropagation algorithm is used to compute the gradient of the error function with respect to the parameters, i.e. ![bold upper W Superscript left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></math>. These weights are then further updated using the stochastic gradient descent approach.

?The translation‐invariance can be achieved in the case of CAE using a Maxpooling layer similar to CNNs. This layer helps with downsampling the latent representation using a constant factor. This factor is usually taken as the maximum value of the overlapping sub‐regions. The advantage of this approach is that it improves the selectivity of the filter as this approach considers the match that occurs between the feature and the input data over the region of interest. The max‐pooling operation used in the case of CAE erases the non‐maximal values in the nonoverlapping sub‐regions, introducing sparsity over hidden representations. This allows the feature detection process to be more broadly applicable, hence the common/trivial solutions are avoided. Further, during the reconstruction part, the sparse latent code formed using this approach decreases the number of filters required for decoding each pixel. Hence, the filters tend to be more general in nature. Subsequently, the max pool layers pose an advantage of not needing L1/L2 regularization overweights or hidden units.

 

## 7.9 Variational Autoencoders

There arise several challenges to performing inference and learning in directed probabilistic models with continuous latent variables that have intractable posterior distributions. In many cases, these posterior distributions cannot be computed analytically, making traditional approaches like exact Bayesian inference or Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) (Gilks et al. [1995](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0102)) computationally expensive. The variational Bayesian (VB) methodology is based on the notion of approximating intractable posterior distributions with more manageable alternatives. Rather than directly engaging with the intricacies of the complex posterior distribution, a selection is made from a family of distributions, referred to as the variational distribution. The optimization challenge consequently transforms into determining the member within this chosen family that best approximates the true posterior distribution. The closeness of approximation is measured by assessing the KL divergence, a mathematical metric used to quantify the dissimilarity between the variational distribution and the true posterior.

A common strategy in *probabilistic modeling* is the adoption of the mean‐field approximation (Honkela and Valpola [2004](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0148)), wherein the variational distribution is assumed to exhibit factorization properties, thereby helping the optimization process. This factorization implies that the complex problem can be deconstructed into simpler, independent components. However, despite this simplification, the calculation of expectations associated with this variational distribution may still pose computational challenges and remain intractable. To mitigate the challenges presented, one may employ the reparameterization trick (Kingma and Welling [2013](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0174)). This technique enables the representation of a random variable in terms of a deterministic function of another variable, coupled with a controlled source of randomness. This transformation facilitates differentiation through the previously random sampling process. Thus this method makes the process of optimizing a mathematical model suitable for use with SGD.

The stochastic gradient variational Bayes (SGVB) estimator is an estimator for the variational lower bound, a critical metric in probabilistic modeling and variational inference (VI). It is derived through the application of the reparameterization trick combined with Monte Carlo sampling to provide approximations for the expectations involved in the optimization process. This methodology facilitates the utilization of standard stochastic gradient ascent techniques in optimizing the variational lower bound. Meanwhile, the auto‐encoding variational Bayes (AEVB) algorithm is introduced while dealing with i.i.d. datasets and continuous latent variables. This algorithm leverages the SGVB estimator for the optimization of a recognition model. The role of this recognition model is to facilitate efficient approximate posterior inference through a process known as ancestral sampling. Ancestral sampling entails the incremental generation of samples layer by layer within the generative model. When this recognition model is implemented as a neural network, it gives rise to the concept of a VAE (Kingma and Welling [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0175)) (see [Fig. 7.15](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0015)). A VAE encompasses both an encoder network (the recognition model) and a decoder network (the generative model), thus enabling the acquisition of a probabilistic mapping between the data space and a lower‐dimensional latent space. Specifically, the encoder approximates the true posterior distribution of latent variables given the observed data, while the decoder generates data samples based on these latent variables.

The utility of the learned approximate posterior inference model, represented by the encoder network, extends beyond the training of the generative model. It finds application in various domains, including data point recognition, denoising by reconstructing clean data from noisy inputs, representation learning for extracting meaningful latent features, and data visualization techniques.

 

### 7.9.1 Latent Variable Inference: Lower Bound Estimation Approach

A *lower bound* estimator, characterized as a stochastic objective function, is derived for a range of directed graphical models featuring continuous latent variables. This analysis assumes an i.i.d. dataset with latent variables linked to each data point. The primary objectives encompass two phases: firstly, the calculation of ML or maximum A posteriori (MAP) inference concerning global parameters, and secondly, the VI of the latent variables.

Consider a dataset denoted as ![bold upper X](images/c07-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></mrow></math> comprising ![upper N](images/c07-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> i.i.d. samples, where each sample corresponds to either a continuous or discrete variable. These data are generated through a stochastic process involving an unobserved continuous random variable ![bold-italic z Subscript i](images/c07-i0139.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math>. This generative process encompasses two sequential steps. The initial step involves producing a value ![bold-italic z Subscript i](images/c07-i0140.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> drawn from a prior distribution ![p Subscript bold-italic theta Sub Superscript asterisk Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0141.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, followed by the subsequent step of generating a value ![bold x Subscript i](images/c07-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> from a conditional distribution ![p Subscript bold-italic theta Sub Superscript asterisk Baseline left-parenthesis bold x vertical-bar bold-italic z right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Both the prior distribution ![p Subscript bold-italic theta Sub Superscript asterisk Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and the conditional likelihood ![p Subscript bold-italic theta Sub Superscript asterisk Baseline left-parenthesis bold x vertical-bar bold-italic z right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> are assumed to originate from parametric distribution families identified as ![p Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![p Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline left-parenthesis bold x vertical-bar bold-italic z right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, respectively. Additionally, the probability density functions (PDF) associated with these distributions demonstrate differentiability at nearly all points w.r.t both model parameters ![bold-italic theta](images/c07-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></math> and latent variables ![bold-italic z](images/c07-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi></mrow></math>. Throughout this generative procedure, the true values of the parameters ![bold-italic theta Superscript asterisk](images/c07-i0150.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></math> and the latent variables ![bold-italic z Subscript i](images/c07-i0151.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> remain unknown. Here, the integral of the marginal likelihood ![p Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis equals integral p Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z right-parenthesis p Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline left-parenthesis bold x vertical-bar bold-italic z right-parenthesis d bold-italic z](images/c07-i0152.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8747;</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi></math> poses significant computational challenges, making it intractable to calculate its derivative. Consequently, determining the true posterior density ![p Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis equals StartFraction p Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline left-parenthesis bold x vertical-bar bold-italic z right-parenthesis p Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z right-parenthesis Over p Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis EndFraction](images/c07-i0153.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></math> becomes an infeasible task. These intractable computations are commonly encountered in scenarios involving moderately complex likelihood functions, as observed in neural networks with non‐linear hidden layers. [Figure 7.14](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0014) shows the *intractable posterior* distribution of the generative model.

To address the aforementioned challenges effectively, a recognition model denoted as ![q Subscript bold-italic phi Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0159.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is introduced, serving as an approximation to the true posterior ![p Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. In contrast to typical factorized approximate posteriors in mean‐field VI, ![q Subscript bold-italic phi Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> doesn't necessarily adhere to a factorial structure, and its parameters ![bold-italic phi](images/c07-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></math> are not derived from closed‐form expectations. Instead, a methodology is proposed for jointly learning the recognition model parameters ![bold-italic phi](images/c07-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></math> alongside the generative model parameters ![bold-italic theta](images/c07-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></math>. Here the latent variables ![bold-italic z](images/c07-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi></mrow></math> can be interpreted as latent representations. Therefore, ![q Subscript bold-italic phi Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0166.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is also referred to as a probabilistic encoder because, given an input data point ![bold x](images/c07-i0167.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>, it generates a distribution encompassing the potential values of the latent representation ![bold-italic z](images/c07-i0168.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi></mrow></math>. Similarly, ![p Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline left-parenthesis bold x vertical-bar bold-italic z right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0169.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is termed a probabilistic decoder since, given a latent code latent representation ![bold-italic z](images/c07-i0170.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi></mrow></math>, it produces a distribution covering the possible corresponding values of ![bold x](images/c07-i0171.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>. This encoder–decoder framework plays a pivotal role in unraveling the hidden structures within the data.

Within the ELBO, the KL term acts as a regularizer, imposing constraints on the form of the approximate posterior. Meanwhile, the second term is termed a reconstruction term as it quantifies the likelihood of the data's reconstruction by the decoder. The objective is to differentiate and optimize the lower bound with regard to both the variational parameters ![bold-italic phi](images/c07-i0179.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></math> and the generative parameters ![bold-italic theta](images/c07-i0180.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></math>. However, the gradient concerning the variational parameters ![bold-italic phi](images/c07-i0181.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></math> poses challenges. The conventional method, the Monte Carlo gradient estimator, exhibits significant variance, rendering it impractical for the intended purposes.

 

### 7.9.2 Reparameterization Trick

The challenges associated with estimating the lower bound and its parameter derivatives prompted the introduction of a pragmatic estimation method. This approach relies on an approximate posterior distribution, denoted as ![q Subscript bold-italic phi Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> tailored to capture the latent variables given the observed data ![bold x](images/c07-i0183.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math>. Within this framework, a *reparameterization* technique is employed, wherein the continuous random variable ![bold-italic z tilde q Subscript bold-italic phi Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0184.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is expressed as a deterministic variable ![bold-italic z equals g Subscript bold-italic phi Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic epsilon comma bold x right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0185.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mstyle mathvariant="bold-italic"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi></mstyle><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Here ![bold-italic epsilon](images/c07-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mstyle mathvariant="bold-italic"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi></mstyle></math> is an auxiliary noise variable characterized by an independent marginal distribution ![p left-parenthesis bold-italic epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mstyle mathvariant="bold-italic"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and ![g Subscript bold-italic phi Baseline left-parenthesis period right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>.</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> represents a vector‐valued function parameterized by ![bold-italic phi](images/c07-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></math>. This transformation enables us to efficiently compute gradients and derivatives, facilitating parameter optimization.

The reparameterization proves advantageous as it allows to reformulate the expectation w.r.t ![q Subscript bold-italic phi Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. This transformation yields a Monte Carlo estimate of the expectation that can be easily differentiated w.r.t ![bold-italic phi](images/c07-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></math>. Given the deterministic mapping of ![bold-italic z](images/c07-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi></mrow></math>

### 7.9.3 Illustration: Variational Autoencoder Implementation

In this section, the focus is on an illustrative example involving the application of a neural network as the probabilistic encoder, represented as ![q Subscript bold-italic phi Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. This encoder plays a crucial role in approximating the posterior distribution within the generative model, ![p Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline left-parenthesis bold x comma bold-italic z right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Furthermore, the AEVB algorithm is employed to jointly optimize two parameter sets denoted as ![bold-italic theta](images/c07-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold-italic phi](images/c07-i0204.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></math>.

![Figure 7.15 VAE architecture. ¶ Source: Addo et al. (2022)/MDPI/CC by 4.0.](images/c07f015.png)

[**Figure 7.15**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0015) VAE architecture. ¶ Source: Addo et al. ([2022](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0004))/MDPI/CC by 4.0.

Assume that the prior distribution governing the latent variables adopts a specific form, characterized as the centered isotropic multivariate Gaussian, and denoted as ![p Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z right-parenthesis equals script í’© left-parenthesis bold-italic z semicolon 0 comma bold upper I right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0205.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#54441;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo>;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. In the case of the data distribution, ![p Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline left-parenthesis bold x vertical-bar bold-italic z right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0206.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, two scenarios are considered: a multivariate Gaussian for continuous data and a Bernoulli for binary data. In both cases, the distribution parameters are derived from ![z](images/c07-i0207.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> using a neural network referred to as an MLP. It is important to note that the true posterior distribution, ![p Subscript bold-italic theta Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0208.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, remains intractable. In these scenarios, it can be assumed that the true posterior distribution has an approximate Gaussian shape with an almost diagonal spread. Thus, it is feasible to employ a variational approximate posterior ![q Subscript bold-italic phi Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic z vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c07-i0209.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> that resembles a multivariate Gaussian with a diagonal spread pattern.

## 7.10 Conclusion

This chapter gives a comprehensive outline of deep unsupervised learning. Here we discuss two main categories of deep unsupervised learning: probabilistic and non‐probabilistic models. Here, we focus on two powerful structures used in unsupervised learning: DBNs and AE. Both these architectures are crucial pillars in the field of neural networks as they facilitate the extraction of meaningful features from complex high‐dimensional data. We talk about RBMs and its training criterion. Following this, we introduce DBNs where the basic elements of the DBN architecture are discussed in detail along with the contrastive divergence training. DBNs come under the category of probabilistic models and it is known for its ability to learn complex features in an unsupervised manner. The strength of DBN lies in its ability to undergo unsupervised training and subsequent fine‐tuning using methods such as backpropagation. The training of the DBN as well as its extensions are discussed in detail. the higher‐level abstractions learned by DBN is used for various application such as speech recognition, image processing, computer vision, etc.

Autoencoders, on the other hand, learn representations of the data that are compact and efficient. Their ability to summarize the data representation is instrumental in applications such as dimensionality reduction, denoising, compression, etc. The learning of AE happens through the encoder and decoder framework. It is through this encoder–decoder setup that the AE learn meaningful information from the raw input data. We further discuss the complete architecture of the AE. We defined the training methodology of these structures in general. Later on, we cover the extensions of AEs such as DAE, CAE, and VAE being a few of them. The applications of AE span various domains of data analysis and pattern recognition. As we move forward exploring more Deep learning architectures, these concepts will continue to evolve and get extended to develop more complex architectures and models.
