### 8.6.1 cGAN Training and Outcomes Highlights

The *conditional adversarial neural network* was trained on MNIST images, where each image was conditioned on a class label represented as a one‐hot vector. In the generator network, a random noise vector ![bold-italic z](images/c08-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi></mrow></math> of length 100 was sampled from a uniform distribution within a unit hypercube. Both the noise vector ![bold-italic z](images/c08-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi></mrow></math> and the class label vector ![bold y](images/c08-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math> were processed through hidden layers with ReLU activation. These hidden layers had sizes of 200 and 1000 units, respectively, and the outputs of these two sets of hidden layers were combined into a single hidden layer with 1200 units. Finally, there was a final output layer with a sigmoid activation function responsible for generating 784‐dimensional MNIST samples.

The discriminator network processed the input image ![bold x](images/c08-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> through a MaxOut layer with 240 units and 5 pieces or groups. In this setup, each of these five groups within the MaxOut layer operated as a distinct set of neurons, with the output being determined by the neuron within each group that exhibited the highest activation for the given input. On the other hand, the class label ![bold y](images/c08-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math> was processed through a MaxOut layer with 50 units and 5 pieces. Both hidden layers were then combined into a joint MaxOut layer with 240 units and 4 pieces before being passed through a sigmoid layer.

The training process for the model employed SGD with mini‐batches of 100 samples. Initially, a learning rate of 0.1 was used, and this learning rate was gradually reduced exponentially to reach 0.000001, with a decay factor of 1.00004. Additionally, momentum was incorporated into the training process, starting with an initial value of 0.5 and gradually increasing to 0.7. To prevent overfitting, a dropout with a probability of 0.5 was applied to both the generator and discriminator networks. The stopping point during training was determined by relying on the log‐likelihood estimate obtained from the validation set.

Furthermore, conditional adversarial networks were employed for the automated tagging of images with multilabel predictions. In this approach, image characteristics are extracted using a pre‐trained convolutional model trained on the ImageNet dataset, while textual representations are generated from a collection of user‐generated tags, titles, and descriptions sourced from the YFCC100M dataset (Thomee et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0349)). The training process encompasses the utilization of fixed convolutional and language models during adversarial network training. Experiments were conducted on the MIR Flickr 25,000 dataset, with the exclusion of images that lacked any tags. The model's training process closely resembled that of the MNIST dataset training. The hyperparameters and architectural decisions were determined through a combination of cross‐validation and a blend of random grid search and manual selection.

 

## 8.7 CycleGAN

CycleGAN (Zhu et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0399)) is a novel method presented to tackle the problem of image‐to‐image translation without the need for paired training data. Image‐to‐image translation (Isola et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0159)) involves transforming an image from one representation to another, such as converting grayscale images to color or mapping edge‐maps (simplified sketches outlining the shapes and contours of objects in an image) to photographic images. Extensive research efforts spanning the domains of computer vision, image processing, computational photography, and graphics have yielded robust translation systems in supervised settings (Eigen and Fergus [2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0087); Hertzmann et al. [2023](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0128); Johnson et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0163)). These systems operate effectively when provided with pairs of example images. However, acquiring such paired data can be challenging and resource‐intensive for various applications. For instance, datasets suitable for tasks like semantic segmentation (Cordts et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0068)) are relatively scarce and typically of limited scale. Acquiring input–output pairs for graphics‐related tasks, such as artistic stylization, can be even more demanding, given the intricacy of the desired output, often necessitating the involvement of artistic expertise. In numerous cases, such as object transfiguration, where, for instance, a zebra needs to be transformed into a horse, defining the precise desired output becomes a complex process.

Numerous methods were designed to overcome the need for paired training examples. For instance, Rosales et al. Resales et al. ([2003](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0283)) propose a Bayesian framework that combines a prior derived from a patch‐based Markov random field computed from a source image and a likelihood term obtained from multiple style images. More recently, approaches like CoGAN (M.‐Y. Liu and Tuzel [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0208)) and cross‐modal scene networks (Aytar et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0019)) utilize a weight‐sharing strategy to learn a shared representation across domains. Concurrently, Liu and collaborators (M.‐Y. Liu et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0209)) extend the above framework by incorporating a combination of VAE and GAN. Another parallel line of research (Shrivastava et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0317); Taigman et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0342); Bousmalis et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0047)) promotes the sharing of specific content features between input and output, even in the presence of style differences. These methods also leverage adversarial networks and introduce additional terms to ensure the output's proximity to the input within predefined metric spaces, such as class label space, image pixel space, and image feature space.

In contrast to the methods mentioned earlier, CycleGAN does not depend on a task‐specific, pre‐defined similarity measure between the input and output, nor does it make an assumption that the input and output must exist within the same low‐dimensional embedding space. This characteristic renders CycleGAN to be a versatile solution applicable to a wide range of vision and graphics tasks. The fundamental assumption here is that an underlying connection exists between these domains, implying that they represent different portrayals of the same underlying scene. The primary goal is to uncover this hidden relationship through the training of a mapping function represented as ![upper G colon upper X right-arrow upper Y](images/c08-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>Y</mi></math>. This entails utilizing one set of images in the domain ![upper X](images/c08-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and another set in the domain ![upper Y](images/c08-i0150.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>. The objective is to ensure that the resulting output, denoted as ![ModifyingAbove bold y With Ì‚ equals upper G left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0151.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for any ![x](images/c08-i0152.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> in ![upper X](images/c08-i0153.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>, closely resembles the images in ![upper Y](images/c08-i0154.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>. This is achieved by training an adversary to differentiate between ![ModifyingAbove bold y With Ì‚](images/c08-i0155.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math> and ![bold y](images/c08-i0156.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math>. Thus, the optimal ![upper G](images/c08-i0157.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> consequently transforms domain ![upper X](images/c08-i0158.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> into a domain ![modifying above upper Y with caret](images/c08-i0159.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#374;</mi></mrow></math> that follows the same distribution as ![upper Y](images/c08-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>. It is important to note that this approach does not ensure a one‐to‐one correspondence between individual input and output images, as there exist infinitely many mappings ![upper G](images/c08-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> that can induce the same distribution over ![ModifyingAbove bold y With Ì‚](images/c08-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math>. Additionally, in practice, optimizing the adversarial objective on its own often leads to a phenomenon referred to as *mode collapse*, where all input images map to the same output image, hindering the optimization process.

To address these challenges, a structured approach is introduced that relies on the concept of cycle consistency. This implies that when a sentence undergoes translation, such as from English to French and subsequently from French to English, it should be possible to restore the original sentence. In mathematical terms, if there's a translator ![upper G colon upper X right-arrow upper Y](images/c08-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>Y</mi></math> and another translator ![upper F colon upper Y right-arrow upper X](images/c08-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>F</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>X</mi></math>, both ![upper G](images/c08-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper F](images/c08-i0166.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> should function as inverses of each other, establishing one‐to‐one mappings between the two domains. To ensure this property, both ![upper G](images/c08-i0167.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper F](images/c08-i0168.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> are trained simultaneously, and a *cycle consistency loss* (Zhou et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0398)) is introduced. This loss function encourages the condition ![upper F left-parenthesis upper G left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis almost-equals bold x](images/c08-i0169.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></math> and ![upper G left-parenthesis upper F left-parenthesis bold y right-parenthesis right-parenthesis almost-equals bold y](images/c08-i0170.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></math>. By combining this loss with adversarial losses applied to domains ![upper X](images/c08-i0171.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper Y](images/c08-i0172.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>, a comprehensive objective for unpaired image‐to‐image translation is formulated. Here the two domains ![upper X](images/c08-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper Y](images/c08-i0174.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math> has training samples ![left-brace x Subscript i Baseline right-brace Subscript i equals 1 Superscript upper N](images/c08-i0175.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></math> where ![x Subscript i Baseline element-of upper X](images/c08-i0176.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>X</mi></math> and ![left-brace y Subscript i Baseline right-brace Subscript i equals 1 Superscript upper N](images/c08-i0177.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></math> where ![y Subscript i Baseline element-of upper Y](images/c08-i0178.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>Y</mi></math>. The data distribution is denoted as ![bold x tilde p Subscript d a t a Baseline left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0179.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![bold y tilde p Subscript d a t a Baseline left-parenthesis bold y right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0180.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. As depicted in [Fig. 8.8](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0008), this model presents two mapping functions: ![upper G colon upper X right-arrow upper Y](images/c08-i0181.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>Y</mi></math> and ![upper F colon upper Y right-arrow upper X](images/c08-i0182.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>F</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>X</mi></math>, along with corresponding adversarial discriminators, ![upper D Subscript upper Y](images/c08-i0183.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></math> and ![upper D Subscript upper X](images/c08-i0184.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></math>. Here ![upper D Subscript upper Y](images/c08-i0185.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></math>'s role is to encourage ![upper G](images/c08-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> to translate ![upper X](images/c08-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math> into outputs that are indistinguishable from those in domain ![upper Y](images/c08-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>, while ![upper D Subscript upper X](images/c08-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></math> performs a similar task in the reverse direction with ![upper F](images/c08-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math>. The objective includes two types of terms: adversarial losses, which aim to align the distribution of generated images with the data distribution in the target domain, and cycle consistency losses, which serve to ensure that the learned mappings ![upper G](images/c08-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper F](images/c08-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> do not contradict each other.

where ![upper G](images/c08-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> is tasked with generating images ![upper G left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0196.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> that closely resemble samples from domain ![upper Y](images/c08-i0197.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>, while ![upper D Subscript upper Y](images/c08-i0198.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></math>'s role is to differentiate between generated samples ![upper G left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0199.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and authentic samples ![bold y](images/c08-i0200.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math>. The objective here is for ![upper G](images/c08-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> to minimize this function, while its adversary ![upper D](images/c08-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> aims to maximize it. This can be mathematically represented as ![min Underscript upper G Endscripts max Underscript upper D Subscript upper Y Endscripts upper J left-parenthesis upper G semicolon upper D Subscript upper Y Baseline semicolon upper X semicolon upper Y right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>min</mi></mrow><mi>G</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mi>max</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

Nonetheless, if a network possesses sufficient capacity and complex function‐processing capabilities, it has the potential to transform the same input images into multiple random permutations within the target domain. Therefore, relying solely on adversarial losses cannot ensure that the learned function can accurately map an individual input, represented as ![x Subscript i](images/c08-i0204.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> to a desired output, denoted as ![y Subscript i](images/c08-i0205.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>. *Cycle consistency* is used to address this challenge and narrow down the space of possible mapping functions. Hence for every image ![bold x](images/c08-i0206.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> from domain ![upper X](images/c08-i0207.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>, the image translation cycle should have the ability to bring ![bold x](images/c08-i0208.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> back to its original form: ![bold x right-arrow upper G left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis right-arrow upper F left-parenthesis upper G left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis almost-equals bold x](images/c08-i0209.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></math>. This property is referred to as *forward cycle consistency*. Similarly, for each image ![y](images/c08-i0210.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> from domain ![upper Y](images/c08-i0211.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>, the functions ![upper G](images/c08-i0212.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper F](images/c08-i0213.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> should also exhibit backward cycle consistency: ![y right-arrow upper F left-parenthesis bold y right-parenthesis right-arrow upper G left-parenthesis upper F left-parenthesis bold y right-parenthesis right-parenthesis almost-equals bold y](images/c08-i0214.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></math>. The overall cycle consistency loss function can be expressed as follows:

### 8.7.1 CycleGAN Training and Outcomes Highlights

The architectural framework for the generative networks is drawn from the work of Johnson and their colleagues Johnson et al. ([2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0163)), who demonstrated impressive results in neural style transfer and super‐resolution. This network structure comprises three convolutional layers, along with several residual blocks (He et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0126)), two *fractionally strided convolutions* with a stride of ![one half](images/c08-i0216.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>, and a final convolutional layer responsible for mapping features to RGB values. For images of size ![128 times 128](images/c08-i0217.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>128</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>128</mn></math>, six blocks are used, while for images of ![256 times 256](images/c08-i0218.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>256</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>256</mn></math> resolution and higher, nine blocks are employed. In the case of the discriminator networks, the architecture employed consists of a ![70 times 70](images/c08-i0219.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>70</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>70</mn></math> PatchGANs (Ledig et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0197)). These discriminator networks are designed to classify whether ![70 times 70](images/c08-i0220.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>70</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>70</mn></math> overlapping image patches are genuine or generated.

In the model training procedure of cost function ![upper J](images/c08-i0221.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>J</mi></mrow></math>, the *negative log‐likelihood* objective has been replaced with a least‐squares loss. This change in the loss function is known to be more stable during training and results in higher‐quality outcomes. Specifically, for ![upper J left-parenthesis upper G semicolon upper D semicolon upper X semicolon upper Y right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0222.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, the approach is to train the generator ![upper G](images/c08-i0223.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> to minimize ![double-struck upper E Subscript bold x tilde p Sub Subscript d a t a Subscript left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis Baseline left-bracket left-parenthesis upper D left-parenthesis upper G left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis minus 1 right-parenthesis squared right-bracket](images/c08-i0224.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>. The discriminator ![upper D](images/c08-i0225.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is also trained to minimize ![double-struck upper E Subscript bold y tilde p Sub Subscript d a t a Subscript left-parenthesis bold y right-parenthesis Baseline left-bracket left-parenthesis upper D left-parenthesis bold y right-parenthesis minus 1 right-parenthesis squared right-bracket plus double-struck upper E Subscript bold x tilde p Sub Subscript d a t a Subscript left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis Baseline left-bracket left-parenthesis upper D left-parenthesis upper G left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis right-parenthesis squared right-bracket](images/c08-i0226.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8764;</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>. Meanwhile, when the model's performance fluctuates during training, instead of updating the discriminators solely based on images generated by the latest generators, an image buffer storage mechanism is employed to retain the 50 most recent images generated by the generator. This buffer likely maintains a history of generated images over training iterations. This provides a more stable and consistent set of training examples for the discriminator, facilitating better convergence of the GAN. Further, the networks start training with a constant learning rate of 0.0002 for 100 epochs, followed by linear decay to zero over the next 100 epochs. In all the experiments the parameter ![lamda](images/c08-i0227.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math> is set to be 10 and the Adam solver has a batch size of 1.

The CycleGAN model is assessed in comparison to several baseline methods through a combination of qualitative and quantitative metrics. This evaluation encompasses two main objectives: first, the translation of semantic labels into images, a task conducted using the Cityscapes dataset (Cordts et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0068)), and second, the transformation of maps into aerial photographs using data sourced from Google Maps. Furthermore, perceptual studies are conducted on Amazon Mechanical Turk to gauge the realism of the model's generated outputs. In these perceptual studies, participants are presented with pairs of images, one being authentic and the other generated either by the CycleGAN or alternative methods. Participants are then instructed to determine which image they believe to be real.

While perceptual studies are the established benchmark for evaluating graphical realism, the evaluation of the Cityscapes labels‐to‐photo task employs an automated quantitative metric like the FCN score, as depicted in [Table 8.1](#c08.xhtml#c08-tbl-0001). The FCN metric assesses the interpretability of the generated photos using an off‐the‐shelf semantic segmentation algorithm known as the FCN. The FCN generates a label map for a given generated photo, which can then be compared to the input ground truth labels using standard semantic segmentation metrics such as per‐pixel accuracy, per‐class accuracy, and mean class IoU. The underlying concept is that if a photo is generated from a label map specifying “car on the road,” it is considered successful if the FCN applied to the generated photo correctly identifies “car on the road.”

[**Table 8.1**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-tbl-0001)  Comparison of FCN scores of CycleGAN with various baseline models using the Cityscapes dataset.

| Methods || CoGAN || BiGAN || SimGAN || Feature loss + GAN || pix2pix || CycleGAN |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Per‐pixel acc || 0.40 || 0.19 || 0.20 || 0.06 || 0.71 || 0.52 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Per‐class acc || 0.10 || 0.06 || 0.10 || 0.04 || 0.25 || 0.17 |
| Class IoU || 0.06 || 0.02 || 0.04 || 0.01 || 0.18 || 0.11 |

 

### 8.7.2 Applications of CycleGAN

CycleGAN demonstrates its versatility in various tasks, even when paired training data is limited or unavailable. The major applications of CycleGAN are as follows:

*   **Collection style transfer:** This application involves training the model on landscape photographs from sources like Flickr and WikiArt. Unlike traditional *neural style transfer*, this method aims to mimic the style of entire collections of artworks, allowing for the generation of photos in the style of specific artists like Cezanne, Monet, Van Gogh, or Ukiyo‐e. The dataset includes a substantial number of images for each artist.
*   **Object transfiguration:** In this application, the model is trained to translate one object class from the ImageNet dataset to another. Each object class contains around 1000 training images. Unlike some approaches that focus on translating objects within the same category, this method aims to transform objects between visually similar categories.
*   **Season transfer:** This application involves training the model on a dataset of winter and summer photos of Yosemite, downloaded from Flickr. The goal is to translate images between these two seasonal contexts, allowing for transformations from winter scenes to summer scenes and vice versa.
*   **Photo generation from paintings:** For this task, the model translates paintings into photographs. To improve the quality of translations, an additional loss is introduced to encourage color composition preservation between input and output. This helps in ensuring that the generated photos maintain the color integrity of the original paintings.
*   **Photo enhancement:** In this application, the model is trained on flower photos from Flickr. The source domain comprises smartphone photos with deep depth of field (DoF) due to a small aperture, while the target domain consists of DSLR photos with shallower DoF due to a larger aperture. The model successfully generates photos with shallower DoF, enhancing the aesthetic quality of smartphone photos.

 

## 8.8 StyleGAN

Computer vision applications demand higher resolution and quality of images. It has been observed through various applications that networks inspired from GANs have been able to produce high‐resolution and good‐quality images over the years. The style transfer technique in computer vision is an application that is explored a lot using different architectures inspired from GANs. The *StyleGAN* architecture was introduced to control the image synthesis process and this architecture was motivated by the style transfer literature (X. Huang and Belongie [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0152)). StyleGAN was first introduced by NVIDIA researchers in late 2018 (Karras et al. [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0169)). Following the main version, other subsequent versions such as StyleGAN2 (Karras et al. [2020a](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0170)) and StyleGAN2‐ADA (Karras et al. [2020b](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0171)) were also released which refined the architecture as well as training methodology. The StyleGAN architecture makes use of the intermediate latent space to perform controlled image modifications, i.e. the architecture will be able to modify a given image rather than the randomly generated one by GANs (Abdal et al. [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0002)).

The GAN inspired architectures have seen their rapid utilization in the field of computer vision with fast‐paced improvements in image quality and resolution generated by such networks. DCGAN introduced in [Section 8.5](#c08.xhtml#c08-sec-0008) was the first milestone to use the fully CNN in GANs. Following this various other architectures came up in different computer vision applications with improvements in different training aspects such as loss functions (Mao et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0218); Arjovsky et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0018)), normalization or regularization (Miyato et al. [2018](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0232); Gulrajani et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0117)), as well as based on the architecture (Gulrajani et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0117)). The computational power was always a question for achieving high‐quality training and most of the testing was performed on poor‐quality and low‐resolution image datasets due to the high computational demand. This computation issue was addressed in the work of Karras *et al*. Karras et al. ([2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0168)) where they collected and created a high‐quality human face dataset CelebA‐HQ and introduced a progressive methodology for training GANs over higher‐resolution input for image generation tasks. The architecture was called ProGAN and it was the first GAN model to generate realistic ![1024 times 1024](images/c08-i0228.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1024</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1024</mn></math> high‐resolution human face images. However, the training and generation using complex datasets such as ImageNet was still a challenge. Later on, in Brock et al. ([2018](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0048)), using the BigGAN model, it was argued that the training of GANs can be improved by using a larger batch size. Following this Karras et al., came up with another much more diverse and high‐quality human face dataset called Flickr‐Faces‐HQ (FFHQ). Using this dataset StyleGAN was introduced which improved the performance of GANs especially on the human face image generation tasks.

StyleGAN architecture re‐designs the generator architecture to expose novel approaches that would accommodate the controlling of the image synthesis process. The generator, in this case, adjusts to the “style” of the image at each convolutional layer. It starts with a learned constant input and the modification to adjust the “style” is learned based on the latent code. This would allow the architecture to directly control the strength of the features of the image even at different scales. Additionally, noise is also injected into the network which enables it to perform scale‐specific interpolation operations and mixing. This architecture does not change or modify the discriminator network or the loss function and focuses on only improving the generator part of the GAN network.

Unlike the traditional generator, in StyleGAN the input latent code is embedded into an intermediate latent space which captures the variation represented in the network. Also, the input latent space must be aligned with the probability density of the training data which might lead to some entanglement. It is claimed that the latent space is unrestrictive, the degree of entanglement is explained using two automated metrics: perceptual path and linear separability. Using these metrics, later it is shown that StyleGAN generator architecture allows more linear as well as less entangled representations with different variation factors compared to that of the traditional generator architecture.

![Figure 8.10 (a) Traditional vs (b) style‐based generator. ¶ Source: Karras, Laine, and Aila 2019 / IEEE / Public Domain.](images/c08f010.png)

[**Figure 8.10**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0010) (a) Traditional vs (b) style‐based generator. ¶ Source: Karras, Laine, and Aila [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0169) / IEEE / Public Domain.

In a traditional generator, the input latent code is provided using an input layer which is the first layer of the feedforward network, as shown in [Fig. 8.10](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0010)a. For StyleGAN, the input layer is removed completely, instead starting part is basically learning from a constant. Let us consider the latent space being represented as ![script í’µ](images/c08-i0229.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#54453;</mi></mrow></math> and the latent code as ![bold-italic z](images/c08-i0230.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi></mrow></math>. Now, a *non‐linear mapping network* given by ![f colon script í’µ right-arrow script í’²](images/c08-i0231.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#54453;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#54450;</mi></math> produces ![bold w element-of script í’²](images/c08-i0232.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#54450;</mi></math>, as shown in [Fig. 8.10](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0010)b. For the sake of simplicity, the dimensions of both these spaces are set to 512. the mapping ![f](images/c08-i0233.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> is created using MLP of 8 layers, as shown in [Fig. 8.10](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0010). This mapping basically is an affine transformation that learned and specialized ![bold w](images/c08-i0234.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math> to various styles ![bold y](images/c08-i0235.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math>. The styles ![bold y equals left-parenthesis bold y Subscript s Baseline comma bold y Subscript b Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0236.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mi>b</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> basically control the adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) (X. Huang and Belongie [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0152); Ghiasi et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0100); Dumoulin et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0085); Dumoulin et al. [2018](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0086)) operation which comes after each convolution layer in the synthesis network. The synthesis network consists of 18 layers. The AdaIN operation can be represented as the following:

[(8.14)](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-disp-0014)![upper A d a upper I upper N left-parenthesis bold x Subscript i Baseline comma bold y right-parenthesis equals bold y Subscript s comma i Baseline StartFraction bold x Subscript i Baseline minus mu left-parenthesis bold x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis Over sigma left-parenthesis bold x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis EndFraction plus bold y Subscript b comma i](images/c08-math-0014.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>A</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>I</mi><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mfrac><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> 

where each of the feature maps given by ![bold x Subscript i](images/c08-i0237.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is normalized individually and then the scaling is performed followed by adding bias using some scalar component of style ![bold y](images/c08-i0238.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math>. The dimension of ![bold y](images/c08-i0239.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math> is two times the number of feature maps for each layer. In [Fig. 8.10](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0010), we can see that the first step is to do a mapping from the input to the intermediate latent space ![script í’²](images/c08-i0240.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#54450;</mi></mrow></math>. This mapping is then used to control the AdaIN for each convolutional layer. The AdaIN operation is particularly suitable for this purpose due to its efficiency and ability to provide compact representation. Following this, Gaussian noise is added before evaluating the non‐linearity. The noise input helps in introducing stochastic detail to the generation process. This noise image is passed onto each of the feature maps with the help of the learned scale factors. This is then finally added to the output of the corresponding convolution as shown in the figure. “A” in [Fig. 8.10](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0010)b corresponds to the learned affine transformation and “B” is the addition of learned per‐channel scaling factors with the noise input. Compared to other style transfer approaches, StyleGAN performs a spatially invariant style ![bold y](images/c08-i0241.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math> from vector ![bold w](images/c08-i0242.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math> instead of using a fixed image.

 

### 8.8.1 StyleGAN Properties and Outcome Highlights

The redesign of the generator not only helps with the controlled image synthesis but also improves the image quality considerably. For evaluation purposes, the metric that is used for StyleGANs is the FID (Heusel et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0129)). It is claimed to be a much better metric than the inception score in capturing the similarity of generated images compared to the real image. This score also helps with capturing the level of disturbance as well. Since, it's a distance measure, for similarity the lower the value the better the result. FID is the distance ![d](images/c08-i0243.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> between two Gaussians with one having mean ![bold-italic mu bold-italic 1](images/c08-i0244.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi></mrow><mn mathvariant="bold-italic">1</mn></msub></math> and covariance ![bold upper Sigma 1](images/c08-i0245.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> obtained from a particular probability distribution ![p 1](images/c08-i0246.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>. The other Gaussian has mean ![bold-italic mu bold-italic 2](images/c08-i0247.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi></mrow><mn mathvariant="bold-italic">2</mn></msub></math> and covariance, ![bold upper Sigma 2](images/c08-i0248.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math> which is obtained from another distribution ![p 2](images/c08-i0249.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>. The FID distance is given by:

The FID here was calculated using 50,000 images randomly drawn from the training set (Karras et al. [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0169)).

The evaluation of StyleGAN was performed on two different datasets n CELEBA‐HQ (Karras et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0168)) and FFHQ (Karras et al. [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0169)). [Table 8.2](#c08.xhtml#c08-tbl-0002) shows the results related to the quality of images generated using the FID metric with best scores indicated in bold for each dataset. The starting baseline model was that of ProGAN (Karras et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0168)) which was then improved using bilinear upsampling/downsampling operations (R. Zhang [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0392)). Further, the comparison of performance is done for (c) adding the mapping network along with AdaIN operation (d) removing the traditional input layer and learning from the constant tensor instead, as shown in [Fig. 8.10](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0010). In column (e), the noise input is introduced, and then finally, (f) the mixing regularization is added. The results keep improving as we progress along the table which shows that modifying the network to (e) from the base architecture (b) has improved the FIDs significantly.

The main objective of StyleGAN generator was to make controlled image synthesis possible and this was achieved using scale‐specific modifications to different styles. There is a mapping network and affine transformations which allows the network to draw samples corresponding to each of the styles from the distribution that is learned by the generator. The synthesis network then generates a novel image based on these style collections. Additionally, the modification of a certain subset of styles affects only some specific aspects of the image, meaning, the styles are localized within the network.

Next, let us understand the localization aspect of the network. Considering the AdaIN operation shown in [Eq. (8.14)](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0014) each of the channels is first normalized to zero mean and unit variance. Following this, to the normalized channels, the scales and biases are applied based on the style.

*   **Style mixing:** The localization of styles in the network is further facilitated by using *mixing regularization*. In this process, two random latent codes are used to produce a given percentage of images during training instead of just using the usual one latent code approach. Let's say we pass two latent codes ![bold-italic z 1](images/c08-i0250.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![bold-italic z 2](images/c08-i0251.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math> through the mapping network to obtain ![bold w 1](images/c08-i0252.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![bold w 2](images/c08-i0253.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math> which help in controlling the styles such that ![bold w 1](images/c08-i0254.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> comes before the crossover point followed by ![bold w 2](images/c08-i0255.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math>. This type of regularization approach prevents the network from getting confused about the correlation between adjacent styles. Using this technique, the localization improves during the training. It also improves the tolerance of the model to adverse operations along with retaining high‐level, meaningful attributes of the image.
*   **Stochastic variation:** The aspects that introduce randomness in human faces can be many, such as hairs, freckles, pores, etc. These aspects can be indeed randomized without any impact on the perception of the image. To achieve this *stochastic variation* in the image, the StyleGAN generator adds *per‐pixel noise* after each convolution. This makes sure that the generator can produce different noise realizations of the same image. It can be noted that these noise realizations affect only the stochastic aspect of the image. The effect of the noise is localized in the network. At any point in the generator, the network is always pushed toward introducing some novelty content as possible. The localized effect for the stochastic variation is ensured by adding a fresh set of noise to each layer. This makes sure that there are no side effects from the earlier activations.
*   **Disentanglement:** The main goal of *disentanglement* is that the latent space consists of linear subspaces, where each of these subspaces controls an individual factor of variation. Additionally, the sampling probability of each of these variation factors in ![script í’µ](images/c08-i0256.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#54453;</mi></mrow></math> should match the corresponding density of the training set. In the case of StyleGAN, the sampling from ![script í’²](images/c08-i0257.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#54450;</mi></mrow></math> is basically induced from the mapping ![f left-parenthesis bold-italic z right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0258.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. The mapping can be manipulated so that the factors of variation are more linear. Therefore, realistic images can be easily generated based on disentangled representation compared to entangled representation. The metric introduced for quantifying this disentanglement includes *Perceptual path length* and *linear separability*. Both these disentanglement methods can be used as regularizers during training.

Perceptual path length quantifies the drastic variations that the image undergoes as interpolation is performed in the latent space. For example, the perceptually smoother transition is observed in a less curved latent space compared to a highly curved latent space. The basis for this metric is from the perceptual pairwise image distance (R. Zhang et al. [2018](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0394)) which stands for the weighted difference between two VGG16 embeddings (Simonyan and Zisserman [2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0320)). here the weights are fit in such a way that they agree with human perceptual similarity judgments. If we subdivide an interpolation path in the latent space into linear segments, the total perceptual length of this path can be defined as the sum of perceptual differences over each of these segments, using the image distance metric. The other metric that can be used to quantify the disentanglement of the latent space is linear separability. Using this metric, we can quantify how well the points in latent space can be separated into two distinct portions using a linear hyperplane. This approach would provide us with sets that correspond to a specific binary characteristic of the image.

Overall, the architecture is capable of performing better *interpolation*, along with adding better disentangling of latent variation factors. Also, the added features in the generator helped the model to perform unsupervised separation of higher‐level characteristics and stochastic variation in the synthesized images.

 

## 8.9 StackGAN

Creating photo‐realistic images from textual descriptions is a significant challenge with wide‐ranging applications, such as enhancing photos through editing and facilitating computer‐aided design tasks. In recent times, GANs, have exhibited promising capabilities in the synthesis of real‐world images. Specifically, when conditioned on provided text descriptions, cGANs (S. E. Reed et al. [2016a](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0280), [2016b](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0281)) have demonstrated the ability to produce images closely aligned with the intended textual meaning. However, augmenting existing state‐of‐the‐art GAN models with additional upsampling layers for the purpose of generating high‐resolution images typically leads to training instability and the generation of nonsensical outputs. The primary challenge in generating high‐resolution images with GANs lies in the fact that the distributions representing natural images and the implied model distributions may not effectively overlap within the expansive, high‐dimensional pixel space (Sønderby et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0326); Arjovsky and Bottou [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0017)). This issue becomes more pronounced as the resolution of the images in question increases. Even though prior works indicate the successful generation of credible ![64 times 64](images/c08-i0259.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>64</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>64</mn></math> images conditioned on textual descriptions, however, these images often lacked intricate details and vivid object components.

![Figure 8.11 StackGAN architecture. ¶ Source: ¶ H. Zhang et al. 2017/IEEE/Public Domain.](images/c08f011.png)

[**Figure 8.11**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0011) StackGAN architecture. ¶ Source: ¶ H. Zhang et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0393)/IEEE/Public Domain.

Therefore, to tackle the problem of text‐to‐photo‐realistic image synthesis more effectively, the approach with stacked generative adversarial networks (StackGAN) decomposes it into two more manageable sub‐problems. To create high‐resolution images with realistic details, a simple yet efficient StackGAN method was introduced (see [Fig. 8.11](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0011)). This method breaks down the text‐to‐image generation process into two stages:

*   **Stage I GAN:** This stage sketches the fundamental shape and primary colors of the object based on the provided text description. It also generates the background layout from a random noise vector, resulting in a low‐resolution image.
*   **Stage II GAN:** In the second stage, the low‐resolution image from Stage I is refined to correct any defects and enhance the object's details. It achieves this by re‐evaluating the text description, ultimately producing a high‐resolution, photo‐realistic image.

The improved likelihood of the model distribution, derived from a somewhat aligned, lower‐resolution image, overlapping with the distribution of the actual image, serves as the fundamental reason why Stage II GAN can produce superior high‐resolution images. This capability allowed StackGAN to generate the first photorealistic ![256 times 256](images/c08-i0260.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>256</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>256</mn></math> resolution images based on textual descriptions.

During the implementation of StackGAN, the initial process involves the encoding of a textual description denoted as ![bold t](images/c08-i0261.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">t</mi></mrow></math>, using an encoder, resulting in the generation of a text embedding ![bold-italic psi Subscript t](images/c08-i0262.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>. However, the latent space associated with the text embedding typically possesses high dimensionality, often exceeding 100 dimensions. When confronted with limited data, this high dimensionality can lead to non‐smoothness within the latent data manifold. Hence, a novel approach called *conditioning augmentation* was introduced to produce additional conditioning variables ![ModifyingAbove bold c With Ì‚](images/c08-i0263.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math>. Contrary to the fixed conditioning text variable ![bold c](images/c08-i0264.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow></math> described in prior studies, a distinct approach involves the random sampling of latent variables ![ModifyingAbove bold c With Ì‚](images/c08-i0265.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math>. These variables are drawn from an independent Gaussian distribution represented as ![script í’© left-parenthesis bold-italic mu left-parenthesis psi Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis comma bold upper Sigma left-parenthesis bold-italic psi Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0266.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#54441;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> where both the mean ![bold-italic mu left-parenthesis bold-italic psi Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0267.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and the diagonal covariance matrix ![bold upper Sigma left-parenthesis bold-italic psi Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0268.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> are determined as functions of the text embedding. Consequently, conditioning augmentation helps in augmenting the number of training pairs, which is particularly beneficial when working with a limited set of image‐text pairs.

To further promote smoothness within the conditioning manifold and prevent overfitting (Larsen et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0192)), an additional regularization term becomes part of the generator's training objective:

(8.16)![upper K upper L left-parenthesis script í’© left-parenthesis bold-italic mu left-parenthesis bold-italic psi Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis comma bold upper Sigma left-parenthesis bold-italic psi Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis double-vertical-bar script í’© left-parenthesis 0 comma bold upper I right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c08-math-0016.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>K</mi><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#54441;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#54441;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

The above term measures the KL divergence between the conditioning Gaussian distribution, which is modeled by ![script í’© left-parenthesis mu left-parenthesis bold-italic psi Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis comma normal upper Sigma left-parenthesis bold-italic psi Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0269.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#54441;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#931;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and a standard Gaussian distribution, represented as ![script í’© left-parenthesis 0 comma upper I right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0270.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#54441;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. This technique promotes smoothness within the latent conditioning manifold by permitting minor, random adjustments within it, ultimately enhancing the variety of synthesized images.

Let ![bold-italic psi Subscript t](images/c08-i0271.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> represent the text embedding obtained from the textual description using a pre‐trained encoder (S. E. Reed et al. [2016a](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0280)). The *Gaussian conditioning variables* ![ModifyingAbove c 0 With Ì‚](images/c08-i0272.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math> linked to this text embedding are sampled from a Gaussian distribution ![script í’© left-parenthesis mu 0 left-parenthesis bold-italic psi Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis comma normal upper Sigma 0 left-parenthesis bold-italic psi Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0273.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#54441;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#931;</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. This sampling procedure aims to capture the semantic essence of the textual description represented by ![bold-italic psi Subscript t](images/c08-i0274.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> while introducing valuable variations. While conditioned on ![ModifyingAbove bold c 0 With Ì‚](images/c08-i0275.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math> and a stochastic variable ![bold-italic epsilon](images/c08-i0276.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi></mrow></math>, Stage I GAN undergoes a training process. This results in the maximization of ![upper J Subscript upper D 0](images/c08-i0277.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></msub></math>, which evaluates the authenticity of the generated images, and the simultaneous minimization of ![upper J Subscript upper G 0](images/c08-i0278.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></msub></math>. The latter focuses on aligning the generated images with the provided textual description, and this iterative training procedure progressively enhances the performance of both the discriminator ![upper D 0](images/c08-i0279.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> and the generator ![upper G 0](images/c08-i0280.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>.

Here, ![bold-italic upper I 0](images/c08-i0281.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math> represents the real image, the text description ![bold t](images/c08-i0282.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">t</mi></mrow></math> originates from the actual data distribution ![p Subscript d a t a](images/c08-i0283.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi></mrow></msub></math>, and ![bold-italic epsilon](images/c08-i0284.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi></mrow></math> constitutes a noise vector, drawn randomly from the distribution ![p Subscript bold-italic epsilon](images/c08-i0285.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi></mrow></msub></math>.

The initial output of Stage I GAN often results in low‐resolution images that lack detailed object parts and may even exhibit shape distortions. To overcome these shortcomings, Stage II GAN uses low‐resolution images and text embedding, aiming to correct imperfections in the Stage I results. This reintroduction of textual information previously overlooked enables Stage II GAN to generate more complex and photo‐realistic details in the final images. To achieve this, Stage II GAN considers the *low‐resolution output*, represented as ![bold s 0 equals upper G 0 left-parenthesis bold-italic epsilon semicolon ModifyingAbove bold c With Ì‚ Subscript 0 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0286.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi><mo>;</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and incorporates Gaussian latent variables ![ModifyingAbove bold c With Ì‚](images/c08-i0287.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math> in the training process for both the discriminator D and the generator ![upper G](images/c08-i0288.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math>. This training involves an optimization approach, where the objective is to maximize ![upper J Subscript upper D](images/c08-i0289.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></math> while simultaneously minimizing ![upper J Subscript upper G](images/c08-i0290.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>G</mi></msub></math>.
