In contrast to the original GAN framework, this stage does not use the random noise variable ![bold-italic epsilon](images/c08-i0291.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi></mrow></math> assuming that necessary randomness is already contained within ![bold s 0](images/c08-i0292.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math>. The Gaussian conditioning variables ![ModifyingAbove bold c With Ì‚](images/c08-i0293.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math> in this stage and the ![ModifyingAbove bold c With Ì‚ Subscript 0](images/c08-i0294.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math> in Stage I GAN both derive from the same pre‐trained text encoder, resulting in the generation of identical text embeddings, denoted as ![bold t](images/c08-i0295.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">t</mi></mrow></math>.

 

### 8.9.1 StackGAN Training and Outcomes Highlights

During the implementation of Stage I GAN generator, the process of obtaining the *text conditioning variable* ![ModifyingAbove bold c With Ì‚ Subscript 0](images/c08-i0296.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math> is as follows: The text embedding ![bold-italic psi Subscript t](images/c08-i0297.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is initially fed into a fully connected layer, resulting in the generation of ![mu 0](images/c08-i0298.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math> and ![sigma 0](images/c08-i0299.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math>, for a Gaussian distribution defined as ![script í’© left-parenthesis mu 0 left-parenthesis bold-italic psi Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis comma normal upper Sigma 0 left-parenthesis bold-italic psi Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0300.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#54441;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#931;</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Subsequently, ![ModifyingAbove bold c With Ì‚ Subscript 0](images/c08-i0301.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math> is sampled from this Gaussian distribution and concatenated with a noise vector to facilitate the generation of an image with dimensions ![upper M 0 times upper N 0](images/c08-i0302.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> through a series of upsampling blocks.

The text embeddings ![bold-italic psi Subscript t](images/c08-i0303.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> are first reduced in dimensionality by the discriminator ![upper D 0](images/c08-i0304.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> using a fully connected layer. Then, this condensed text information is spatially duplicated to create a multidimensional tensor with dimensions ![upper B Subscript d Baseline times upper B Subscript d Baseline times upper C Subscript d](images/c08-i0305.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>. Simultaneously, the associated image data undergoes downsampling until it reaches a spatial dimension of ![upper B Subscript d Baseline times upper B Subscript d](images/c08-i0306.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>. Next, the image's feature map is combined with the spatially duplicated text tensor along the channel dimension. A ![1 times 1](images/c08-i0307.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> convolutional layer is applied to this combined tensor to extract important features representing the relationship between the textual and visual elements. Finally, a single‐node fully connected layer is used to determine a decision score, which indicates the discriminator's judgment.

The Stage II generator uses an encoder‐decoder network architecture with residual blocks. It takes a *text embedding* ![bold-italic psi Subscript t](images/c08-i0308.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#968;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> and transforms it into the text conditioning vector ![ModifyingAbove bold c With Ì‚](images/c08-i0309.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></math>, which is replicated spatially into a tensor with dimensions ![upper B Subscript g Baseline times upper B Subscript g Baseline times upper C Subscript g](images/c08-i0310.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>g</mi></msub></math>. Concurrently, the Stage I GAN's output, denoted as ![s 0](images/c08-i0311.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>, undergoes several downsampling blocks in the form of an encoder until it reaches the spatial dimensions ![upper B Subscript g Baseline times upper B Subscript g](images/c08-i0312.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>g</mi></msub></math>. The features extracted from both the image and text are concatenated along the channel dimension and are passed through a series of residual blocks. Ultimately, a sequence of upsampling layers in the decoder is employed to generate a high‐resolution image with dimensions ![upper M times upper N](images/c08-i0313.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>M</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>N</mi></math>. This generator plays a crucial role in enhancing input images by rectifying imperfections and introducing realistic details.

The discriminator in this stage shares similarities with the Stage I discriminator but incorporates additional downsampling blocks due to the larger image size. To promote improved alignment learning between the image and conditioning text, the approach uses a matching‐aware discriminator for both stages (S. Reed et al. [2016b](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0281)). During training, the discriminator considers real images paired with their corresponding text descriptions as positive sample pairs. Meanwhile, negative sample pairs include two groups: one with real images and mismatched text embeddings, and the other with synthetic images and their corresponding text embeddings.

During the training phase, the process begins by training ![upper D 0](images/c08-i0314.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> and ![upper G 0](images/c08-i0315.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> of the Stage I GAN for 600 epochs while keeping Stage II GAN fixed. Then, the training shifts to iteratively train ![upper D](images/c08-i0316.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper G](images/c08-i0317.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> of the Stage II GAN for another 600 epochs, with Stage I GAN fixed. All networks are trained using the Adam solver, with a batch size of 64 and an initial learning rate of 0.0002. The learning rate is reduced to half of its previous value every 100 epochs. The experiments used three different datasets: CUB (Wah et al. [2011](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0362)), which includes 200 bird species with 11,788 images; Oxford‐102 (Nilsback and Zisserman [2008](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0249)), comprising 8189 flower images across 102 categories; and MS COCO (T.‐Y. Lin et al. [2014b](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0203)), a more challenging dataset with images featuring multiple objects and diverse backgrounds. MS COCO had 80 k training images and 40 k validation images, each with 5 descriptions, while the CUB and Oxford‐102 datasets had 10 descriptions for each image.

A numerical evaluation technique called the *Inception score* (Salimans et al. [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0303)) is employed for quantitative assessment.

(8.21)![upper I equals exp left-parenthesis double-struck upper E Subscript bold x Baseline upper K upper L left-parenthesis p left-parenthesis bold y vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis double-vertical-bar p left-parenthesis bold y right-parenthesis right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c08-math-0021.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>I</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></msub><mi>K</mi><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

Here, ![bold x](images/c08-i0318.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> represents an individual‐generated sample, and ![bold y](images/c08-i0319.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math> corresponds to the label predicted by the Inception model. The underlying concept of this metric revolves around the idea that effective models should produce various meaningful images. Consequently, the KL divergence between the overall distribution of labels ![p left-parenthesis bold y right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0320.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and labels given a specific image ![p left-parenthesis bold y vertical-bar bold x right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0321.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> will be large. Although the inception score has been shown to correlate with human perceptions of visual quality, it does not evaluate the alignment between the generated images and the provided text descriptions. To address this aspect, human evaluations are also conducted. The Inception scores and average human ranks for the proposed StackGAN and the compared methods such as GAN‐INT‐CLS (S. Reed et al. [2016b](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0281)) and GAWWN (S. E. Reed et al. [2016a](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0280)) are listed in [Table 8.3](#c08.xhtml#c08-tbl-0003).

## 8.10 Diffusion Models

In the past, probabilistic models have struggled with a challenging dilemma characterized by a balancing act between two opposing objectives: *tractability* and *flexibility*. Models that are tractable, such as Gaussian or Laplace distributions, are straightforward to study and apply to data. Nonetheless, they encounter difficulties when attempting to encompass the intricate patterns within complex datasets. Conversely, flexible models can mold themselves to the patterns within any given dataset by employing a non‐negative function ![phi left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0336.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> to establish their distribution ![p left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis equals StartFraction phi left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis Over upper Z EndFraction](images/c08-i0337.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>Z</mi></mfrac></math>, where ![upper Z](images/c08-i0338.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math> represents a normalization constant. Nevertheless, calculating this normalization constant is a computationally expensive task. Dealing with these adaptable models frequently necessitates the use of resource‐intensive *Monte Carlo* techniques for tasks like assessment, training, or generating samples.

Several analytical approximations are available that improve, yet do not completely eliminate, this tradeoff. Examples include mean field theory and its extensions (Tanaka [1998](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0345)), variational Bayes (M. I. Jordan et al. [1999](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0165)), contrastive divergence (Welling and Geoffrey E. Hinton [2002](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0368)), minimum probability flow (Sohl‐Dickstein et al. [2011](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0324)), minimum KL contraction (Lyu [2011](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0214)), proper scoring rules (Gneiting and Raftery [2007](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0105)), score matching (Hyvärinen and Dayan [2005](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0157)), pseudolikelihood (Besag [1975](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0035)), loopy belief propagation (K. Murphy et al. [2013](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0237)), and many others. Furthermore, non‐parametric approaches can also demonstrate significant effectiveness.

In recent years, an innovative method emerged for building probabilistic models, offering multiple advantages. This methodology provides exceptional flexibility in model structure, ensures precise data sampling, enables seamless integration with other probability distributions, and facilitates cost‐efficient evaluation of both the model's log‐likelihood and the likelihood of individual states. This approach relies on the utilization of a Markov chain to systematically transition from one distribution to another, drawing inspiration from *non‐equilibrium statistical physics* (Jarzynski [1997](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0161)) and *Sequential Monte Carlo* (Neal [2001](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0240)). Specifically, it involves the construction of a generative Markov chain, which helps in the transformation of a straightforward, well‐defined distribution, such as a Gaussian, into the desired target data distribution through a diffusion process.

The fundamental concept underlying diffusion models is rather straightforward. They start with an initial input image and progressively introduce Gaussian noise to it through a sequence of steps, which we refer to as the forward process. Importantly, this is distinct from the forward pass of a neural network. It serves as a crucial step in generating the target data for our neural network. Subsequently, a neural network is trained to reconstruct the original data by reversing the noise application process. This ability to model the inverse process enables the generation of novel data, which is commonly referred to as the reverse diffusion process or the sampling process of a generative model.

In recent years, numerous generative models based on diffusion have been introduced, all sharing similar foundational concepts. These include diffusion probabilistic models (Sohl‐Dickstein et al. [2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0325)), noise‐conditioned score networks (Y. Song and Ermon [2019](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0327)), and denoising diffusion probabilistic models (Ho et al. [2020](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0144)).

![Figure 8.12 Forward diffusion process. ¶ Source: ¶ Reproduced from paper (Ho et al. 2020) / Neural Information Processing Systems Foundation.](images/c08f012.png)

[**Figure 8.12**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0012) Forward diffusion process. ¶ Source: ¶ Reproduced from paper (Ho et al. [2020](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0144)) / Neural Information Processing Systems Foundation.

 

### 8.10.1 Forward Diffusion Process

Consider a data point sampled from a real data distribution, denoted as ![bold x 0](images/c08-i0339.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math> drawn from the distribution ![q left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0340.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Let's define a forward diffusion process where Gaussian noise with a variance of ![beta Subscript t](images/c08-i0341.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is incrementally added to ![bold x 0](images/c08-i0342.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></math> over the course of ![upper T](images/c08-i0343.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> steps. This produces a sequence of noisy samples: ![bold x 1 comma bold x 2 comma ellipsis comma bold x Subscript upper T Baseline](images/c08-i0344.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>T</mi></msub></math>. More specifically, at each step of the *Markov chain*, Gaussian noise with variance ![beta Subscript t](images/c08-i0345.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is introduced to ![bold x Subscript t minus 1](images/c08-i0346.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, resulting in a new latent variable ![bold x Subscript t](images/c08-i0347.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> with a distribution of ![q left-parenthesis bold x Subscript t Baseline vertical-bar bold x Subscript t minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0348.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. This diffusion process can be formulated as follows:

In this case, the distribution ![q left-parenthesis bold x Subscript t Baseline vertical-bar bold x Subscript t minus 1 Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0349.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> shown in [Fig. 8.12](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0012) is a normal distribution characterized by a mean, denoted as ![bold-italic mu Subscript t](images/c08-i0350.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, which is equal to ![StartRoot 1 minus beta Subscript t Baseline EndRoot bold x Subscript t minus 1](images/c08-i0351.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msqrt><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>, and a standard deviation, denoted as ![bold upper Sigma Subscript t](images/c08-i0352.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#931;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>, which is a diagonal matrix consisting of variances ![beta Subscript t](images/c08-i0353.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math>.

The *forward trajectory*, starting from the initial data distribution and undergoing ![upper T](images/c08-i0354.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> diffusion steps, can be written in closed form as follows:

### 8.10.2 Reverse Diffusion Process

Reversing the above forward process and sampling from ![q left-parenthesis bold x Subscript t minus 1 Baseline vertical-bar bold x Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0366.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> enables us to reconstruct the true sample from a Gaussian noise input, ![bold x Subscript upper T Baseline tilde script í’© left-parenthesis 0 comma bold upper I right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0367.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#54441;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. In practical terms, the knowledge of ![q left-parenthesis bold x Subscript t minus 1 Baseline vertical-bar bold x Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0368.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is limited, and estimating it becomes intractable since it uses complex computations related to the data distribution. Consequently, one can opt for an approximation of ![q left-parenthesis bold x Subscript t minus 1 Baseline vertical-bar bold x Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0369.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> through the utilization of a parameterized model, denoted as ![p Subscript theta](images/c08-i0370.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></msub></math> (see [Fig. 8.13](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0013)). Given that ![q left-parenthesis bold x Subscript t minus 1 Baseline vertical-bar bold x Subscript t Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0371.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> also exhibits Gaussian characteristics, particularly when ![beta Subscript t](images/c08-i0372.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub></math> is sufficiently small, there is the flexibility to choose ![p Subscript theta](images/c08-i0373.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></msub></math> to be Gaussian and focus solely on parameterizing the mean and variance:

### 8.10.3 Diffusion Process Training

A diffusion‐based generative model can be trained by maximizing the log‐likelihood of the sample generated at the end of the reverse process to ensure that it closely matches the original data distribution. During training, the approach draws inspiration from VAEs and reformulates the training objective using a *variational lower bound*, referred to as ELBO, as demonstrated in Eq. (7.42). After various calculations, this final term for the variational lower bound loss, denoted as ![script upper L Subscript v l b](images/c08-i0374.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#8466;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>v</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub></math>, is derived for individual timesteps:

The term ![q left-parenthesis bold x Subscript t minus 1 Baseline vertical-bar bold x Subscript t Baseline comma bold x 0 right-parenthesis](images/c08-i0379.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is referred to as *forward process posterior distribution*. The deep‐learning model's task during training is to estimate the parameters of this Gaussian posterior in such a manner that it minimizes the KL divergence.

At training and inference times, the ![beta](images/c08-i0387.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></math>'s, ![alpha](images/c08-i0388.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math>'s and ![x Subscript t](images/c08-i0389.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> are known. Consequently, the model's sole task is to predict the noise at each timestep. The final loss function is a result of reducing it to a mean squared error between the noise introduced in the forward process and the noise the model predicts.

 

## 8.11 Conclusion

GANs represent a groundbreaking advancement in the field of computer vision for generative architectures. The results achieved by GANs have exceeded the performance of earlier methods in deep unsupervised learning, which were known for their remarkable capabilities. Over the years, different types of GANs have emerged, each with their own unique architecture and applications. From the original vanilla GAN to more specialized variants like DCGAN, CycleGAN, and cGAN, GANs have demonstrated their versatility in generating realistic data, transferring styles, and solving complex problems in domains ranging from image synthesis to text‐to‐image translation. The central concept of every GAN variant is based on a two‐player minimax game. The adversarial training framework puts the generator against the discriminator in an ongoing feedback loop, facilitating the creation of realistic and high‐quality synthetic data.

One key aspect of GANs' versatility is their ability to serve not only as data generators but also as tools for feature learning and representation learning. Beyond their primary objective of generating data, some GAN models incorporate secondary objectives, such as learning meaningful features or representations through related semantic tasks. These learned features can subsequently be employed for classification or recognition tasks in unsupervised settings, extending the utility of GANs beyond generative tasks. However, GANs also pose challenges, including issues related to training stability, mode collapse, and ethical concerns surrounding the generation of deepfake content and potential misuse. Despite these challenges, ongoing research and development in the GAN domain are actively addressing these issues.

Moreover, the development of GANs has given rise to the emergence of diffusion models as a significant advancement within this field. These models, which fall under the umbrella of generative models, have gained a lot of attention due to their unique approach to probabilistic generative modeling. Unlike traditional GANs, which rely on adversarial training, diffusion models work by gradually improving a data sample, making it more realistic through a series of diffusion steps. This distinctive approach has shown promise in generating high‐quality samples and addressing some of the stability issues associated with GANs. Diffusion models provide an alternative viewpoint on generative modeling, and their incorporation into the field reflects an explorative for data generation and representation learning.

# 9  
Deep Bayesian Networks

 

## 9.1 Introduction

Deep learning (DL) models can be seen as very powerful approximations, that are able to perform complex machine learning tasks. The power of these machines relies, roughly speaking, on the high (often tremendous) number of parameters for the models, that endow the structure with a high expressive capability in the space of the input pattern. This is the ultimate reason why these machines have been successfully used in complex pattern recognition tasks, such as image processing, speech recognition, and other natural language processing tasks, and in complex generative tasks, including realistic synthetic image generation, just to cite some well‐known applications.

The drawback of the structural complexity of DL machines is overfitting (Szegedy et al. [2013](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0338)). Overfitting is a universal phenomenon particularly important in DL that can be controlled by controlling the capacity of the machine in various ways, among them dropout (N. Srivastava et al. [2014](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0330)), cost functions that force sparsity in the parameters, and controlling the Frobenius norm of the weights of the machine (often called weight decay), are strategies that have been addressed in this book. These strategies have an interpretation from the point of view of Bayesian learning (Gal and Ghahramani [2016](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0096); Q. Li and N. Lin [2010](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0199)).

Bayesian learning is a way to address the overfitting phenomenon by modeling the uncertainty of the weights. This is done by imposing a prior probability distribution in the weights of the neural network, and this strategy has proven to be particularly advantageous in presence of small datasets. But beyond the potential improvement of the generalization properties in neural networks, the use of Bayesian techniques has another interesting property. Bayesian neural networks are able to estimate the model uncertainties. Not only the uncertainty on the model parameters, which can be obtained by the inference of a posterior probability distribution of these parameters, but it is also possible to estimate the uncertainty in the performance of the machine through the construction of predictive posterior distribution. This provides the user with additional knowledge, which can be used to determine whether the machine is producing a reliable prediction.

 

## 9.2 Bayesian Models

Throughout this book, we have presented the main deep learning architectures, ranging from the standard MLP to the transformers, and generative approaches. Most of these models are trained using the backpropagation algorithm that is constructed over the criterion of the maximization of the output likelihood conditional to the available training input patterns. The NLL is also used in Bayesian inference, but it is applied in a different way.

 

### 9.2.1 The Bayes' Rule

Bayesian inference is rooted in the Bayes' theorem or Bayes' rule, which is summarized here. Assume two random variables ![u](images/c09-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> and ![v](images/c09-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow></math>. Assume that the first variable ![u](images/c09-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> is observed, and a probabilistic model in relation with the latent or unobservable variable ![v](images/c09-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow></math> can be established with the form ![p left-parenthesis u vertical-bar v right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, this is the probability of the observation ![u](images/c09-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> varies depending on the chosen hypothesis for ![v](images/c09-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow></math>.

Now, assume that while variable ![v](images/c09-i0014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow></math> is unobservable, we have a specific probabilistic model ![p left-parenthesis v right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0015.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for this variable. This is what we call a prior probability, which is what we know about it before having any additional knowledge. Roughly speaking, the goal of the Bayesian inference is to guess the most probable value of ![v](images/c09-i0016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow></math> given the observation of ![u](images/c09-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>, which depends on ![v](images/c09-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>v</mi></mrow></math>. where the constant term, that can be neglected, is the logarithm of the marginal likelihood, which does not depend on the parameters. If, for the set of parameters, the corresponding prior model is simply the multivariate Gaussian distribution ![p left-parenthesis bold-italic theta right-parenthesis proportional-to exp left-parenthesis minus StartFraction lamda Over 2 EndFraction parallel-to bold-italic theta parallel-to squared right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8733;</mo><mi>exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mrow><mo>&#8741;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>&#8741;</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, then the above expression can be written as ![log p left-parenthesis bold upper Y vertical-bar bold upper X comma bold-italic theta right-parenthesis minus StartFraction lamda Over 2 EndFraction parallel-to bold-italic theta parallel-to squared](images/c09-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mrow><mo>&#8741;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>&#8741;</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math> and therefore, [Eq. (9.6)](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0006) can be called a MAP criterion.

The prior distribution plays the role of *prior* belief or knowledge about the problem. The no free lunch theorem (NFL) theorems (Wolpert [1996a](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0374), [1996b](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0375)) express in the sentence “there is no such thing as a free lunch” that we cannot find a single optimization for all problems. The first theorem states that any two algorithms perform equally when their performance is averaged over all possible problems. The second theorem says that if an algorithm outperforms another one for a given cost function, then the reverse situation must be true for all other cost function dynamics (Wolpert and Macready [1997](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0376)). If the algorithm does not contain prior information, the algorithm cannot learn from the data in a way that can generalize to test data. In Bayesian learning, this prior knowledge can be specified by the use of priors.

 

## 9.3 Bayesian Inference Methods for Deep Learning

A difference between a classical approach and a Bayesian approach is in how the posterior for the parameters is chosen. In a classical approach, the parameter of the prior is adjusted by a cross‐validation of parameter ![lamda](images/c09-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math>. In a Bayesian approach, the way in which this parameter is adjusted is different, based on a probabilistic criterion, which can provide a better estimation of the posterior. Moreover, the Bayesian perspective allows to extract additional knowledge of the structure and the process. In particular, the Bayesian model encodes the uncertainties present in the learning model. The likelihood constructed with the training data contains the information related to the of the model, this is, the uncertainties due to the noise or error present in the process. The posterior expresses what is usually called the Epistemic Uncertainty, or the uncertainty in the model parameters due to the limited information carried by the data.

Therefore, a Bayesian model not only provides a probabilistic way to explain the regularization of the structure but also a way to quantify the uncertainties of the model (Hubin and Storvik [2023](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0156)). Indeed, a posterior distribution of the test samples, usually called the can be constructed by marginalization through the posterior probability of the model parameters. In order to construct such posterior, we first need a posterior probability of the prediction ![f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> as ![p left-parenthesis f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis vertical-bar bold x comma bold-italic theta right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and then the marginal predictive posterior is found as

[(9.9)](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-disp-0009)![p left-parenthesis f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis vertical-bar bold x comma bold upper X right-parenthesis equals integral p left-parenthesis f left-parenthesis bold x right-parenthesis vertical-bar bold x comma bold-italic theta right-parenthesis p left-parenthesis bold-italic theta vertical-bar bold upper Y comma bold upper X right-parenthesis d bold-italic theta](images/c09-math-0009.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8747;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></math> 

The difficulty with this inference is that the computation of the parameter posterior is intractable due to its high dimensionality and the fact that it is a nonconvex problem (MacKay [1992](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0217)). In order to circumvent this difficulty, two different frameworks for inference have been developed. The first one falls in the family of the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods (Hastings [1970](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0121)), and the second one is based on variational inference (VI) (Blei et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0043)). In this section, these fundamental ideas used in Bayesian inference for DL are reviewed.

The literature in Bayesian inference for DL is very extensive. The interested reader can find a variety of tutorials (Lampinen and Vehtari [2001](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0190); Goan and Fookes [2020](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0106); H. Wang and Yeung [2020](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0364); Jospin et al. [2022](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0166)) that introduce the basics and the different approaches to the problem of training a neural network from a Bayesian perspective.

 

### 9.3.1 Markov Chain Monte Carlo Methods

The original MCMC algorithm was introduced in Metropolis and Ulam ([1949](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0226)) and Hastings ([1970](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0121)), and the idea behind the algorithm consists of constructing a Markov chain of the parameters where at each time instant a parameter is sampled with a probability that depends on the previously visited samples, in order to construct a stationary distribution of these parameters (Hitchcock [2003](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0142); Chib and Greenberg [1995](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0056)). In this chapter, we present the basic MCMC algorithm, which is the Metropolis–Hasting algorithm.

The Metropolis–Hasting algorithm starts with an initial arbitrary value ![bold-italic theta left-parenthesis 0 right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> for the set of parameters. For a given sample ![bold-italic theta left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, a proposal (prior) probability distribution ![q left-parenthesis bold-italic theta vertical-bar bold-italic theta left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> around this sample is used. Then, a new sample ![bold-italic theta left-parenthesis n plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is drawn from this distribution. The new sample is then tested by computing a posterior distribution ![p left-parenthesis bold upper Y vertical-bar bold upper X comma bold-italic theta left-parenthesis n plus 1 right-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0038.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. This is, in a deep learning setup, the probabilistic output of the learning machine. The corresponding posterior probability for the sample is

We can ignore the denominator in the Bayes' rule here because it is not available, and we simply state that the posterior is proportional to the prior times the likelihood. Then, an *acceptance probability* is stated as

The quotient of this expression has, in the numerator, the posterior of the new sampled parameters ![bold-italic theta left-parenthesis n plus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, which depends (through the prior), on the previous set of parameters, and also on the training data. If the new posterior is higher than the previous one, the quotient is higher than 1, and then ![r equals 1](images/c09-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, which means that the new sample has to be accepted. If the previous posterior was higher, then the result of ![r](images/c09-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> is the quotient, so the sample must be accepted with a probability that is high if both posteriors are similar, and with a low probability if the new posterior is low compared to the previous one. This allows the system to occasionally pick the new set of parameters even if the posterior is worse. Notice that the prior of the previous sample is simply computed as a distribution around the new sample. If the distribution is symmetric, this is ![q left-parenthesis bold-italic theta vertical-bar bold-italic theta Superscript prime Baseline right-parenthesis equals q left-parenthesis bold-italic theta prime vertical-bar bold-italic theta right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, for example, when the prior is a simple circularly symmetrical Gaussian, the formula is simplified as

Usual proposal distributions ![q](images/c09-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi></mrow></math> are Gaussian distributions, since it is sufficient for those proposals to produce samples that move from one sample to another one with a nonzero likelihood in the targets. Therefore, a reasonable option is

where ![bold upper M](images/c09-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi></mrow></math> is a given covariance matrix and ![s squared](images/c09-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> is a scale factor. In some cases, it is possible to compute the Hessian of the cost function surface at point ![bold-italic theta left-parenthesis n right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and then the distribution will follow the curvature of this surface (Roberts and Rosenthal [2001](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0289)). In many cases, however, the Hessian cannot be easily computed or it has an unreasonable computational burden, and then one can choose an identity matrix for the covariance. In this case, the distribution is symmetric, and the acceptance probability is the one in [Eq. (9.13)](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0013).

 

### 9.3.2 Hamiltonian MCMC

The Hamiltonian MCMC variant (Neal et al. [2011](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0242)) (see also Betancourt ([2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0036))) is an improvement of the MH MCMC algorithm that uses a Hamiltonian function to guide the process so the chosen sample of the parameters has a reduced correlation with the previous sample while maintaining a high probability of acceptance. The Hamiltonian is defined as a function ![upper H left-parenthesis bold-italic theta comma bold p right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, where ![bold p](images/c09-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi></mrow></math> is defined as the momentum of a particle at position ![bold-italic theta](images/c09-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></math>. The Hamiltonian is constructed as

(9.18)![upper H left-parenthesis bold-italic theta comma bold p right-parenthesis equals u left-parenthesis bold-italic theta right-parenthesis plus k left-parenthesis bold p right-parenthesis](images/c09-math-0018.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> 

where ![u left-parenthesis upper Theta right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mstyle mathvariant="normal"><mi>&#920;</mi></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is called the potential energy and it is defined as the negative logarithm of a function proportional to the probability density of the distribution of the parameters, and ![k left-parenthesis bold p right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is defined as the kinetic energy, typically defined as ![k left-parenthesis bold p right-parenthesis equals one half bold p Superscript down-tack Baseline bold upper M Superscript negative 1 Baseline bold p](images/c09-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi></math>, where ![bold upper M](images/c09-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi></mrow></math> is a positive definite matrix. This function represents the total energy of a particle, and it has the properties of a Hamiltonian function.

The distribution that is used to sample the parameters is then constructed with the potential function as

Then, the new position is chosen with a probability ![r](images/c09-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> by using the Metropolis–Hasting criterion

and the algorithm ([9.22](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0022)) is iterated until convergence.

The Hamiltonian MCMC is a powerful algorithm for Bayesian inference, but it has two main parameters, ![mu](images/c09-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper L](images/c09-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>, that need to be chosen in advance or through some sort of cross‐validation. This is not straightforward, provided that in general there are no clear criteria to select it, and the usual practice is to make use of heuristics (Neal et al. [2011](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0242)). In order to avoid this inconvenience, the software packages for inference using MCMC usually implement the no‐U‐turn sampler (NUTS) (Hoffman et al. [2014](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0146)).

 

### 9.3.3 Variational Inference

The MCMC algorithms are very efficient in sampling from an exact posterior (Bardenet et al. [2017](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0023)), but their drawbacks are obvious from the analysis of the previously introduced algorithms. These methods may have poor scalability when the number of parameters is large, which is the case of DL. The methods based on VI, also used in [Section 7.9](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0018) to train autoencoders, have a better scalability in DL, and this is why they have more popularity in this field.

![Figure 9.3 Example of neural network regression and confidence intervals with MCMC in a neural network with five hidden layers of 10 nodes each.](images/c09f003.png)

[**Figure 9.3**](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0003) Example of neural network regression and confidence intervals with MCMC in a neural network with five hidden layers of 10 nodes each.

In VI, rather than using an exact posterior and sample from it, a parametric function ![q Subscript bold-italic phi Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic theta right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is used that depends on a set of parameters ![bold-italic phi](images/c09-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></math> to approximate the actual posterior. This approximation is usually called variational. In order to approximate the actual posterior with the parametric one, the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence could be used, which is defined here as

which means that maximizing the KL divergence between the posterior and the approximate posterior ![q Subscript bold-italic phi](images/c09-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></msub></math> is equivalent to minimizing ![script upper F left-parenthesis bold-italic theta comma bold upper X comma bold upper Y right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#8497;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, which is the evidence lower bound (ELBO), also called the negative variational free energy (Neal and Geoffrey E. Hinton [1998](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0241); Yedidia et al. [2000](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0385)), also used in [Section 7.9.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0019).

The most common choice for the variational distribution ![q Subscript bold-italic phi Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic theta right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is a Gaussian with a diagonal covariance matrix ![bold-italic sigma Subscript i](images/c09-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mrow><mstyle mathvariant="bold-italic"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#963;</mi></mstyle></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></math> with elements ![sigma Subscript i Superscript 2](images/c09-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math> in its diagonal and with a mean ![bold-italic mu](images/c09-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mstyle mathvariant="bold-italic"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi></mstyle></math>, both vectors with the same length as the total number of parameters in set ![bold-italic theta](images/c09-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></math>.

A common way to optimize the ELBO is the use of stochastic variational inference (SVI) (van de Schoot et al. [2021](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0307); Hubin and Storvik [2023](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0156)). The methodology consists of applying stochastic gradient descent to the inference. This is useful when the datasets used for training are large, but the convergence is slow when compared to the standard gradient descent applied to a likelihood function. The usual functions for ![q Subscript bold-italic phi Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic theta right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> are multivariate Gaussians (Graves [2011](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0113)), Gamma functions and Dirichlet distributions (Jospin et al. [2022](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0166)). The method presented in Ghahramani and Beal ([2000](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0099)) factorizes the elements of the ELBO to separately treat the data and the parameters, which simplifies the procedure and gives an optimization algorithm that is a generalization of the Expectation–Maximization algorithm. The algorithm also applies a Gaussian prior for the parameters with an identity matrix as a covariance matrix.

 

### 9.3.4 Bayes by Backpropagation

The Bayes by backpropagation algorithm (Blundell et al. [2015](#b03.xhtml#bref-bib-0044)) uses an approximation to the ELBO function as

Once the algorithm has converged, a MAP prediction of a test sample ![bold x Superscript asterisk](images/c09-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></math> can be done with the use of the MAP estimation of the parameters provided by the variational posterior ![q Subscript bold-italic phi Baseline left-parenthesis bold-italic theta right-parenthesis](images/c09-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#966;</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. The confidence interval of the prediction can be estimated by sampling equation of ([9.9](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0009)), the predictive posterior in the usual case where the integral is not tractable. The procedure consists of simply drawing samples of the parameters from the parameter posterior, and obtaining predictions of ![bold x Superscript asterisk](images/c09-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msup></math> with these sampled parameters. Then, a statistical measure of the obtained outputs (for example, ![2 sigma](images/c09-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><mi>&#963;</mi></math> or 95% confidence intervals) can be computed for a regression application or the posterior Bernoulli or Multinoulli probability in a classification application.

 

## 9.4 Conclusion

Neural networks are particularly underspecified by the training data, given that the number of parameters is in many cases much higher than the number of training samples. The use of Bayesian approaches is a compelling way to regularize neural networks. Most importantly, Bayesian methods offer a way to quantify the uncertainty of the model parameters by the inference of a parameter posterior with the possibility to compute a predictive posterior, from which to calculate (often numerically) confidence intervals in the prediction.

In this chapter, we covered the basic elements of Bayesian learning. We first stated the relationship between the regularization and the parameter priors, and then we summarized the two main methodologies for Bayesian inference, which are the MCMC and the VI frameworks.

Among the MCMC methods, the standard Metropolis–Hasting algorithm has been summarized, with a variant that includes the Hessian of the cost function surface, and the Hamiltonian Metropolis–Hasting algorithm, that uses a Hamiltonian function (modeling the trajectory of the parameter as a particle with kinetic and potential energy). While the MCMC methods. While the MCMC methods are able to produce inference sampling from the exact posterior, they may present scalability problems.

VI methods are more popular in Bayesian learning because they have better scalability properties through the use of an approximate parametric variational posterior. The Bayes by backpropagation has been presented as it is a standard methodology for Bayesian inference in DL. This method can be seen as an extension to the standard backpropagation algorithm that, instead of optimizing a likelihood function, can optimize a posterior distribution of the model weights.

# Notation

 

In the nomenclature of this book, scalar variables are represented with a lowercase normal letter, while the constants are represented with normal uppercase letters. The vectors are represented as bold lowercase letters (e.g. ![bold w](images/both02-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math>), and they are assumed to be column vectors. Matrices and multidimensional arrays are represented as bold uppercase letters (e.g. ![bold upper W](images/both02-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow></math>). When functions map to ![double-struck upper R](images/both02-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math>, they are also represented with normal face, and when they map to a vector space, they are represented in boldface.

Below is an exhaustive list of the notation used in the book. The list is simply grouped in functions, Greek symbols (including scalars, vectors, and arrays), matrices and vectors represented with Latin characters, other symbols, and scalars represented with Latin characters.
